gaps: DATA MIGRATION FROM THE LIVE PHP/POSTGRES SYSTEM IS COMPLETELY ABSENT. The catalog importer (medicines_export.csv, 318 rows) seeds only the medicine catalog. There is no examined path to migrate existing batches/stock-on-hand, open sessions, historical sales, inventory_movements, audit_log, GRNs, returns, or supplier records from the production Postgres app to SQLite. A pharmacy cannot go live with zero stock and zero sales history. Cutover/parallel-run strategy, opening-balance reconciliation, and migrated-audit-chain continuity are unaddressed across all 12 plan themes.

NO END-TO-END / SYSTEM-LEVEL ACCEPTANCE TEST exists. Every test is a unit or single-service DB-integration test. Nothing drives a full day (open shift -> GRN -> POS sales cash+card+controlled -> return/adjudicate -> void -> close -> Z-report -> reconcile) and asserts the books balance and the audit chain is continuous. The never-leave-stock-inconsistent guarantee is only asserted per-service, never across the whole workflow.

INJECTED MID-TRANSACTION FAILURE TESTS ARE MISSING despite CLAUDE.md explicitly requiring them. Reliability tests cover business-rule REJECTIONS only; no test forces a fault (disk-full, killed process, SQLITE_BUSY, failed audit insert) partway through a sale/return/GRN and proves stock+ledger+money are consistent on recovery. The most load-bearing pharmacy-safety claim is unproven.

POWER-LOSS / CRASH DURABILITY ON A SINGLE PC IS UNVERIFIED. PRAGMA synchronous left at WAL-default NORMAL means the last committed sale can be lost on power loss; no busy_timeout (confirmed absent), no integrity_check on startup or before destructive ALTER-TABLE migrations. For an unattended retail counter on AlmaLinux this is the most likely real-world data-loss vector and it is only noted, never tested or decided (no documented UPS assumption).

AUDIT TAMPER-EVIDENCE IS GONE, NOT JUST SIMPLIFIED. The HMAC chain (prev_hmac/row_hmac) is entirely unimplemented (confirmed: only a deferral comment in Audit.h, columns always empty) and there is no offline verifier. A regulator-facing medical audit log that is merely UPDATE/DELETE-trigger-blocked is not tamper-evident against anyone with file/SQLite access. The plan lists HMAC as a workstream but never decides whether shipping with empty chain columns is acceptable, and no external retention/compliance requirement is cited to justify it.

26 Audit::write CALL SITES IGNORE THE RETURN VALUE (confirmed), so a failed audit insert silently lets the business transaction commit. Flagged as scattered findings rather than one enforced invariant; there is no single throwing choke point guaranteeing audit-failure aborts every money/stock mutation. The append-only audit guarantee is defeatable by any audit-write error.

REGULATORY/COMPLIANCE REQUIREMENTS ARE NEVER STATED. No summary or plan item cites the actual legal regime (DRAP/Pakistan controlled-drug register format, narcotic record retention period, FBR tax-receipt requirements, data-retention duration, patient-PII privacy). Compliance is treated as match-the-PHP-app; the PHP app's own compliance is assumed, never validated against an external standard. Faithful reproduction may faithfully reproduce non-compliance.

BACKUP RESTORE IS UNIMPLEMENTED AND UNTESTED (confirmed: no restore code in src). The plan calls for a rehearsed recovery runbook but there is nothing to rehearse; plus no -wal/-shm sidecar handling, no retention/pruning, world-readable backup files exposing bcrypt PINs and patient records, and an unchecked WAL-checkpoint result. A single-PC system with no tested restore is one disk failure from total loss.

WAYLAND COMPATIBILITY ON THE ACTUAL TARGET IS UNVERIFIED. AlmaLinux 10 GNOME defaults to Wayland, but the AppImage bundles only libqxcb + libqoffscreen (confirmed; no Wayland platform plugin). Listed P2 but never tested on the real target. No examined evidence the AppImage even launches on a clean AlmaLinux 10 box.

NO RELEASE-GATING CI EXISTS (confirmed: no .github, no CTest/add_test in CMakeLists, no runner script). All-tests-pass is unenforced; a red build can ship. No automated post-build smoke test of the packaged binary either. The strong unit suite gives false confidence because nothing prevents regressions or a broken AppImage from being released.

CONCURRENCY / SECOND-CONNECTION SAFETY IS ASSUMED AWAY EVERYWHERE. Receipt-, grn-, and adjustment-number minting use read-then-insert with the PHP advisory locks dropped and no busy_timeout. Every summary excuses this with single-PC/single-connection, but auto-backup, an external WAL reader, a future second window, or a restore tool each introduce a second connection. The single-connection assumption is never enforced or documented as a hard constraint, leaving latent TOCTOU windows.

FLOATING-POINT IN A MONEY TEST ASSERTION violates the no-float rule (CAST AS REAL / toDouble / 0.005 epsilon) and can mask sub-cent rounding bugs in the exact path CLAUDE.md says must match PHP bit-for-bit. Until fixed, the money-parity guarantee has a hole in its own verification harness.

NO TRUE PHP-ORACLE PARITY HARNESS. Money/FEFO/cost/tax/SaleCalculator are checked against hand-transcribed golden constants, not live PHP output, and composed cross-class flows (SaleCalculator+CostBlender+report aggregation) are never compared end-to-end to the PHP app on shared fixtures. Reports explicitly never assert exact PKR amounts. Bit-for-bit is claimed but not mechanically guaranteed for composed flows.

MONEY int64 OVERFLOW IS UNGUARDED AND UNTESTED. PHP bcmath is arbitrary-precision; the C++ Money silently overflows in fromString/mul with no guard or boundary test. Low probability at pharmacy scale, but a silent wrong total is the worst failure class for a money system.

OPERATIONAL OWNERSHIP / UPDATE DELIVERY UNADDRESSED. No examined plan for who installs updates on the single AlmaLinux box, how a patched AppImage is delivered/verified on-site, how schema migrates forward in-field, or how a failed in-field migration rolls back. Migration runner has no pre-migration backup/integrity_check and no rollback test.

VALIDATION-AT-IMPORT AND BAD-DATA RESILIENCE under-examined: CatalogImporter never validates enum fields (form/schedule/tax) and silently drops ragged rows; CostBlender returns silent 0.0000 on degenerate input (units_per_purchase=0) instead of throwing like PHP, with no schema CHECK. A future re-import of a different export could silently post zero-cost batches.

PATIENT-DATA / PII HANDLING DROPPED OR UNEXAMINED: parked carts drop customer name/phone/CNIC that PHP persists; backups are world-readable; no examined data-at-rest encryption decision for a DB holding patient identifiers and controlled-drug dispensing records. Medical-record privacy obligations are never assessed.
top_risks: Data-loss / inconsistency on crash or power loss: synchronous=NORMAL, no busy_timeout, no integrity_check, no tested restore, and ZERO injected-mid-transaction-failure tests mean the core never-leave-stock-inconsistent guarantee is unproven exactly where it matters most — an unattended single PC.

No data migration from the live PHP/Postgres system: only the 318-row catalog seeds. Going live would discard all existing stock, sales history, audit chain, and controlled-drug register continuity. A hard blocker absent from every plan theme.

Audit trail is neither tamper-evident (HMAC chain empty/unimplemented) nor fail-safe (26 write sites ignore failure), so a regulator-facing controlled-substance/narcotic register can be silently altered or silently fail to record — a compliance and legal exposure for a drug-dispensing system.

Compliance is defined only as match-the-PHP-app with no external regulatory requirement cited (controlled-drug register, retention period, tax receipt, patient-PII privacy); faithfully reproducing an unvalidated spec may faithfully reproduce non-compliance.

No release gate: no CI, no CTest registration, no packaged-binary smoke test, and a money-parity test that itself uses floating point — a red or broken build can ship and the strongest safety claim (bit-for-bit money) has a hole in its own verifier.
Target-platform launch unverified: AlmaLinux 10 defaults to Wayland but the AppImage bundles no Wayland platform plugin and there is no evidence it starts on a clean target box.
critique.verdict: NOT production-ready: the per-module port is genuinely strong on money/stock/FEFO math, but cross-cutting medical-retail essentials — data migration/cutover, crash/power-loss durability with tested restore, fail-safe and tamper-evident audit, injected-failure and end-to-end acceptance tests, a release-gating CI, externally-grounded regulatory compliance, and verified launch on the actual Wayland AlmaLinux target — are missing or unproven, and these are blockers for a system that dispenses drugs and handles cash.

findings.title: fromString() and mul() can silently overflow int64; PHP bcmath cannot
findings.detail: Money stores value as qint64 at scale 4, so the representable range is ±(2^63-1)/10000 ≈ ±9.22e14. fromString() computes `intVal * 10000 + fracVal` (Money.cpp:58) with no overflow check: any integer part above ~922 trillion overflows to undefined/garbage. mul(qint64 qty) does `m_units * qty` (Money.h:28) with no guard — used by SaleCalculator::lineSubtotal (qty × unit_mrp), CostBlender numerator (unitCost × paidQty), Returns and StockAdjuster value calcs. PHP's Money is bcmath (arbitrary precision) and NEVER overflows, so a sufficiently large qty or unit price diverges silently from the spec (and is C++ signed-overflow UB). Realistic pharmacy values won't hit this, but it's an unbounded silent-divergence path on a money type that CLAUDE.md says must match PHP bit-for-bit.
findings.recommendation: Add overflow detection (e.g. __builtin_mul_overflow / __builtin_add_overflow, or check operands against limits) in fromString, operator+/-, and mul; on overflow throw or clamp deterministically and surface an error rather than wrap. Document the supported magnitude range and reject out-of-range parse input the way upstream validation expects.

findings.title: No test asserts bit-for-bit parity with actual PHP Money output (no oracle)
findings.detail: money_tests.cpp is large but every expectation is a hand-written literal; nothing compares against output captured from the PHP bcmath implementation. CLAUDE.md explicitly requires the money path to 'Match these results bit-for-bit and cover them with tests.' The subtle risk area is exactly the divByInt scale-4-vs-PHP-scale-8 equivalence and the SaleCalculator/CostBlender flows — I confirmed equivalence analytically/empirically here, but the repo has no regression guard tying the C++ results to PHP. If anyone touches the rounding or division logic, the suite won't catch a re-introduced divergence from the spec.
findings.recommendation: Generate a fixtures file by running the PHP Money/SaleCalculator/CostBlender over a broad grid (random and boundary inputs, both signs, >4dp, tie cases) and assert the C++ output equals each PHP string. Commit the generator so fixtures are reproducible.

findings.title: divByInt and arithmetic operators lack direct parity coverage for cross-class flows
findings.detail: divByInt is tested with ~20 direct cases (money_tests.cpp:545-567) and operator+/-/mul mostly via distributive identities and parse round-trips. There is no test exercising SaleCalculator::lineTotal (subtotal − discount + tax) or CostBlender::blendedCostPerBaseUnit / mrpPerBaseUnit against expected PHP values, even though those are the actual money-correctness surfaces the pharmacy depends on. The divByInt header even carries an unproven-in-tests claim ('8-dp truncation can't change a 4-dp HALF_UP decision'); I verified it holds, but no test pins it at the tie boundary (remainder*2 == divisor and remainder just under half).
findings.recommendation: Add tests for SaleCalculator (lineSubtotal/lineTotal/change with discount+tax) and CostBlender (FOC quantities, units_per_purchase>1, fractional unit costs) with PHP-derived expectations, plus explicit divByInt tie-boundary cases (e.g. value where quotient frac is exactly 0.5 and 0.49996) for both signs.

findings.title: Money has no decimal×decimal multiply; relies on the invariant that all multipliers are integer quantities
findings.detail: PHP Money::mul accepts string|int|float and is general decimal×decimal. C++ Money only offers mul(qint64). I confirmed every current PHP mul call multiplies a decimal by an integer quantity (SaleCalculator qty, CostBlender paidQty, Returns qty, StockAdjuster |qtyDelta|), so the narrower API is currently sufficient. But this is an undocumented invariant: if a future port step needs a percentage tax/discount (decimal × decimal), the type silently cannot express it and a developer may force-fit it (e.g. via divByInt or float), diverging from bcmath's scale-8 working precision.
findings.recommendation: Document the integer-multiplier invariant prominently on mul(), and if any decimal×decimal need arises, add a mulDecimal that computes at a wider working scale then rounds, mirroring bcmath SCALE_WORK=8 semantics, rather than improvising at the call site.

findings.title: Parsing leniency differs from bcmath prefix-parsing and '+' handling
findings.detail: PHP routes inputs through bcmath, which parses a leading numeric prefix and ignores trailing junk (e.g. '12abc' -> 12, 'abc' -> 0) and does not strip a leading '+'. C++ fromString returns 0 for any string where intStr.toLongLong fails (Money.cpp:39-41), so '12abc' -> 0 (divergence), while it explicitly strips a leading '+' (Money.cpp:25-27) which bcmath would not. Inputs are validated upstream so impact is low, but the comment 'mirrors Money::s leniency' (Money.cpp:40) is inaccurate — the leniency rules are not the same.
findings.recommendation: Either tighten upstream validation so only canonical decimal strings reach Money, or make fromString match bcmath's prefix-parse behavior; at minimum correct the misleading comment so future maintainers don't assume parity that isn't there.

findings.title: lineSubtotal can silently overflow int64 for extreme qty x MRP; PHP bcmath cannot
findings.detail: lineSubtotal does Money::fromString(unitMrp).mul(qtyBaseUnits). Money holds the value as int64 at scale 4 (m_units = value * 10000) and mul does m_units * qty with no overflow check. unit_mrp is DECIMAL(12,2), so a near-max MRP parses to ~10^14 at scale 4; multiplied by a large qtyBaseUnits (qty_sold_display up to 9999 x a large sold_unit_factor) the product can approach or exceed INT64_MAX (~9.2e18), wrapping to a wrong/negative subtotal. PHP's bcmath is arbitrary-precision and simply returns the correct large value. SaleService caps qtyDisplay at 9999 but does not bound sold_unit_factor or unit_mrp magnitude, so the guard is incomplete. This is a corner case (requires unrealistic data) but it is a silent wrong-money result rather than a thrown error.
findings.recommendation: Add an overflow-safe multiply in Money::mul (e.g. detect via __builtin_mul_overflow or check operands against a derived bound) and throw/return a sentinel on overflow so the sale aborts in a transaction rather than storing corrupt totals. Add a salecalc test at the DECIMAL(12,2) x large-qty boundary to lock the behavior.

findings.title: Internal scale-4 truncation diverges from PHP scale-8 working precision for MRP with >4 decimals (latent)
findings.detail: PHP lineSubtotal computes Money::mul at SCALE_WORK=8 then rounds the product HALF_UP to 2. The C++ port parses unitMrp into Money (rounding/truncating the MRP to scale 4 in Money::fromString), multiplies by the integer qty (exact at scale 4), then rounds to scale 2. If a unit MRP ever carried more than 4 decimal places, the C++ result could differ from PHP because the per-unit value is rounded before multiplication while PHP rounds only the final product. Today this is harmless because mrp_per_unit and unit_mrp are DECIMAL(12,2), so MRP never has >2 (let alone >4) decimals. It becomes a real bit-for-bit divergence the moment any caller feeds a higher-precision unit price (e.g. a future per-fraction price or a cost-based line).
findings.recommendation: Document the DECIMAL(12,2) precondition in SaleCalculator.h/Money.h (it is partially noted) and add a regression test using a >4-decimal unit price to pin the divergence so a future schema/precision change is caught. Alternatively, perform the qty x price multiply against the raw decimal string at a wider working scale to mirror PHP exactly.

findings.title: PHP SaleCalculator::sum() helper not ported (no parity coverage of the round-once sum boundary)
findings.detail: pos/backend/services/SaleCalculator.php exposes a sum() method that accumulates at SCALE_WORK and rounds once to scale 2. The C++ namespace omits it. In practice neither Sale.php nor SaleService.cpp call sum() (both inline the per-line accumulation), so this is not an active bug. However, the omission means the subtotal-summation rounding boundary has no dedicated unit test on the C++ side, and SaleService/PosTerminalPage each re-implement the accumulation independently (one summing scale-2 line subtotals, which is the PHP behavior). The duplicated accumulation logic is a maintainability/parity risk if the rounding convention ever needs to change.
findings.recommendation: Either port sum() and route both SaleService and PosTerminalPage subtotal accumulation through it (single source of truth for the round-once boundary), or explicitly document why it was dropped. Add a salecalc test asserting sum-of-lines parity with PHP for a multi-line cart that exercises rounding at the seam.

findings.title: lineTotal (per-line discount/tax) is dead in the sale path but untested against negative-clamp policy mismatch
findings.detail: Both PHP and C++ always store line_tax='0', line_discount='0', and line_total = line_subtotal; the lineTotal(subtotal, discount, tax) function is never invoked by the sale write path. The tests do exercise lineTotal including a -50.00 (no-clamp) case, correctly matching PHP which does not clamp at line level (only grand_total is clamped/validated). This is fine, but the kept-for-parity dead function plus its deliberately-negative test could mislead a future maintainer into thinking per-line tax/discount is wired up. No correctness issue.
findings.recommendation: Add a one-line comment on lineTotal noting it is retained for parity only and that the sale path stores line_total=line_subtotal with zero per-line tax/discount, matching Sale.php.

findings.title: UI silently clamps over-subtotal discount to a zero grand total instead of mirroring the server's hard rejection
findings.detail: recompute() computes grand = subtotal - discount and, if negative, sets grand = Money() (0.00) for display. The server (SaleService, matching Sale.php) instead throws 'Discount cannot exceed subtotal' when discount > subtotal. So a cashier can type a discount larger than the subtotal, see a 0.00 grand total that looks acceptable, attempt to complete the sale, and only then hit a server-side error. The authoritative server check prevents any bad data, so this is purely a UX/parity gap, not a money bug.
findings.recommendation: In recompute(), when discount > subtotal, surface the same validation message inline and disable the complete-sale action, so the UI fails fast with the same rule the server enforces.

findings.title: FEFO date boundary uses UTC in SQL but local date in the domain default — diverges from PHP near midnight
findings.detail: The batch prefilter in both src/data/BatchRepository.cpp:75 and src/service/SaleService.cpp:253 uses `expiry_date > date('now')`, but SQLite's date('now') is UTC. The PHP source-of-truth (pos/backend/services/Sale.php:238) uses Postgres `expiry_date > CURRENT_DATE`, which is the server's LOCAL date, and Fefo.php filters with `$exp > new DateTimeImmutable('now')` (local). Worse, the C++ domain filter in Fefo.cpp:22 compares against `today` whose default is `QDate::currentDate()` (LOCAL) — see Fefo.h:47 — while SaleService calls `Fefo::allocate(batches, qtyNeeded, medicineId)` (SaleService.cpp:273-274) with no `today`, so it gets local date. The SQL prefilter (UTC) and the domain re-filter (local) therefore use two different 'today' values. In Pakistan (UTC+5), between 00:00 and ~05:00 local, date('now') (UTC) is still the previous day, so a batch expiring 'today local' would pass the SQL filter but be (correctly, per PHP) excluded by the domain filter — or vice versa near the other edge. This produces behavior that does not match PHP at the day boundary and is internally inconsistent (SQL says sellable, domain says no).
findings.recommendation: Make every FEFO/expiry date comparison use local date consistently. Either pass an explicit `today = QDate::currentDate()` and bind it into the SQL as a parameter (e.g. `expiry_date > :today`), or use `date('now','localtime')` in SQLite. Audit InventoryRepository.cpp:95 and :131 too — they have the same `date('now')` UTC issue for near-expiry/sellable reporting. Add a test that pins `today` and a batch expiring exactly today to lock the boundary against the PHP spec.

findings.title: available accumulator is a 32-bit int with no overflow guard; differs from PHP array_sum semantics
findings.detail: Fefo.cpp:36-39 sums currentQty into a plain `int available`. currentQty is also `int` (Fefo.h:12). For realistic pharmacy quantities this never overflows, but the values flow from arbitrary DB content (current_qty is an integer column with no enforced upper bound here), and `available` plus `remaining`/`totalQtyNeeded` are all 32-bit. PHP uses array_sum over PHP integers (64-bit on the target) and (int)min, so an extreme dataset could in principle diverge or overflow silently in C++ before it does in PHP. There is no test exercising very large quantities.
findings.recommendation: Use qint64 (or long long) for available/remaining/totalQtyNeeded and the qty fields, matching PHP's 64-bit int width, or add an explicit bound check. Add a large-quantity test case.

findings.title: Domain re-filter can silently throw InsufficientStock for rows the SQL caller already filtered, masking real-world boundary bugs
findings.detail: Because allocate() re-applies the full filter (Fefo.cpp:18-26) on top of the SQL prefilter, any disagreement between the two filters (see the UTC/local finding) silently reduces `available` and can raise InsufficientStockException even though stock physically exists and the SQL said it was sellable. The exception's `available` would then under-report, and the cashier sees 'insufficient stock' on a medicine that has stock. The exhaustive unit tests never feed allocate() the exact rows the SQL produces (they construct FefoBatch directly), so this integration seam is untested. This mirrors PHP's defensive double-filter, but PHP keeps both filters on the SAME clock, so PHP cannot hit the divergence.
findings.recommendation: Either (a) fix the clock consistency so SQL and domain filters always agree, then keep the defensive re-filter as a true no-op; or (b) add an integration test that inserts batches via the repository, runs candidateBatchesForSale()/SaleService, and asserts allocate() never drops a SQL-returned row. Consider logging when the re-filter actually drops a row, since post-fix it should never happen.

findings.title: No concurrency/locking equivalent to PHP's SELECT ... FOR UPDATE in the SaleService FEFO loop (no test asserts single-writer safety)
findings.detail: PHP Sale.php:228-240 explicitly locks candidate batches with `FOR UPDATE` before allocating and decrementing, to prevent two sales racing on the same batch. The C++ port (SaleService.cpp:248-288) reads candidate batches then UPDATEs current_qty within a transaction, relying on SQLite's whole-DB write lock instead. For a single-PC SQLite deployment this is acceptable (per CLAUDE.md), but it is a deliberate semantic substitution with no test or assertion documenting that current_qty cannot go negative under concurrent access (e.g. a background report process). The UPDATE writes the precomputed qtyAfter (SaleService.cpp:279,284) rather than `current_qty = current_qty - :d`, so if the row changed between SELECT and UPDATE the decrement would be wrong/lost.
findings.recommendation: Document the single-writer assumption near the loop, and prefer `UPDATE batches SET current_qty = current_qty - :d WHERE id = :id AND current_qty >= :d` so a concurrent/stale read cannot drive stock negative; verify affected-row count. Add a test (or at least a CHECK(current_qty >= 0) in schema) asserting stock never goes negative.

findings.title: assertSortedByExpiry uses only QDate ordering and ignores the id tie-break, so a sorted-but-wrong-tie input passes silently
findings.detail: Fefo.cpp:58-69 asserts only that expiry is non-decreasing; it does NOT verify the id ASC tie-break the allocator relies on. PHP's assertSortedByExpiry (Fefo.php) likewise only checks expiry_date, so this is faithful to PHP — but it means the 'defensive' assert in SaleService.cpp:272 gives false confidence: a caller could pass batches with equal expiry but descending ids and the assert passes, then allocate() internally re-sorts anyway. The assert is therefore near-useless as a guard (allocate re-sorts unconditionally at Fefo.cpp:29-34). Not a divergence from PHP, but a maintainability/clarity trap.
findings.recommendation: Either drop the assertSortedByExpiry call in SaleService (allocate already re-sorts, so it is redundant), or strengthen the assert to include the id tie-break and document that allocate() does not depend on input order. Keep parity with PHP intentional and commented.

findings.title: Invalid/unparseable expiry is treated as 'skip' identically to PHP, but parse failures are silent with no audit/log
findings.detail: Fefo.cpp:22 silently drops a batch whose QDate is invalid (mirrors PHP's try/catch returning false in Fefo.php). The upstream parse at SaleService.cpp:265 / BatchRepository.cpp:85 uses QDate::fromString(..., 'yyyy-MM-dd'); if a row's expiry_date is stored in any other format (e.g. with a time component, which Postgres DATE never had but a SQLite TEXT column could acquire via a buggy importer per the medicines_export.csv seed note), the date silently becomes invalid and the batch becomes permanently unsellable with no diagnostic. Test #10 covers a deliberately-null QDate but not a malformed non-empty string.
findings.recommendation: Log (at warn level) when a batch row's expiry_date fails to parse, so corrupt seed/import data surfaces rather than silently zeroing out sellable stock. Add a test feeding a non-empty but malformed expiry string through the repository layer.

findings.title: No test pins FEFO against a fixed 'today' / no PHP cross-check fixture, despite CLAUDE.md requiring bit-for-bit expiry parity
findings.detail: CLAUDE.md mandates that batch/expiry/FEFO logic be 'covered by tests comparing results against PHP behavior.' The current suite (fefo_tests.cpp) is thorough but entirely self-referential: it uses today.addDays(offset) and asserts internal invariants, never comparing against captured PHP outputs, and never pins an absolute date. The most failure-prone real-world case — a batch expiring exactly at the local/UTC day boundary — is only tested in the offset==0 case under a single clock and cannot detect the UTC/local divergence described above because both the SQL layer and any PHP comparison are absent from the pure test. There is also no test crossing the day boundary in a non-UTC timezone.
findings.recommendation: Add a small golden-vector test that mirrors a handful of PHP Fefo::allocate inputs/outputs (capture them from the PHP app) including the expiry==today and expiry==tomorrow boundary, run under a forced non-UTC TZ in CI, asserting identical allocations. This directly satisfies the CLAUDE.md bit-for-bit requirement.

findings.title: Invalid input silently returns 0.0000 instead of throwing — diverges from PHP and can post corrupt batches
findings.detail: PHP CostBlender::blendedCostPerBaseUnit and mrpPerBaseUnit THROW \InvalidArgumentException when paidQty<0, focQty<0, or unitsPerPurchase<1 (CostBlender.php:27-29,42), which aborts the entire SERIALIZABLE GRN post. The C++ port instead returns Money().toString(ScaleCost) == "0.0000" and returns normally. The caller GrnService::post reads upp = mq.value(1).toInt() (GrnService.cpp:101) with NO upp>=1 validation, and the SQLite schema column units_per_purchase has NO CHECK >= 1 (sql/schema_sqlite.sql:91; mirrors db/schema/init.sql:147). So a medicine with units_per_purchase=0 (plausible from a bad CSV import via CatalogImporter, or NULL coerced to 0) flows straight through: blendedCost="0.0000", mrpPerBase="0.0000", totalBase=(paid+foc)*0=0, and GrnService happily INSERTs a batch with current_qty=0, cost_per_unit=0, and emits a no-op GRN_RECEIPT movement — silently corrupting inventory where PHP would hard-fail the receipt. This is a genuine behavioral divergence on the stock/cost path that CLAUDE.md says must match bit-for-bit.
findings.recommendation: Either (a) make CostBlender signal the error the way PHP does (throw / return an explicit failure the caller must handle) instead of masquerading invalid input as a valid 0.0000 cost, or (b) add an explicit unitsPerPurchase>=1 (and paid/foc>=0) guard in GrnService::post that aborts the post with a user-facing error, AND add CHECK("units_per_purchase" >= 1) to the medicines table. The current 'return 0.0000' is only safe because callers happen never to pass bad data — but nothing enforces that.

findings.title: Tests codify the divergent silent-zero behavior as expected rather than flagging it
findings.detail: The test suite asserts blendedCostPerBaseUnit(-1,0,...)=="0.0000", (0,-1,...)=="0.0000", (5,5,...,upp0)=="0.0000", and mrpPerBaseUnit(...,0)/(...,-1)=="0.0000". These lock in the C++-only silent-zero behavior, which is the OPPOSITE of the PHP spec (PHP throws). Because the spec is 'reproduce PHP behavior', these tests give false confidence that the port matches — they actually encode a deviation. There is no test asserting that an invalid GRN line is rejected end-to-end.
findings.recommendation: Decide the contract (throw vs. caller-validates), then change these assertions to verify the intended error path. Add a GrnService-level test that a units_per_purchase=0 medicine causes post() to fail and roll back, matching PHP's abort.

findings.title: Unguarded int64 overflow in Money::mul used by blendedCostPerBaseUnit / lineTotal
findings.detail: Money::mul does fromUnits(m_units * qty) with no overflow check; CostBlender calls Money::fromString(unitCost).mul(paidQty). m_units is unitCost*10000 (scale-4). Overflow requires unitCost*10000*paidQty > INT64_MAX, i.e. ~9.2M packs at max DECIMAL(12,4) cost — not a realistic pharmacy GRN, so practical risk is low. But signed-int64 overflow is undefined behavior, and the same Money type is reused on hotter paths. PHP's bcmath has arbitrary precision so it never overflows here, making this a (remote) parity gap.
findings.recommendation: Add a checked-multiply (e.g. __builtin_mul_overflow or a range assert) in Money::mul, or at least clamp/validate paidQty*unitCost magnitude in GrnService before calling. Low priority given realistic ranges.

findings.title: blendedCostPerBaseUnit ignores FOC-only and partial-pack scenarios that PHP's int totalBaseUnits also computes the same way — verify totalBase int math in caller
findings.detail: CostBlender itself computes totalBaseUnits as qint64 (CostBlender.cpp:13-14), which is correct. But the GrnService caller independently recomputes const int totalBase = (line.paidQty + line.focQty) * upp as a 32-bit int (GrnService.cpp:129) and uses it for received_qty/current_qty/qty_delta. This is a separate, narrower type than CostBlender's qint64 path. For very large receipts (millions of base units) the caller's int could overflow while CostBlender's qint64 would not, producing an inconsistent batch qty vs. cost basis. Within normal pharmacy volumes this is fine, but the two code paths disagree on width for the same quantity.
findings.recommendation: Use qint64 for totalBase in GrnService::post to match CostBlender's internal width and the batches.current_qty domain, keeping the qty and cost computations consistent.

findings.title: No FOC > paid sanity check; blended cost can collapse toward zero with large FOC, matching PHP but worth a guardrail note
findings.detail: blended_cost = (unitCost*paid)/((paid+foc)*upp). This intentionally dilutes per-unit cost by free goods and matches PHP exactly (verified). However neither PHP nor the port bounds foc relative to paid, so a data-entry error (e.g. paid=1, foc=999) yields a near-zero cost basis that then drives margin/valuation reports. This is faithful to the spec (not a port bug), but it is a real-world business-rule blind spot on the cost path with no validation anywhere.
findings.recommendation: No change required for parity. Optionally flag in UI (GrnLineDialog) when foc >> paid, since blended cost feeds valuation/P&L. Leave domain math as-is to preserve PHP fidelity.

findings.title: gtin13From diverges from PHP ltrim — breaks bit-for-bit barcode matching for short (EAN-8/UPC) GTINs
findings.detail: PHP MedicineSearch derives the 13-digit match key as `ltrim($gtin14,'0') ?: '0'`, stripping ALL leading zeros. The C++ gtin13From() strips leading zeros only down to a MINIMUM of 13 digits (`while (s.size() > 13 && startsWith('0'))`). For a GTIN-14 that was padded from an EAN-8 or UPC-A (e.g. EAN-8 '96385074' → normalizeGtin → '00000096385074'), PHP yields gtin13 '96385074' (8 chars) while C++ yields '0000096385074' (13 chars). searchForPos then binds these differing values into `primary_barcode IN (:g14,:g13)`, so a stored EAN-8/UPC barcode that PHP would match, the Qt app will NOT match (or vice-versa). CLAUDE.md and the audit brief require GTIN matching to be bit-for-bit identical to PHP; this is a genuine divergence on a stock/pricing-adjacent path.
findings.recommendation: Match PHP exactly: in searchForPos derive the 13-digit key with full leading-zero strip (Qt equivalent of `ltrim(gtin14,'0') ?: '0'`), independent of the public gtin13From() helper (which the tests document as the 'min 13' contract). Add a test feeding a stored EAN-8/UPC barcode and asserting the scanned padded GTIN matches it the same way PHP does.

findings.title: searchForPos omits the PHP raw-barcode exact-match clause (m.primary_barcode = :raw)
findings.detail: PHP matches a scanned barcode with `(m.primary_barcode IN (:g14,:g13) OR m.primary_barcode = :raw)` — i.e. it also tries the raw scanned string verbatim. The Qt query only binds :g14/:g13 (and the generic LIKE). If a medicine's primary_barcode is stored in a non-canonical form the parser doesn't reproduce (e.g. stored with a check digit the GS1 path strips, or a 12-digit UPC stored unpadded while the scan padded it), PHP still hits via the raw clause but Qt misses. Additionally the Qt code binds the sentinel value ' ' (a single space) when there's no GTIN, relying on no barcode ever equalling ' '; that's a fragile substitute for binding NULL/omitting the clause.
findings.recommendation: Add `OR m.primary_barcode = :raw` bound to the trimmed query, matching PHP. Replace the ' ' sentinel with a clause that is conditionally appended only when scan.isBarcode (or bind NULL, which never equals a stored barcode).

findings.title: Scanned-barcode POS UX not ported: no clean-GTIN substitution, no parsed-field chip, no heuristic-verify warning
findings.detail: In the PHP terminal, when a scan parses as a structured barcode the UI: (a) replaces the 30-50 char raw scanner string in the search box with the clean GTIN (`value=searchChip['gtin'] ?? searchQuery`), (b) renders a barcode chip showing GTIN / lot / expiry, and (c) shows a 'heuristic — verify lot/exp' warning badge when the FNC1 separator was missing and field boundaries were guessed. PosTerminalPage feeds the raw text straight to searchForPos and surfaces none of this. For a pharmacy the heuristic-verify warning is a real safety signal (a mis-cut lot/expiry from a separator-less scan could attach the wrong batch info); silently dropping it loses the PHP guardrail. The parser already exposes the data (lot/expiry/serial and could expose a 'heuristic' flag) — only the UI surfacing is missing.
findings.recommendation: After Barcode::parse in the POS flow, when isBarcode && a GTIN is present, replace the search field text with the canonical GTIN and show a chip with gtin/lot/expiry. Expose a 'usedHeuristic' bool from the parser (currently the strict-vs-heuristic distinction is computed but discarded) and render the verify warning, mirroring terminal.php.

findings.title: GTIN mod-10 check digit never validated (PHP exposes check_digit_ok)
findings.detail: PHP computes and returns check_digit_ok (validateGtinMod10) for every GTIN/GS1/DigitalLink parse. The C++ port has no check-digit validation at all and ParsedBarcode has no such field. A transposed/mis-scanned digit yields a structurally-valid-but-wrong GTIN that silently fails to match any product (acceptable) — but the app can't distinguish 'unknown product' from 'corrupt scan', and can't warn the cashier. Low severity because an invalid check digit just produces a no-match lookup, but it's a lost diagnostic the PHP spec provides.
findings.recommendation: Port validateGtinMod10 (GS1 mod-10, 3/1 alternating weights) and expose a checkDigitOk flag on ParsedBarcode; optionally surface a soft 'check digit failed — re-scan' hint in the POS UX. Cover with tests against known-good and known-bad GTINs.

findings.title: Dropped barcode formats (HIBC / IFA-PPN / ISO 15434 / AIM symbology prefix) silently fall through to free-text search
findings.detail: PHP handles AIM symbology identifiers (]C1/]d2/]Q3/]e0 — some scanners ALWAYS prepend these), the ISO 15434 envelope ([)>RS06GS...), HIBC (leading '+') and IFA PPN ('9N'). The C++ parser handles none. The most impactful is the AIM prefix: a scanner configured to emit ]d2 in front of a GS1-DataMatrix payload will cause the C++ parse() to fail all the AI/GTIN/DigitalLink branches (the string no longer starts with 01/00/02 or https) and fall through to PlainText, so even a normal pharma GS1 scan won't extract a GTIN. The CLAUDE.md header comment acknowledges the subset, but an AIM-prefix-emitting scanner is a common real-world config, not an exotic format.
findings.recommendation: At minimum strip a leading AIM identifier (^\](.)(.) ) before the format dispatch, matching QrParser step 1, so GS1 scans with ]C1/]d2/]Q3/]e0 prefixes still decode. Decide explicitly (and document in CLAUDE.md/MEMORY php-vs-qt-port-gaps) whether HIBC/PPN/ISO15434 are in-scope for the target pharmacy's stock; if any imported devices use them, port them with tests.

findings.title: Digital Link parser ignores AI 02 and does not URL-decode query values, unlike PHP
findings.detail: Two parity gaps in parseDigitalLink: (1) PHP urldecode()s query-string AI values; the C++ inserts them raw, so a percent-encoded lot/serial in a `?10=...` query (e.g. a '/' encoded as %2F) is stored encoded and won't match. (2) fillFromAis prefers AI 01 then 02, but a Digital Link carrying only /02/<gtin> (inner-pack) would be picked up by fillFromAis while PHP's parseDigitalLink only reads pairs['01'] for the GTIN — a subtle behavioral difference (C++ is arguably more lenient here, but it's an undocumented divergence). The C++ path also never reaches the AI-02-requires-01 exclusivity rule that the AI-string path enforces.
findings.recommendation: URL-decode query-string values (QUrl::fromPercentEncoding) to match PHP. Decide and document whether Digital Link /02/ should yield a GTIN; align with PHP (which uses only /01/).

findings.title: Heuristic boundary-AI list is a narrower subset than PHP without documented stock justification
findings.detail: PHP HEURISTIC_BOUNDARY_AIS = {01,10,11,13,15,17,21,240,241,710-714}; C++ isBoundaryAi = {01,10,11,15,17,21}. Because C++ only recognizes a smaller fixed/var AI set this is internally consistent, but it means a separator-less (heuristic) scan whose lot or serial is immediately followed by an AI 13 (pack date) or 240/710 boundary will mis-cut differently than PHP — the C++ greedy walk will swallow the boundary AI and its value into the variable field. PHP's refineLotSerial() post-pass (which fixes the common '21-inside-serial' mis-cut) is also entirely absent in C++, so heuristic lot/serial splits can differ from PHP for codes that hit that pattern. For pharma the heuristic path feeds lot/expiry that staff act on, so silent divergence matters even if rare.
findings.recommendation: Either (a) document in CLAUDE.md/MEMORY exactly which heuristic mis-cuts the Qt port intentionally diverges on and why they can't occur with this pharmacy's packs, or (b) port the refineLotSerial scoring pass and widen the boundary list for the AIs you support, and add heuristic-mis-cut test vectors mirroring QrParser's documented example.

findings.title: No tests for the actual lookup integration (parse → searchForPos g14/g13 binding) or the gtin13 mismatch
findings.detail: The unit tests exhaustively cover Barcode::parse in isolation but nothing tests the integration point that matters for stock/pricing correctness: that a scanned GTIN actually matches a medicine's stored primary_barcode via searchForPos, across the EAN-8/UPC/EAN-13/GTIN-14 storage variants. Given findings #1 (gtin13 divergence) and #2 (missing raw clause), there is no regression test that would catch a scan that should match a product but doesn't — exactly the kind of silent POS failure (cashier can't find the scanned item) that the audit brief flags. The ' ' sentinel binding also has no test asserting it never collides with a real barcode.
findings.recommendation: Add a DB-backed test (the harness already passes a QSqlDatabase into run_*_tests) that inserts medicines with primary_barcode stored as EAN-8, UPC-12, EAN-13 and GTIN-14, then asserts searchForPos returns the right row for each corresponding scanned form — and compare the matched key derivation against PHP's ltrim semantics.

findings.title: Audit verb diverges from PHP source of truth (CONTROLLED_DISPENSED vs NARCOTIC_DISPENSED)
findings.detail: PHP Sale.php:340 writes the controlled-dispense audit row with action 'NARCOTIC_DISPENSED'. The Qt port writes 'CONTROLLED_DISPENSED' instead. CLAUDE.md and the porting brief make audit who-did-what-when a compliance requirement and the PHP app the spec. Any forensic query, compliance export, or future audit-trail report that filters audit_log.action by the PHP verb will silently miss every controlled dispense recorded by the Qt app, and a mixed-history database (PHP rows + Qt rows) will have two different verbs for the identical event. The narcotic-register/compliance reports happen to read from sales/sale_items (not audit_log) so they still work, which masks the divergence.
findings.recommendation: Rename the verb to 'NARCOTIC_DISPENSED' to match PHP exactly, or if a more generic name is genuinely wanted, document the deliberate deviation in CLAUDE.md and migrate any consumers. Add an assertion-level test that the row is written with the agreed verb.

findings.title: Controlled-dispense audit payload omits fields PHP records (cashier_id, medicine_ids)
findings.detail: PHP (Sale.php:341-347) records receipt_number, cashier_id, witness_id, prescriber_license_number, and medicine_ids in the controlled-dispense audit detail. The Qt port records only receipt_number, witness_id, and prescriber_license. The omitted medicine_ids in particular is the compliance-relevant payload (which scheduled drugs were dispensed), and cashier_id is needed when the acting-user column is later trimmed. This weakens the append-only audit trail the brief calls out as critical for a medical-retail system and breaks payload parity with the PHP records.
findings.recommendation: Include cashier_id and the list of medicine ids (and ideally witness_at) in the JSON detail so the Qt audit row carries the same evidentiary content as PHP.

findings.title: No end-to-end test for the SCHEDULE_G / SCHEDULE_H tier — the exact controlled-vs-gated boundary
findings.detail: The only SCHEDULE_G coverage is a pure-policy assert that requiresWitness('SCHEDULE_G')==false. There is no integration test that a cart containing ONLY a SCHEDULE_G (or SCHEDULE_H) medicine (a) commits successfully with NO prescriber license and NO witness, AND (b) still persists has_controlled_drug=1. This is precisely the regression-prone boundary: a one-line change to isGatedSchedule() (e.g. gating SCHEDULE_H) or to anyControlled() would silently either over-block routine schedule-G dispensing or stop flagging it as controlled, and no test would catch it. CLAUDE.md mandates tests on anything touching controlled dispensing.
findings.recommendation: Add integration cases: SCHEDULE_G-only cart commits with no license/witness and sets has_controlled_drug=1; SCHEDULE_H behaves identically; and a mixed NARCOTIC+SCHEDULE_G cart still triggers the full gate. Compare has_controlled_drug semantics against PHP.

findings.title: has_controlled_drug is server-derived in Qt but client-trusted in PHP — undocumented behavioral divergence
findings.detail: PHP binds :hcd from the client-supplied flag (!empty($input['has_controlled_drug']), Sale.php:202). The Qt port instead derives hasControlled from a server-side DISTINCT controlled_schedule query (anyControlled(schedules)). The Qt behavior is more correct and harder to spoof, but it is a genuine divergence from the spec: a PHP sale of a controlled drug where the client omitted the flag would store has_controlled_drug=false, whereas Qt stores 1. This affects the compliance report's 'has_controlled_drug = 1 OR EXISTS(...)' predicate parity and historical data comparisons. The deviation is reasonable but is not noted in CLAUDE.md/PHP_APP_MAP.md as an intentional correction.
findings.recommendation: Keep the safer server-derived behavior but record it as an explicit, intentional deviation in CLAUDE.md (like the Money/DB corrections), and add a test asserting has_controlled_drug is set from schedule regardless of any client flag.

findings.title: Witness PIN is not re-verified inside SaleService; only the resolved user id is re-validated
findings.detail: SaleService trusts input.controlledWitnessUserId and only re-checks that it is an active, non-deleted MANAGER/ADMIN and != cashier; the bcrypt PIN verification happens only in the UI (PosTerminalPage.cpp:498 verifyManagerOverride). A caller that constructs a SaleInput directly (test harness, future second entry point, scripted import) could supply any valid manager id as 'witness' without ever proving possession of that manager's PIN, defeating the two-person attestation. This matches PHP (Sale.php also trusts the int witness id), so it is parity-correct under the single-PC trusted-process model — but it means the domain/service layer alone does not enforce the human two-person guarantee; the guarantee lives entirely in one UI path.
findings.recommendation: Either accept and explicitly document that witness-PIN proof is a UI-layer responsibility (and ensure every future commit path routes through that verification), or have SaleService accept the witness PIN and call verifyManagerOverride itself so the two-person rule is enforced at the trust boundary regardless of caller.

findings.title: Aggregate policy helper anyRequiresPrescriberLicense and the prescriber-license-only path lack direct tests
findings.detail: Tests cover requiresWitness(NARCOTIC/SCHEDULE_G) and isControlled(NONE), and the integration cases exercise the combined gate. But anyRequiresPrescriberLicense, anyControlled (especially with a mix of NONE + controlled in one list), and anyRequiresWitness are not asserted directly. Because the gate currently couples license and witness to the same isGatedSchedule predicate, a future requirement that splits them (license required for SCHEDULE_H but witness only for NARCOTIC) would change requiresPrescriberLicense independently and is presently untested.
findings.recommendation: Add pure-policy asserts for the three any* helpers including mixed-schedule lists, and an explicit assert that requiresPrescriberLicense and requiresWitness can be reasoned about independently.

findings.title: Schedule-gate query result is empty-tolerant on failure, silently bypassing the controlled gate on DB error
findings.detail: The DISTINCT controlled_schedule lookup runs before the transaction and only appends schedules 'if (sq.exec())'. If the query fails (locked db, transient error), schedules stays empty, hasControlled becomes false, and the sale proceeds with NO controlled gate — a narcotic could be dispensed without license/witness and recorded as non-controlled. PHP runs its has_narcotic EXISTS query with execute() and would throw a PDOException on failure (fail-closed). The Qt path fails open on this safety-critical check.
findings.recommendation: Treat a failed schedule query as a hard SaleError (fail closed), e.g. throw with sq.lastError().text() when exec() returns false, so a DB hiccup can never silently disable the controlled-substance gate.

findings.title: Prescriber license is stored and audited in plaintext with no format/length validation
findings.detail: The prescriber license is accepted as any non-empty trimmed string, persisted to prescriber_license_number (schema VARCHAR(50)) and copied verbatim into the audit JSON. There is no length cap matching the column (a >50-char value would fail the INSERT mid-transaction and abort an otherwise valid sale rather than being rejected up front with a clear message) and no minimal sanity check. PHP behaves the same (trim only), so this is parity-correct, but for a DRAP-regulated narcotic field a length/format guard mirroring the column would give a cleaner error and prevent a late transaction abort.
findings.recommendation: Validate the trimmed license length against the 50-char column and optionally a basic non-whitespace/format check, raising a SaleError with a clear message before the transaction opens.

findings.title: Manager-PIN override has no rate limiting — brute-force regression vs PHP
findings.detail: PHP ManagerOverride::verify (../pos/backend/services/ManagerOverride.php:35-39) gates every attempt through RateLimit::check keyed on action+IP, emits an OVERRIDE_RATE_LIMITED audit row, and refuses after the limit; it also RateLimit::reset on success. The Qt verifyManagerOverride has NONE of this — it bcrypt-scans all active managers/admins on every call with no attempt counter, no lockout, and no rate-limit audit event. The login path has lockout (secondsLockedOut/registerFailedLogin) but the override path is wide open. At the POS a malicious or curious cashier can repeatedly fire the discount/void/witness override dialog and brute the (typically 4-6 digit numeric) manager PIN with no throttle. This is a direct security downgrade from the source-of-truth spec.
findings.recommendation: Add an attempt counter + backoff lockout to verifyManagerOverride mirroring the login lockout (per-action key, e.g. reuse the failed_attempts/locked_until mechanism or a small override_attempts table), write an OVERRIDE_RATE_LIMITED audit row when tripped, and reset on success. Cover with a test that the Nth attempt is refused.

findings.title: verifyManagerOverride has zero direct unit tests
findings.detail: Grep of tests/ for verifyManagerOverride, OVERRIDE_GRANTED, OVERRIDE_DENIED, forbidUserId, and isActiveManagerOrAdmin returns nothing. The function is the single security gate for discount/void/witness overrides yet only its downstream effects are exercised indirectly through SaleService (sale_tests.cpp section 13, which passes discountAuthorizedBy directly and never goes through PIN verification). The core behaviors are untested: correct PIN of a manager grants and returns the right userId/role; the forbidUserId cashier is excluded even if its own PIN is supplied; a CASHIER's correct PIN is never accepted (role filter); an inactive/soft-deleted manager is rejected; empty PIN is rejected; and OVERRIDE_GRANTED vs OVERRIDE_DENIED audit rows are written with the right actor and action. CLAUDE.md mandates tests on this class of path.
findings.recommendation: Add a UserRepository override test case: seed an ADMIN, a MANAGER, a CASHIER, and an inactive MANAGER; assert grant/deny outcomes for each PIN, the forbidUserId exclusion, empty-PIN rejection, and that the matching audit row (action='discount', correct role/userId) is written for both grant and deny.

findings.title: OVERRIDE_DENIED audit drops forbid_user_id context recorded by PHP
findings.detail: PHP writes OVERRIDE_DENIED with {action, forbid_user_id} (ManagerOverride.php:75-76), so a denied attempt is traceable to which cashier attempted it. The Qt version writes only {"action":"..."} with actor userId 0 and no forbid_user_id, so a denied override is anonymous — you cannot tell from the audit log which terminal/cashier triggered the failed manager-PIN attempt. For a medical-retail audit trail this loses meaningful who-attempted-what evidence on the deny path (the grant path is fine).
findings.recommendation: Include forbidUserId in the OVERRIDE_DENIED detail JSON (and consider recording it as the actor) to match PHP and keep failed overrides attributable to the acting cashier.

findings.title: Role checks are case-sensitive with no normalization
findings.detail: isManagerial compares role exactly against 'MANAGER'/'ADMIN', and verifyManagerOverride / isActiveManagerOrAdmin use SQL role IN ('MANAGER','ADMIN'). The schema CHECK constraint (sql/schema_sqlite.sql:33) does enforce uppercase, so this is currently safe, but the policy is a pure, DB-agnostic class that a future caller could feed a differently-cased role (e.g. from an import or a relaxed constraint), which would silently mis-classify a manager as a cashier and force an unnecessary override — or worse, mis-classify the other direction. The coupling between the pure policy's correctness and an external CHECK constraint is implicit and undocumented.
findings.recommendation: Either normalize (role.trimmed().toUpper()) inside isManagerial, or add a comment/assert documenting that callers must pass the canonical uppercase role; add a test for a lowercase 'manager' to lock in the chosen behavior.

findings.title: No automated parity test that a MANAGER-role cashier self-authorizes without a PIN prompt
findings.detail: PHP terminal.php:306 self-authorizes for both MANAGER and ADMIN ($isManagerOrAdmin). The disc-auth tests cover CASHIER (needs override) and the ADMIN userId (self-authorizes), but section 13 only exercises self-authorization via the ADMIN seed user; there is no case where a MANAGER-role user is the cashier and self-authorizes. The pure-policy asserts (lines 1043-1048) similarly test CASHIER and ADMIN but never MANAGER. Since MANAGER is the more common discount-granting role in a pharmacy, the self-authorization path for MANAGER is unverified end-to-end.
findings.recommendation: Add a SaleService case where the cashier is a MANAGER applying a positive discount with no discountAuthorizedBy, asserting success and discount_authorized_by == the manager's own id; add isManagerial('MANAGER') and requiresManagerOverride('MANAGER', true)==false policy asserts.

findings.title: Manager override result userId trusted by UI but not bound to the verified scan in PosTerminalPage
findings.detail: PosTerminalPage sets in.discountAuthorizedBy = res.userId from verifyManagerOverride, then SaleService re-validates that this id is a different active manager/admin (SaleService.cpp:191) — good defense in depth. However, this means verifyManagerOverride is effectively called twice for the same sale-discount intent only when going through the UI is correct, but the authoritative gate is the SaleService re-check, NOT the PIN verification: a caller that constructs a SaleInput directly with discountAuthorizedBy set to any valid manager id bypasses PIN verification entirely (the PIN is only checked in the UI layer). This is acceptable for a single-PC desktop app where the UI is the only entry point, but it is worth noting that the PIN is a UI-layer control, not a domain/service-layer invariant, unlike narcotic witness which is also only id-validated at the service layer.
findings.recommendation: Document that PIN verification is a UI-layer control and the service layer trusts a validated authorizer id; if scriptable/headless sale entry is ever added, move PIN verification (or a verified-token) into the service boundary.

findings.title: 90-day rotation silently never triggers when pin_changed_at is NULL/unparseable (diverges from PHP)
findings.detail: pinAgeDays() runs CAST(julianday('now') - julianday(pin_changed_at) AS INTEGER) and, when the value is NULL (q.value(0).isNull()) or the query fails, returns 0. main.cpp:119 then computes `mustRotatePin || pinAgeDays >= RotationDays`, so a NULL or unparseable pin_changed_at yields age 0 and the PIN NEVER expires. julianday() returns NULL on any non-ISO timestamp string, so a row that stores e.g. a TIMESTAMPTZ-flavored value or an empty string would silently bypass the rotation policy forever. The PHP source-of-truth (Auth.php:128-132) does the opposite: `new DateTimeImmutable((string)$row['pin_changed_at'])` on a bad/empty value throws or resolves to 'now', and the policy is enforced via a hard redirect to /account/change-pin. The Postgres schema (phase4_pin_policy.sql:10,26) makes the column NOT NULL with a backfill, but the SQLite port has no equivalent guarantee shown here, so a migration/import gap turns a security control off with no signal.
findings.recommendation: Treat unknown/NULL/unparseable pin_changed_at as 'rotation due' (return a large sentinel, matching the header comment 'Large if unknown'), not 0. Enforce NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP on users.pin_changed_at in the SQLite schema and backfill on migration, mirroring phase4_pin_policy.sql. Add a test asserting a NULL pin_changed_at forces rotation.

findings.title: pinAgeDays header contract ('Large if unknown') contradicts the implementation ('return 0')
findings.detail: UserRepository.h:102 documents pinAgeDays as 'Days since pin_changed_at (for the 90-day rotation policy). Large if unknown.' but UserRepository.cpp:315-318 returns 0 on the unknown/NULL/query-failure path. A future reader trusting the header would assume an unknown age forces rotation, when in fact it suppresses it. This is the same root cause as the rotation-NULL bug and makes the divergence easy to reintroduce.
findings.recommendation: Make the code match the documented intent (return e.g. INT_MAX or RotationDays when unknown), or fix the comment — but the safe choice for an auth control is to honor the header and treat unknown as expired.

findings.title: No direct unit tests for Bcrypt (cost, $2y$/$2b$ interop, malformed hash, salt uniqueness)
findings.detail: Bcrypt is exercised only indirectly via PinPolicy reuse/current-hash tests, which would still pass even if the cost factor were wrong, if $2y$ interop were broken, or if hash() silently returned an empty string. There is no test asserting: hash() emits a $2b$ string at cost 12 (the header at Bcrypt.h:12 claims parity with PHP's cost 12 but nothing verifies it); a PHP-generated $2y$12$... hash verifies true here (the central migration promise in Bcrypt.h:6-8); a $2b$ hash made here verifies under the same plaintext; verify() returns false for malformed/short/'*'-prefixed stored hashes; and that two hashes of the same PIN differ (random salt). For a system whose CLAUDE.md mandates tests on the auth path and that migrates staff PIN hashes from PHP, this is the biggest test gap in the area.
findings.recommendation: Add a bcrypt_tests case: assert hash() starts with '$2b$12$' and length 60; embed a known PHP password_hash($2y$12$...) constant and assert verify(plain,hash)==true and verify(wrong,hash)==false; assert verify against a hash produced by hash(); assert verify returns false for '', 'notahash', and a truncated hash; assert hash(pin)!=hash(pin).

findings.title: No test for the 90-day rotation boundary (RotationDays is asserted nowhere)
findings.detail: The sanity block asserts MinLen/MaxLen/HistoryKeep but not RotationDays, and there is no test covering pinAgeDays() / the `>= RotationDays` decision in main.cpp:119 at all (e.g. age 89 not due, 90 due, NULL handling). Rotation is a stated security requirement and currently has the NULL bug above precisely because it is untested.
findings.recommendation: Add tests around UserRepository::pinAgeDays / the rotation decision: seed pin_changed_at at now-89d (not due), now-90d (due), now-NULL (should be due once fixed), and assert PinPolicy::RotationDays==90.

findings.title: verify() length-mismatch early-return is a minor timing/parity wrinkle
findings.detail: verify() recomputes the candidate hash, then if recomputed.size() != hashBytes.size() returns false before the constant-time XOR loop. For correctly-formed bcrypt hashes both are always 60 bytes, so this rarely fires, but it means the function is not uniformly constant-time across all stored-hash shapes and the comparison is data-length-dependent. This is low risk for local single-PC PIN auth (the salt is in the stored hash, attacker controls plaintext not the stored hash), but it deviates slightly from PHP's password_verify which is documented constant-time and is the parity reference. Note crypt_r already shortcuts to '*'+errno on malformed salts (handled at line 44), so the size check is essentially redundant defense.
findings.recommendation: Either accept as-is (document why it's safe for this threat model) or fold the size difference into the accumulator (e.g. set diff to nonzero when sizes differ, then still walk min length) to keep a single uniform path.

findings.title: crypt_data instances are stack-allocated and large
findings.detail: Both hash() and verify() declare `crypt_data data;` on the stack. glibc/libxcrypt's struct crypt_data is ~32KB (historically up to ~131KB on some libcs). It is correctly initialized (data.initialized=0) and crypt_r is the reentrant variant, so there is no correctness/threading bug. The only concern is stack footprint on threads with small stacks; the main login path is on the GUI thread so this is fine today, but if PIN hashing ever moves to a worker thread with a reduced stack it could overflow.
findings.recommendation: Optional: allocate crypt_data on the heap (or static-thread-local) if hashing is ever moved off the main thread. Harmless to leave as-is for the current single-threaded login flow; note it so it isn't copied into a thread pool later.

findings.title: hash() returns empty QString on RNG/crypt failure with no signal to the caller
findings.detail: If crypt_gensalt_rn or crypt_r fail (e.g. kernel RNG unavailable, returns NULL or '*'), hash() returns an empty QString. Callers (UserRepository PIN create/change paths at lines 56-70, 157-171, 238-260) must defend against an empty hash being written to users.pin_hash / pin_history; an empty stored hash would make verify() (Bcrypt.cpp:35) always return false, silently locking the user out or, worse, persisting an un-loginable credential. The failure is plausible-but-rare, but there is no exception/log distinguishing 'hash failed' from 'hash succeeded'.
findings.recommendation: Have callers check for empty hash and abort the transaction with a clear error (and audit-log the failure), rather than relying on downstream verify() failing. Consider logging the libxcrypt failure in hash() itself.

findings.title: No PRAGMA busy_timeout set — concurrent access yields immediate SQLITE_BUSY
findings.detail: open() sets foreign_keys and journal_mode=WAL but never sets a busy_timeout. SQLite's default busy timeout is 0, so any contention (a backup process reading the file via BackupService, the WAL checkpoint, a transient lock during AppPaths::hardenPermissions/migrateLegacyData copy, or even WAL writer-vs-checkpointer) returns SQLITE_BUSY immediately and surfaces as a hard query failure rather than a brief wait-and-retry. The single-instance QLockFile reduces cross-process contention but does not cover the in-process WAL checkpointer or external file copies. The PHP source used Postgres with a serialization-failure retry loop (Db::transaction retries on SQLSTATE 40001); the Qt port has no equivalent resiliency.
findings.recommendation: Add `PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000;` (or similar) in open() immediately after journal_mode=WAL so transient locks block-and-retry instead of failing. Optionally also wrap critical transactions in a small retry-on-SQLITE_BUSY helper to mirror the PHP retry semantics.

findings.title: Schema migrations run on a live production DB with no pre-migration backup or integrity check
findings.detail: migrate() applies ALTER TABLE / CREATE TABLE / UPDATE statements directly against the operator's production DB on startup. Each migration is transactional (good), but there is no defensive snapshot beforehand, even though a BackupService already exists in the codebase (src/MainWindow.cpp:209). If a migration fails midway on a malformed prod DB, or a future migration is wrong, there is no automatic recovery copy; the operator's only data on a single AlmaLinux PC is at risk. SQLite ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN inside a transaction can also leave a half-applied DDL state harder to reason about than DML.
findings.recommendation: Before running pending migrations on a non-fresh DB, take a timestamped file copy (reuse BackupService) and optionally run `PRAGMA integrity_check` / `PRAGMA foreign_key_check`. Refuse to migrate (or restore the copy) if a migration fails. Surface a clear error if the backup can't be made.

findings.title: isFreshDb/isFirstRun/schemaVersion ignore exec() errors and treat failure as 'no data'
findings.detail: These probes call q.exec(...) without checking the return value and infer state purely from !q.next(). If the SELECT/PRAGMA fails because the DB is locked, corrupt, or partially upgraded, isFreshDb() returns true (no 'users' row visible) and main.cpp:67 will then call bootstrap() against a non-fresh DB — bootstrap runs CREATE statements that will error, but the misclassification masks the real cause. schemaVersion() returns 0 on any PRAGMA failure, which on an existing DB would cause migrate() to attempt re-applying v1..v4 (ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN would then fail with 'duplicate column'). The distinction between 'empty DB' and 'unreadable DB' is lost.
findings.recommendation: Check q.exec() return values; on failure set m_error and propagate a distinct error (e.g. make these methods return a tri-state or signal failure to the caller) instead of silently reporting 'fresh' / 'version 0'. At minimum, log the lastError when these probes fail.

findings.title: synchronous left at WAL default (FULL) — not explicitly chosen; no durability decision documented
findings.detail: open() sets WAL but never sets PRAGMA synchronous. The CLAUDE.md/MEMORY notes call out crash safety as a production-hardening concern. With WAL the safe-and-recommended setting is usually synchronous=NORMAL (durable across app crashes, only risks the last transaction on OS/power loss, and is notably faster). Leaving it implicit means the durability/perf tradeoff is undocumented and could change with the SQLite build. For a POS that must never corrupt stock/sales, this should be a deliberate, tested choice.
findings.recommendation: Explicitly set `PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL;` (or FULL if power-loss durability of the very last sale is required) in open(), and document the rationale. Check the exec result like the other PRAGMAs.

findings.title: Migration registry assumes monotonic, gap-free ordering but does not enforce it
findings.detail: migrate() iterates migrationRegistry() and applies any entry with version > current, then sets user_version = m.version. It relies on the static vector being authored in strictly ascending order. If a future edit inserts an out-of-order or duplicate version (easy to do in a hand-maintained list), the loop would set user_version to a lower value after a higher one, or skip/re-run migrations, with no assertion to catch it. There is also no check that versions are contiguous or that current isn't already higher than the max known version (a DB from a newer build run against an older binary would silently be treated as up-to-date with no warning of a downgrade).
findings.recommendation: Add a one-time assertion/validation that registry versions are strictly increasing and start at 1; in migrate(), detect schemaVersion() > max(registry) (downgrade) and refuse with a clear error rather than proceeding.

findings.title: No test coverage for the migration runner itself (gating, idempotency, rollback, convergence)
findings.detail: Tests only call migrate() once on a fresh bootstrapped DB (run_all.cpp, smoke.cpp) and assert it returns true. There is no test that: (a) migrate() is idempotent (running twice is a no-op), (b) an existing DB at an older user_version is correctly upgraded to N and only the pending migrations run, (c) a failing statement inside a migration rolls back and leaves user_version unchanged, (d) the fresh-bootstrap path and the incremental-upgrade path converge on an identical schema (the documented invariant in the file header). Given this is a medical POS and CLAUDE.md mandates tests on schema/stock paths, the upgrade machinery is undertested.
findings.recommendation: Add a migration test module: build a v0 baseline DB, assert schemaVersion()==0, run migrate(), assert ==max and that v1..v4 columns/tables exist; run migrate() again and assert no error and version unchanged; inject a deliberately failing migration in a test fixture and assert rollback + unchanged user_version; and compare the column sets of a fresh-bootstrapped DB vs a stepwise-upgraded one.

findings.title: Comment-stripping in bootstrap() can corrupt SQL if '--' ever appears inside a string literal
findings.detail: bootstrap() strips '--' line comments by cutting each line at its first '--' BEFORE the string-aware splitter runs. The code comment asserts no '--' appears inside a string literal in the current schema, so it is safe today, but this is a latent footgun: a future schema string default like a CHECK/seed value containing '--' (e.g. a date range, a SQL fragment, or '--' in display text) would be silently truncated, producing wrong DDL/data with no error. The robust splitter immediately below already understands strings; the pre-pass undermines it.
findings.recommendation: Move comment handling into splitSqlStatements (which already tracks inString), skipping from '--' to end-of-line only when not inString, instead of a naive line-level pre-cut. Then strings containing '--' are preserved.

findings.title: open() uses the default (unnamed) connection and is not guarded against being called twice
findings.detail: addDatabase("QSQLITE") registers the default connection without a name. If open() were ever called twice (or a second Database instance constructed) Qt would emit a 'duplicate connection name' warning and replace the connection, and there is no removeDatabase on teardown. It works today because main.cpp constructs exactly one Database, but the class gives no protection or cleanup. WAL/-shm/-wal sidecar files are also not checkpointed/cleaned on shutdown.
findings.recommendation: Use a named connection, guard open() against re-entry (return early if m_db.isValid()/isOpen()), and consider a destructor that closes the connection and optionally runs `PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE)` so the DB file is self-contained for the auto-backup copy.

findings.title: Dropped invariant: no DB-level 'one OPEN session per cashier' unique index
findings.detail: Postgres phase9 adds `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX cashier_sessions_one_open_per_user ON cashier_sessions (cashier_id) WHERE status = 'OPEN'` explicitly as the 'suspenders' to the app-side check, to defend against a race producing two OPEN shifts for one cashier. The SQLite baseline has no such index. The C++ guard (SessionRepository::openSession at src/data/SessionRepository.cpp:51, via openSessionId) is a read-then-write check with no DB constraint backing it. SQLite supports partial unique indexes, so the port could mirror this 1:1. Two simultaneous open attempts (e.g. double-click, or app + a stray second instance before the single-instance lock binds) could both pass the SELECT and create duplicate OPEN sessions, corrupting Z-report/drawer reconciliation.
findings.recommendation: Add `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX "cashier_sessions_one_open_per_user" ON "cashier_sessions"("cashier_id") WHERE "status"='OPEN';` to the baseline (or a numbered migration), and handle the resulting constraint violation in openSession() as the 'already have an open session' error path. Cover with a test that attempts two opens.

findings.title: z_report_archive lacks the append-only immutability trigger present in Postgres
findings.detail: In Postgres, z_report_archive is protected by a BEFORE UPDATE OR DELETE trigger that raises 'z_report_archive is append-only' — it is explicitly described as a regulator's evidence record. The audit_log table got its no-update/no-delete triggers faithfully ported (schema_sqlite.sql:398-405), but the equally append-only z_report_archive created in migration v2 has NO equivalent RAISE(ABORT) triggers. Day-close signed reports can therefore be silently UPDATEd or DELETEd in the SQLite port, defeating the tamper-evidence guarantee. This is an inconsistent application of the same invariant within the same codebase.
findings.recommendation: In the same migration that creates z_report_archive, add BEFORE UPDATE and BEFORE DELETE triggers using the identical RAISE(ABORT) pattern already used for audit_log (schema_sqlite.sql:398-405).

findings.title: phase8 customer_cnic column not ported to sales
findings.detail: Postgres phase8 adds `sales.customer_cnic VARCHAR(20)` (used for receipts on corporate/insurance clients and controlled-drug audit trail). The SQLite sales table has customer_name/customer_phone/customer_remarks but no customer_cnic, and no migration adds it (grep finds zero references in src/). If the operator relies on CNIC capture (DRAP / insurance), this field is missing entirely. If it was deliberately dropped as out-of-scope it should be noted, but CLAUDE.md says deviations from the PHP spec are bugs unless stated.
findings.recommendation: Either add customer_cnic TEXT to sales via a migration (matching the PHP receipt/audit use), or document in the port-gap memory that CNIC capture is intentionally out of scope for the single-PC build.

findings.title: Partial-unique medicine indexes deviate from Postgres unique-without-predicate, risking soft-deleted SKU/barcode collisions on reinsert
findings.detail: Postgres init.sql declares `medicines_sku_key` as a plain UNIQUE index on sku (no WHERE) and `medicines_primary_barcode_idx` as a NON-unique index. The SQLite port instead makes both partial-unique with `WHERE deleted_at IS NULL` (citing phase8_medicines_partial_unique.sql). That phase8 file is referenced but was NOT provided among the trigger files I could read (the dir lists phase8_medicines_partial_unique.sql separately) — so I could not confirm the Postgres source actually makes barcode UNIQUE. If Postgres keeps primary_barcode merely indexed (not unique), the port has SILENTLY ADDED a uniqueness constraint on barcode that the spec does not have, which could reject legitimate duplicate-barcode medicines (combo packs, repackaged generics). Conversely the relaxed sku rule means two soft-deleted rows plus a live row can share an sku — verify history-resolution code (which joins on sku) tolerates that.
findings.recommendation: Read ../db/triggers/phase8_medicines_partial_unique.sql and confirm both the predicate AND whether primary_barcode is truly meant to be unique. Align the SQLite indexes to the actual Phase-8 semantics; add a test inserting a live + soft-deleted medicine with the same sku and barcode.

findings.title: branches.id seed value differs from Postgres ('Main' vs 'CPHC Main') — cosmetic but a spec deviation
findings.detail: Postgres seeds the default branch as name='CPHC Main'; the SQLite baseline seeds name='Main'. The comment says the first-run wizard overwrites it, so the visible impact is limited, but it is an unflagged change to a seeded value. If any code/report references the literal default branch name before the wizard runs (e.g. a receipt header on a pre-wizard test sale), the two builds diverge.
findings.recommendation: Match the Postgres seed ('CPHC Main') unless the rename to 'Main' is intentional, in which case note it.

findings.title: supplier_settled_by FK partially dropped vs Postgres; phase7 partial index on returns missing
findings.detail: Postgres phase7 adds returns.supplier_settled_by with a FK to users(id) ON UPDATE CASCADE ON DELETE SET NULL, plus a partial index `returns_supplier_settled_at_idx ... WHERE supplier_settled_at IS NOT NULL`. The SQLite migration v1 adds the three columns as bare ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN with no FK (SQLite cannot add a column-level FK via ALTER, so a referential gap is unavoidable here) and no supporting index. The FK omission is a known SQLite limitation, but it means a deleted user can leave a dangling supplier_settled_by, and the supplier-returns list query (ReturnRepository.cpp:172 ORDER BY supplier_settled_at) has no index support.
findings.recommendation: Document the unavoidable FK limitation for ALTER-added columns (or rebuild the table to add the FK), and add `CREATE INDEX returns_supplier_settled_at_idx ON returns(supplier_settled_at) WHERE supplier_settled_at IS NOT NULL` to match Postgres.

findings.title: No schema-parity test asserting SQLite baseline matches the Postgres spec
findings.detail: The four findings above (dropped session index, missing z-report trigger, missing customer_cnic, barcode-uniqueness deviation) all slipped through because there is no automated comparison between the SQLite schema and the Postgres source of truth. CLAUDE.md mandates that stock/expiry/pricing invariants be covered by tests against PHP behavior, and these are exactly the constraint surfaces that protect them. A drift test (enumerate tables/columns/CHECK lists/unique constraints in the built SQLite DB and assert the expected set, including the enum CHECK value lists which must match the Postgres ENUM members 1:1) would have caught every item here.
findings.recommendation: Add a schema-introspection test that boots a fresh DB (baseline + all migrations) and asserts the full column set, CHECK enum value lists, and unique/partial-unique indexes against a checked-in expected snapshot derived from init.sql + triggers.

findings.title: CHECK enum value lists are hand-maintained in two places with one documented escape hatch (medicines.form)
findings.detail: Every Postgres ENUM was ported to a TEXT + CHECK(... IN (...)) list, which is correct, EXCEPT medicines.form which is left as bare TEXT with the ~55-value MedicineForm list enforced only in the C++ domain layer (comment at lines 76-77). This is a defensible readability tradeoff, but it means the single most value-heavy enum has NO database-level guard: a direct SQL insert or an import path (e.g. the pending medicines_export.csv import) that bypasses the domain layer can write an arbitrary/garbage form value the rest of the app cannot render.
