The other enums are DB-protected; form is the odd one out.
findings.recommendation: Either add the CHECK list for form (it can live in one generated SQL fragment driven by the same C++ form list to keep a single source of truth), or ensure the CSV/seed import path validates form against the domain enum before insert, and add a test that rejects an invalid form.

findings.title: Receipt label date (local) diverges from stored sold_at (UTC), risking wrong prefix and cross-day collisions
findings.detail: nextReceiptNumber() builds the prefix from QDate::currentDate() (machine-local) as INV-yyyyMMdd-NNNN, and counts same-day sales with date(sold_at,'localtime')=date('now','localtime'). But the INSERT stores sold_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, which SQLite emits in UTC. In PKT (UTC+5) a sale committed between 00:00 and 05:00 local gets a receipt labelled with TODAY's local date while sold_at lands on YESTERDAY (UTC). Consequences: (a) the receipt number's date no longer matches the row's sold_at date, breaking any receipt<->date correlation and operator expectations; (b) the per-day counter (keyed on localtime) and the stored sold_at (UTC) drift, so two distinct UTC days can share one local-date prefix, increasing the chance the NNNN counter restarts while older UTC-dated rows with the same prefix still exist. PHP avoided this: it labels with server-local Ymd and counts WHERE sold_at >= CURRENT_DATE in the same (server) timezone, keeping label, counter, and stored timestamp on one clock. The analytics/report queries here further compound it by filtering date(sold_at,'localtime') against a UTC-stored, UTC-indexed column.
findings.recommendation: Pick one clock and use it everywhere on the sale path. Either store sold_at in local time (e.g. INSERT datetime('now','localtime')) so the label, the counter, sold_at, and the report date filters all agree, or keep UTC storage but derive the receipt prefix and the count from date(sold_at) without 'localtime'. Add a test that commits a sale at a simulated 02:00 local time and asserts the receipt prefix matches date(sold_at) used by the reports.

findings.title: loadReceipt groups/sums sale_items, diverging from PHP per-row receipt and mis-totalling split partial-unit lines
findings.detail: PHP's Printer::reload (../pos/backend/services/Printer.php:58-110) returns one receipt line per sale_items row, ORDER BY si.id, exposing batch_number/expiry per row. Qt's loadReceipt instead GROUPs BY (medicine_id, sold_unit_label, unit_mrp) and SUM(qty_sold_display), SUM(line_total). Two problems: (1) it drops the per-batch breakdown (batch number / expiry) the PHP receipt shows, a parity gap for a pharmacy receipt; (2) qty_sold_display is stored per batch as ceil(deduction/factor) (SaleService.cpp:291-292). When one cart line is FEFO-split across batches, summing those independently-rounded ceils overstates the displayed quantity (e.g. factor=10, 8+7 base units -> ceil(0.8)+ceil(0.7)=2 displayed for what was 1.5 packs), so the reprinted/report receipt can show a different qty than the original sale screen. The committed SaleResult lines in SaleService.cpp:334-341 use the un-split cashier-entered qty and so do NOT match what loadReceipt later reconstructs for the same sale.
findings.recommendation: Mirror PHP: SELECT per sale_items row joined to batches (batch_number, expiry_date), ORDER BY si.id, without GROUP BY/SUM, so the reprint matches the original receipt exactly. If a grouped view is desired for readability, group on stored qty_in_base_units and recompute display qty once from the summed base units, not by summing per-batch ceils. Add a test selling a quantity that FEFO-splits across two batches and assert loadReceipt qty/line_total equal the original SaleResult.

findings.title: Receipt-number uniqueness relies on dropped SERIALIZABLE + advisory lock; only a best-effort fallback remains
findings.detail: PHP guaranteed receipt uniqueness with SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE plus a per-day pg_advisory_xact_lock held until commit (Sale.php:56,386-407), then a 40001 retry-once. The Qt port (correctly, per SaleService.h's note) drops these for single-PC SQLite, keeping only: count(*) -> candidate -> 'does this exact string exist?' -> on collision, mint a random 6-digit suffix. With one serialized connection this is safe today. But the read-then-write count is not protected by the surrounding transaction under SQLite's default journal/locking the way the PHP advisory lock was, so the design is fragile if a second connection (e.g. a background report/export, or a future thread) is ever opened against the same file: two commits could read the same count and the only guard is the random-suffix fallback (which abandons the monotonic INV-...-NNNN format and is itself only probabilistically unique). There is also no UNIQUE-constraint catch-and-retry: the schema has a unique index on receipt_number (sql/schema_sqlite.sql), but a duplicate INSERT would just throw and fail the sale rather than retry a fresh number.
findings.recommendation: Document and enforce single-connection-on-the-write-path as an invariant, and/or set PRAGMA busy_timeout + use BEGIN IMMEDIATE for the sale transaction so the write lock is taken before the count is read. Better: catch the UNIQUE violation on the sales INSERT and retry nextReceiptNumber a bounded number of times before falling back, preserving the monotonic format. Add a concurrency-ish test (the existing uniq test at sale_tests.cpp:788 is sequential).

findings.title: No same-clock guarantee between nextReceiptNumber count and the surrounding transaction's other date logic; count(*) runs an unprepared exec
findings.detail: nextReceiptNumber issues q.exec(...) for the count(*) without checking the return value or q.lastError(); if the query fails (locked DB, malformed pragma state) count silently stays 0 and the candidate becomes INV-yyyyMMdd-0001, which could collide with the day's first sale. The subsequent existence check would then push it to the random fallback, but the failure is swallowed with no log. PHP read the count via Db::fetchOne which would surface a PDO error.
findings.recommendation: Check q.exec() and log/throw on failure (consistent with the rest of commit() which checks every exec). At minimum, treat a failed count query as a hard error rather than count=0.

findings.title: Void/refund status transitions on the sales row are not covered by a sale-path test, and totals exclusion is only spot-checked
findings.detail: Voiding a sale (ReturnService::voidSale) flips sales.status to VOIDED, and reports/analytics exclude VOIDED from every total (SalesReportRepository.cpp:42, AnalyticsRepository.cpp multiple). The sale-commit area writes status='COMPLETED' and the inventory_movements ledger, but there is no test asserting that after a void: (a) the SALE inventory_movements are compensated/reversed in the ledger (qty_before/qty_after restored) consistent with PHP, and (b) the report gross/net correctly drops the voided sale while refunds in range are still counted. Given this is a medical-retail stock+money path, the void-vs-ledger interaction deserves an explicit parity test.
findings.recommendation: Add tests: commit a sale, void it, then assert (1) sales.status='VOIDED', (2) batch current_qty and the inventory_movements ledger reflect the documented void semantics (matching PHP Returns/void behavior), and (3) SalesReportRepository::report excludes it from gross/cash/card but reflects any associated reversal. Compare numbers against the PHP path.

findings.title: Receipt-line name backfill issues one query per line outside the transaction and assumes res.lines index == input.items index
findings.detail: After commit, the code loops res.lines and runs a separate SELECT brand_name FROM medicines per line to fill the display name, using input.items.at(i).medicineId keyed by position. This is an N+1 query for a hot path, and it couples res.lines ordering to input.items ordering. res.lines is pushed exactly once per input line (SaleService.cpp:334-341), so the index alignment holds today, but it is fragile: if the per-line block ever pushes per-allocation lines (as the grouped/split logic might invite), the i-th medicineId lookup silently mislabels rows. The name could instead be selected once in the original batch/medicine query or via a single IN (...) query.
findings.recommendation: Fetch all needed brand_name/strength in one parameterized IN (...) query (you already gather the medicine id set at lines 132-135), or join medicines into the FEFO/select step, and map by medicineId rather than by positional index.

findings.title: discount-authorized-by self-authorization parity nuance vs PHP (managerial cashier path)
findings.detail: When a managerial cashier applies a discount and no explicit authorizer is supplied, the Qt code sets discountAuthBy = m_cashierId (self-authorize) and then writes a DISCOUNT_AUTHORIZED audit row with authorized_by = the cashier (lines 197, 362-369). PHP only writes the DISCOUNT_AUTHORIZED audit row when input['discount_authorized_by'] is non-empty (Sale.php:350), i.e. it does NOT emit a self-authorization audit entry for a managerial cashier who didn't pass an explicit authorizer. The Qt port therefore can produce an extra DISCOUNT_AUTHORIZED audit record (and stores discount_authorized_by = cashier) that the PHP spec would omit. This is an audit-trail divergence on a compliance-sensitive event.
findings.recommendation: Confirm intended behavior; if matching PHP, only set discount_authorized_by and emit the DISCOUNT_AUTHORIZED audit row when an explicit authorizer distinct from the cashier was provided. Cover with a test asserting audit rows for both the managerial-self and manager-override cases.

findings.title: addStock always INSERTs — no merge on (medicine_id, batch_number, expiry_date); will violate the unique index
findings.detail: BatchRepository.cpp:19-35 unconditionally INSERTs a new batches row. The SQLite schema (sql/schema_sqlite.sql) has UNIQUE INDEX batches_med_batch_expiry_key on (medicine_id, batch_number, expiry_date). The PHP source-of-truth Grn::post() does a find-or-create: when a batch with the same (medicine_id, batch_number, expiry_date) exists it UPDATEs received_qty/foc_qty/current_qty and refreshes cost/MRP. In the Qt port a second stock-in of the same batch+expiry hits the unique constraint, q.exec() fails, addStock rolls back and returns -1. Receiving more of an already-stocked batch (a routine pharmacy operation) is therefore impossible through this path. The grn_tests dup-batch merge passes only because that path goes through GrnService, not addStock.
findings.recommendation: Mirror Grn::post(): before insert, SELECT an existing batch by (medicine_id, batch_number, expiry_date); if found, UPDATE quantities/cost/MRP and emit the GRN_RECEIPT movement against the existing batch id with correct qty_before/qty_after; otherwise INSERT. Keep it inside the same transaction.

findings.title: No server-side validation: cost/MRP zero, inactive medicine, and past expiry are all accepted by the repo
findings.detail: addStock performs no business validation. PHP Grn::post() rejects unit_cost <= 0, mrp <= 0, batch_number empty, inactive/deleted medicines, and expiry < today. In the Qt port the only guards live in StockInDialog::accept() (StockInDialog.cpp:96-107), and even those are weaker: cost/MRP are only rejected if isNegative(), so a value of '0' or '0.0000' passes (PHP requires strictly > 0 via Money::cmp(...,'0') <= 0). The repo is also called directly from many tests and could be called from future non-UI callers (GRN Phase 4, import), none of which get the dialog's checks. Validation belongs in the domain/data layer per CLAUDE.md (business rules out of the UI).
findings.recommendation: Move the PHP validation set into addStock (or a shared validator): cost > 0, mrp > 0, batch_number non-empty, expiry >= today, medicine active and not soft-deleted. Return a typed error. Make the dialog reject zero, not just negative.

findings.title: cost_per_unit and mrp_per_unit stored as raw user strings without HALF_UP scale normalization
findings.detail: addStock binds d.costPerUnit and d.mrpPerUnit directly into the INSERT (BatchRepository.cpp:29-30). They come straight from QLineEdit text (StockInDialog.cpp:93-94) constrained only by a regex allowing up to 4 dp (cost) / 2 dp (mrp). CLAUDE.md mandates fixed-point decimal with HALF_UP rounding at every storage boundary: cost stored at scale 4, money at scale 2. A user entering '5.5' for cost stores '5.5' (not '5.5000'); '8.999' would be rejected by the regex but '2.5' for MRP stores '2.5' not '2.50'. Downstream string comparisons and PHP-parity tests assume normalized scale (the GRN path normalizes via CostBlender; this path does not), so blended-cost / display / equality can diverge from PHP.
findings.recommendation: Normalize through Money before storage: cost = Money::fromString(d.costPerUnit).toString(4) (or scale-4 round HALF_UP), mrp = Money rounded to scale 2. Add a test that stock-in of '5.5'/'2.5' persists '5.5000'/'2.50'.

findings.title: onHand() omits the expiry-date filter, overstating sellable stock vs candidateBatchesForSale() and PHP
findings.detail: onHand() (BatchRepository.cpp:97-100) filters only current_qty>0 AND is_quarantined=0 AND is_expired=0, but NOT expiry_date > date('now'). candidateBatchesForSale() (line 74-75), InventoryRepository (line 95), and the PHP MedicineSearch in_stock query all additionally require expiry_date > CURRENT_DATE. Because no ported code ever sweeps is_expired to 1 (see separate finding), a batch that has passed its expiry date but still has is_expired=0 is counted by onHand() as available yet refused by FEFO/candidateBatchesForSale(). onHand therefore reports stock that cannot actually be sold — a parity and correctness gap (e.g. low-stock/reorder math and any UI reading onHand).
findings.recommendation: Add AND expiry_date > date('now') to the onHand() WHERE clause to match the candidate/FEFO/PHP definition of sellable stock.

findings.title: is_expired flag is never set by any ported code; expiry correctness relies solely on date comparison
findings.detail: Grep shows is_expired is only ever READ across the Qt codebase (BatchRepository, InventoryRepository, SaleService, StockAdjustmentRepository) and never written. The schema carries the column and Fefo/queries honor it, but there is no sweeper that flips is_expired=1 once expiry_date passes (and the PHP side has no obvious sweeper either, suggesting it may rely on EXPIRY_WRITEOFF adjustments). The system thus depends entirely on the date('now') comparison. This is acceptable only if combined with consistent date filtering everywhere (which onHand violates) and if EXPIRY_BLOCK/quarantine handling is ported. As-is, expired-but-unflagged stock lingers in counts and there is no audit/movement marking it blocked.
findings.recommendation: Confirm the PHP behavior for is_expired transitions and port it (a sweep that flips is_expired and writes an EXPIRY_BLOCK inventory_movement, or document that date('now') is the single source of truth and make ALL queries consistent). Add a test for an expired batch.

findings.title: date('now') is UTC in SQLite vs PHP CURRENT_DATE (server local) — off-by-one expiry at day boundaries
findings.detail: candidateBatchesForSale() uses expiry_date > date('now') (BatchRepository.cpp:75). SQLite's date('now') returns the current UTC date, whereas the PHP source compares against CURRENT_DATE / new DateTimeImmutable('now') which is the server's local timezone (Pakistan is UTC+5). Near midnight local time the UTC date can be the previous day, so a batch expiring 'today' (local) may still be treated as sellable for several hours longer than in PHP, or vice-versa. For an expiry-critical pharmacy system this is a real, if narrow, divergence. Note Fefo::allocate in C++ takes today=QDate::currentDate() (local) while this SQL pre-filter uses UTC — even internally inconsistent.
findings.recommendation: Use date('now','localtime') in the SQL, or pre-filter in C++ using QDate::currentDate() consistently with Fefo. Pick one local-date source and use it in every batch query.

findings.title: Missing test coverage for addStock's own guardrails (duplicate batch, zero cost, past expiry, scale normalization)
findings.detail: All existing addStock test usages (smoke.cpp, sale_tests, adjustment_tests, etc.) call it on the happy path with distinct batch numbers and well-formed scale-4/scale-2 strings. There is no test that: (a) re-stocks the SAME (medicine, batch_number, expiry) and asserts a merge (it would currently fail by returning -1), (b) rejects cost '0', (c) rejects a past-expiry stock-in at the repo layer, (d) asserts cost persists as '5.0000' / mrp as '2.50' after passing an under-scaled string, (e) verifies onHand vs candidateBatchesForSale agree for an expired-date batch. CLAUDE.md explicitly requires tests on the quantities/pricing/batch-number/expiry paths.
findings.recommendation: Add targeted BatchRepository tests covering duplicate-batch merge, zero/negative cost+MRP rejection, past-expiry rejection, scale normalization of stored cost/MRP, and onHand/candidate parity for an expired batch.

findings.title: branch_id hardcoded to 1 in INSERTs with no constant or validation
findings.detail: addStock hardcodes branch_id=1 literally inside both the batches and inventory_movements INSERT SQL (BatchRepository.cpp:23, :42). This matches the single-branch assumption but is a magic literal embedded in SQL strings rather than a named constant, and there is no FK pre-check, so a misconfigured DB (no branch row id=1) would surface only as an opaque FK error string returned via errorString(). The audit JSON is also hand-built with QString::arg (line 56) rather than a JSON serializer, which is fragile if any field ever becomes non-numeric/string-escaped.
findings.recommendation: Hoist branch_id to a single named constant (or pass it in) shared across repositories, and build audit JSON via QJsonDocument to avoid hand-rolled escaping.

findings.title: low-stock query diverges from PHP: extra expiry_date filter changes on-hand counts
findings.detail: InventoryRepository::lowStock() LEFT JOINs batches with an extra predicate `AND b.expiry_date > date('now')` (src/data/InventoryRepository.cpp:95). The PHP source-of-truth (pos/frontend/pages/inventory/dashboard.php low-stock query, which the comment explicitly says it matches /reports/low-stock) joins only `b.current_qty > 0 AND b.is_quarantined = FALSE AND b.is_expired = FALSE` with NO date check. Consequently a batch that is past its expiry date but not yet flagged is_expired counts toward on-hand in PHP but is excluded in C++. C++ on-hand can therefore be lower than PHP, flagging MORE medicines as below reorder level than the spec does — a quantity-sensitive divergence on a pharmacy reorder screen.
findings.recommendation: Either remove the `AND b.expiry_date > date('now')` clause to match PHP exactly, or, if the intent is that low-stock should reflect sellable stock, change the PHP spec too and document the deliberate deviation in CLAUDE.md. Add a test with a past-date, is_expired=0 batch asserting the chosen behavior.

findings.title: Inconsistent definition of 'today': SQLite UTC date('now') vs QDate local time
findings.detail: lowStock() filters with SQLite `date('now')` which is UTC, while batchList() and expiringSoon() compute the cutoff and the `days` field from `QDate::currentDate()` which is the host local date (src/data/InventoryRepository.cpp:40, :81, :95, :124-125, :150). On the AlmaLinux target in Pakistan (UTC+5) these two clocks disagree for the first 5 hours of each local day, so a batch can be treated as 'expired'/'not expiring' inconsistently between screens, and the displayed `days`-to-expiry can be off by one relative to the WHERE-clause inclusion. PHP uses a single server CURRENT_DATE for everything.
findings.recommendation: Pick one clock and use it everywhere. Simplest: drive all date comparisons from QDate::currentDate() bound as a parameter (e.g. bind today.toString('yyyy-MM-dd') instead of date('now')), so SQL filtering and the computed days field agree and are in the operator's local timezone like PHP.

findings.title: batchList drops the PHP barcode/GTIN exact-match search mode
findings.detail: pos/frontend/pages/inventory/stock.php runs the query through QrParser: when the input parses as a barcode (GS1/GTIN/HIBC/etc.) it switches to an EXACT match on medicines.primary_barcode against both the 14-digit and ltrim'd 13-digit GTIN forms, instead of a LIKE. InventoryRepository::batchList() only implements the free-text LIKE branch (src/data/InventoryRepository.cpp:47-64); scanning a barcode that contains AI prefixes / Digital Link URL will not match the primary_barcode the way the PHP Stock screen does. This is a real workflow gap for a barcode-driven stock screen.
findings.recommendation: Route the search through the ported QrParser (already listed as a planned service) and add the barcode-exact branch matching gtin14/gtin13/raw, mirroring stock.php. At minimum, document the gap in the PHP-vs-Qt port-gaps memory.

findings.title: batchList LIMIT 300 vs PHP LIMIT 200
findings.detail: InventoryRepository::batchList() ends with `LIMIT 300` (src/data/InventoryRepository.cpp:56) whereas the PHP stock.php query uses `LIMIT 200`. With both ordered by expiry_date ASC, brand_name, a different cap means the Qt screen shows a different (larger) truncated set than the spec, and any operator comparing the two will see disagreement on large catalogs.
findings.recommendation: Align the cap with PHP (200) unless there is a documented reason to differ; if the larger cap is intentional, note it in the port-gaps memory.

findings.title: Query exec() return values ignored in totals() — silent zeros on SQL error
findings.detail: InventoryRepository::totals() calls q.exec(...) three times without checking the boolean result (src/data/InventoryRepository.cpp:14-32). If a statement fails (locked DB, schema drift, corrupt batch row) the code silently leaves counts/value at 0 and returns a fully-populated InventoryTotals with bogus zeros. On a money/stock screen, silently reporting 'stock at cost = 0' is dangerous and indistinguishable from genuinely empty inventory. batchList/lowStock/expiringSoon at least guard on exec() returning false, but still swallow the error with no logging.
findings.recommendation: Check each exec() result; on failure log q.lastError() (the project has a logging facility per the production-hardening memory) and surface a distinguishable error state to the caller rather than returning silent zeros.

findings.title: Money mul() can overflow int64 on aggregate stock value with no guard
findings.detail: totals() accumulates value via Money::fromString(cost).mul(qty) where Money holds value*10000 in an int64 and mul does m_units * qty with no overflow check (src/domain/Money.h:28, src/data/InventoryRepository.cpp:30-31). cost_per_unit is DECIMAL(12,4); a single batch near the 12-digit ceiling times a large current_qty, or a very large total inventory sum, can overflow silently and produce a wrong (possibly negative) stock value. Realistic pharmacy data is far from this, so severity is low, but a financial total that can silently wrap is worth a guard or a test asserting headroom.
findings.recommendation: Add an overflow-checked multiply/add in Money (or assert bounds) and a test exercising a high-value batch sum; alternatively document the safe input range.

findings.title: Missing tests for low-stock expiry-exclusion, barcode search, and timezone boundary
findings.detail: tests/cases/inventory_tests.cpp covers happy-path totals deltas, basic low-stock membership, expiring-soon windows, and ascending sort, but does NOT cover: (a) a past-date-but-unflagged batch's effect on lowStock on-hand (the divergence above), (b) any barcode/GTIN search path for batchList, (c) the LIMIT cap, or (d) date-boundary behavior (batch expiring exactly today vs date('now') in a non-UTC tz). Per CLAUDE.md, expiry and quantity paths must be covered by tests comparing against PHP behavior; these branches are exactly the quantity/expiry-sensitive ones.
findings.recommendation: Add cases: a past-date is_expired=0 batch asserting expected on-hand; an expiry-exactly-today batch asserting inclusion matches PHP's <=/> boundary; (once implemented) a barcode-search case; and a LIMIT assertion.

findings.title: expiringSoon lower-bound parity: includes already-past batches like PHP but worth confirming intent
findings.detail: expiringSoon() filters only `expiry_date <= :cutoff` with no lower bound (src/data/InventoryRepository.cpp:131), and reports negative `days` for past-date batches. This matches PHP dashboard.php (expiry_date <= CURRENT_DATE + INTERVAL '60 days', is_expired=FALSE), so behavior is faithful — including the quirk that a past-date batch not yet flagged is_expired shows up in the 'Expiring in 60 days' list with negative days. Flagging so reviewers know it is intentional parity, not a bug, and so it is not 'fixed' in a way that breaks parity.
findings.recommendation: Leave as-is for parity; add a one-line comment noting the absence of a lower bound is deliberate to match PHP, to prevent a future well-meaning 'fix'.

findings.title: listRecent() ignores the cashier-scoping that PHP enforces — cashiers see every user's returns
findings.detail: PHP pos/frontend/pages/pos/returns/history.php (lines 15-28) restricts the return history to the logged-in cashier with `WHERE r.initiated_by = :c` and only shows all rows when the session role is MANAGER or ADMIN. The Qt ReturnRepository::listRecent(int limit) takes no user id or role and runs an unfiltered `SELECT ... FROM returns ... ORDER BY r.id DESC LIMIT ?`. ReturnsPage::reloadRecent() (src/ui/ReturnsPage.cpp:606-609) calls repo.listRecent() unconditionally for all roles. Result: a plain cashier in the Qt app sees every cashier's returns (refund amounts, reasons, receipts), a behavior change vs the source-of-truth PHP app. This is a segregation-of-duties / data-visibility regression on a medical-retail refund ledger.
findings.recommendation: Add an optional initiatedBy/role parameter to listRecent (mirror history.php: managers/admins see all, cashiers see only `r.initiated_by = :uid`). Pass the current user id and role from ReturnsPage when populating the recent table.

findings.title: All four query methods silently swallow exec() failures and return empty results
findings.detail: Every method uses the pattern `if (q.exec()) { ... }` (or `if (!q.exec() || !q.next()) return hdr;`) and silently returns an empty header/vector on failure, with no logging of q.lastError(). listSupplierReturns() in particular selects migration-added columns (supplier_settled_at, supplier_reference — added in Database.cpp v1 migration, absent from the schema_sqlite.sql baseline at sql/schema_sqlite.sql:263). If that migration ever fails to run (e.g. a DB restored from a pre-migration snapshot, or a future baseline refactor), the query errors and the supplier-settlement queue silently shows ZERO rows instead of surfacing an error — supplier-credit returns would quietly disappear from the operator's view. Same risk for a typo'd column or a failed lookup query masquerading as 'no sale found'.
findings.recommendation: Log q.lastError().text() (via the project logger) on every failed exec before returning empty, and consider distinguishing 'query error' from 'no rows' so the UI can show a real error rather than an empty/Not-found state.

findings.title: listPending() and listSupplierReturns() have no test coverage
findings.detail: tests/cases/returns_tests.cpp exercises lookupByReceipt (including the unpadded INV-...-N suffix path and the not-found/blank cases) and listRecent (return number, qty, refund 4 x 8.00 = 32.00, status, linked receipt). But listPending() and listSupplierReturns() are not referenced anywhere under tests/ . These two feed the manager adjudication queue and the supplier-settlement queue — both adjudication-critical screens — and listSupplierReturns depends on migration-added columns plus a non-trivial `ORDER BY (r.supplier_settled_at IS NOT NULL), r.id DESC` and a `settled = !value.isNull()` derivation that should be pinned by a test (insert a RETURN_TO_SUPPLIER row, mark settled, assert ordering/settled flag/supplierReference).
findings.recommendation: Add cases that seed PENDING_REVIEW and RETURN_TO_SUPPLIER returns (settled and unsettled) and assert listPending ordering/fields and listSupplierReturns ordering, settled flag, settledAt, and supplierReference.

findings.title: listRecent ORDER BY r.id DESC diverges from PHP's ORDER BY r.created_at DESC
findings.detail: history.php orders by `r.created_at DESC LIMIT 100`; the Qt listRecent orders by `r.id DESC LIMIT ?`. For an AUTOINCREMENT id these usually coincide, but they can differ if created_at is ever back-dated/imported or if rows are inserted out of timestamp order during a data migration. Also the default limit is 200 here vs PHP's hard 100, a small parity difference in how much history is shown. Low impact, but it is a behavioral deviation from the spec on a screen whose ordering the operator relies on.
findings.recommendation: Order by r.created_at DESC, r.id DESC to match PHP and provide a stable tiebreak; align the default limit with the PHP page (100) unless a larger window is intentional.

findings.title: lookupByReceipt uses LEFT JOIN users while PHP uses INNER JOIN — cosmetic but masks data integrity
findings.detail: PHP initiate.php joins `sales s JOIN users u ON u.id = s.cashier_id` (INNER); the Qt query uses `LEFT JOIN users u` with COALESCE(u.full_name,''). cashier_id is a NOT NULL FK, so in practice the row always matches. The LEFT JOIN is harmless for output but it papers over a would-be FK-integrity violation (orphaned cashier) by showing a blank cashier instead of failing to find the sale, a subtle behavioral divergence. Minor; flagging for parity/clarity.
findings.recommendation: Use INNER JOIN users to match the PHP source-of-truth, or document the intentional deviation in a comment.

findings.title: lookupByReceipt returns full returnable lines even for VOIDED / REFUNDED_FULL sales; guard lives only in UI
findings.detail: PHP initiate.php actively refuses to open a VOIDED/REFUNDED_FULL receipt (lines 123-127: flash error + redirect to /pos/history before listing items). The Qt repo always returns the header + all returnable lines regardless of status; the only thing stopping a refund is ReturnsPage disabling buttons when hdr.status is VOIDED/REFUNDED_FULL (src/ui/ReturnsPage.cpp:430-433,491-493). The write path (ReturnService) presumably re-checks, so this is defence-in-depth rather than an exploit, but the read layer hands the UI 'returnable' lines for sales that are not returnable — easy to misuse from a future caller that doesn't replicate the UI guard.
findings.recommendation: Either skip building lines (or set a clear non-returnable flag) when status is VOIDED/REFUNDED_FULL in the repo, or document that callers must honor the status gate as the UI does.

findings.title: lookupByReceipt suffix-padding logic is duplicated from PHP and subtly differs on multi-dash receipts
findings.detail: PHP builds the candidate via explode('-')/array_pop (operates on the last dash-segment) and pads when `ctype_digit($last) && strlen($last) < 4`. Qt uses lastIndexOf('-') and pads when the tail is all-digit and `tail.size() < 4`. These agree for the canonical INV-YYYYMMDD-NNNN format, but the two implementations are independent copies of a parsing rule that defines whether a customer's typed receipt matches — if the receipt-number format ever changes, both must be updated in lockstep. There is no shared helper, raising drift risk on a customer-facing lookup.
findings.recommendation: Extract the receipt-candidate generation into one shared utility used by both lookup and any other receipt-matching code, and add a focused unit test for multi-segment / already-padded / non-numeric-suffix inputs.

findings.title: GRN DRAFT/CANCELLED lifecycle dropped entirely — only POSTED is ever produced, status machine unimplemented
findings.detail: PHP Grn.php has three operations: createDraft() (inserts status='DRAFT'), post() (DRAFT→POSTED with re-read FOR UPDATE guard), and cancelDraft() (DRAFT→CANCELLED with audit). The Qt port collapses this to a single post() that hard-codes status='POSTED' in the INSERT and never writes DRAFT or CANCELLED. There is no createDraft, no cancelDraft, and no way to reach the CANCELLED state at all. The SQLite schema still carries the GrnStatus CHECK('DRAFT','POSTED','CANCELLED') and a default of 'DRAFT', and grn_documents_status_idx exists, implying the states were intended to be reachable. GrnRepository.list() will therefore never surface a DRAFT or CANCELLED row produced by the app. The header comment acknowledges this is intentional ('can be layered back on later'), but for a production-readiness audit it is a real port-parity gap: users cannot stage/cancel a receipt, and any imported PHP data with DRAFT/CANCELLED rows is unmanageable from the UI.
findings.recommendation: Either implement createDraft/post/cancelDraft to match PHP, or explicitly document the single-step decision in CLAUDE.md/PHP_APP_MAP.md as an accepted scope reduction and confirm no migrated data relies on the other states. If kept single-step, drop the now-dead DEFAULT 'DRAFT' so the schema does not imply a workflow the app cannot drive.

findings.title: grn_number generation has a TOCTOU race and the fallback can still collide / abort the whole post
findings.detail: nextGrnNumber() does SELECT count(*) for today, then probes GRN-YYYYMMDD-NNNN for 3 attempts, then falls back to a random 6-digit suffix. It is called AFTER m_db.transaction() begins (line 68), but the uniqueness is only enforced by the grn_documents_number_key UNIQUE index at INSERT time. Between the SELECT/probe and the INSERT, nothing reserves the number. On a single-PC SQLite build concurrent writers are unlikely, but WAL is enabled (Database.cpp:27) and a second connection (e.g. a report/export thread, or a future multi-window UI) could insert the same number; the loser's INSERT fails the UNIQUE constraint and the entire GRN post aborts with a raw SQLite error surfaced to the cashier. PHP mitigated this with SERIALIZABLE isolation; the Qt port has no equivalent and no retry-on-unique-violation around the INSERT. The random fallback also has no uniqueness check at all, so it can itself collide.
findings.recommendation: Wrap the INSERT in a retry loop that, on a UNIQUE-constraint failure for grn_number, regenerates the number and retries a bounded number of times; verify the random fallback against the table too. Alternatively derive the number from the just-inserted autoincrement id (insert with a placeholder, then UPDATE grn_number = printf('GRN-%s-%04d', date, id)) so it is collision-free by construction.

findings.title: received_qty merge semantics diverge from PHP and the divergence is untested
findings.detail: On a duplicate batch (same medicine+batch#+expiry) the Qt UPDATE sets received_qty = received_qty + delta, while PHP sets received_qty = current_qty + delta. The inline comment calls the PHP behavior 'a quirk that mis-tracks cumulative receipts once stock is sold' and intentionally changes it. This is a behavioral deviation from the source-of-truth spec on a stock-tracking column, which CLAUDE.md says must match PHP bit-for-bit unless explicitly sanctioned. The Qt behavior is arguably more correct, but: (a) it is a silent semantic change to a pharmacy stock field, and (b) grn_tests.cpp test case 4 only asserts current_qty (onHand==5) after the dup merge — it never asserts received_qty, and there is no test that sells stock and then re-receives to exercise the exact case where Qt and PHP differ. So the one place the port knowingly disagrees with the spec has zero coverage proving the chosen value is right.
findings.recommendation: Get the deviation explicitly blessed (note it in CLAUDE.md / the port-gaps memory) and add a regression test: receive a batch, sell part of it (current_qty drops), re-receive the same batch key, and assert received_qty equals the cumulative lifetime receipts (and current_qty the running balance). Lock in the intended numbers so a future refactor cannot silently revert to the PHP formula.

findings.title: No double-post / idempotency guard; the PHP FOR UPDATE re-read protection is absent
findings.detail: Because the port always creates a fresh POSTED document per call, the specific PHP protection — re-read status FOR UPDATE inside the txn so two concurrent posts of the same draft cannot both pass the DRAFT check and double-receive stock, plus DELETE FROM grn_lines for idempotent re-post — has no analogue. In the single-step model there is no draft to re-post, so the exact PHP bug is sidestepped, but the new model introduces its own hazard: if the cashier double-clicks Post (the GrnDialog.postGrn button is not disabled while the service runs, GrnDialog.cpp:162) the service can run twice and receive the same physical stock twice as two separate GRNs, with no detection. Worth a guard since this touches stock quantities.
findings.recommendation: Disable the Post button (or set a busy flag) for the duration of GrnService::post in GrnDialog.cpp, and/or block re-entry in the service. Consider a soft duplicate check on (supplier_id, invoice_number) before posting to warn on an obviously repeated invoice.

findings.title: mrp_per_base_unit stored at scale-4 into a column that is scale-2 in the source schema
findings.detail: grn_lines.mrp_per_base_unit is DECIMAL(12,2) in the Postgres source schema (db/schema/init.sql) but the Qt code inserts CostBlender::mrpPerBaseUnit(...) which is computed and returned at ScaleCost (4 dp). The SQLite column is TEXT and stores the full 4-dp string verbatim, so the value persisted ('8.0000') differs from what the PHP/Postgres pipeline would store ('8.00' after the column's scale-2 coercion). PHP also computes mrp at scale 4 but Postgres rounds it to 2 on insert; SQLite does not, so the stored representation diverges. Low impact (it is a per-base reference MRP and grn_lines is rarely re-read for math), but it is a quiet scale mismatch on a money/MRP field that the money-fidelity rule cares about.
findings.recommendation: Round mrp_per_base_unit to ScaleMoney (2) before inserting into grn_lines to match the column semantics, or change the SQLite column comment/scale to scale-4 deliberately and document it. Add an assertion in grn_tests for the stored grn_lines.mrp_per_base_unit string.

findings.title: Audit detail JSON is hand-built with string interpolation rather than escaped
findings.detail: The GRN_POSTED audit row builds its JSON detail via QStringLiteral("{\"grn_number\":\"%1\",...}").arg(grnNumber, subtotalStr). grn_number and subtotal are system-generated and safe today, but this is fragile: any future field carrying user text (e.g. notes, invoice_number, supplier name) interpolated the same way would produce invalid JSON or allow audit-record JSON injection. Since the audit_log is the compliance trail, malformed/forgeable detail is a maintainability and integrity smell even if currently benign.
findings.recommendation: Build the audit detail with QJsonObject/QJsonDocument(Compact) so values are always escaped, and route all Audit::write detail payloads through it. This also future-proofs adding notes/invoice fields to the audit detail.

findings.title: GrnRepository.list has no pagination/filtering and re-runs a correlated line-count subquery per row
findings.detail: list() hard-caps at LIMIT 200 (default) with ORDER BY id DESC and a correlated scalar subquery SELECT count(*) FROM grn_lines WHERE l.grn_id = g.id per returned row. grn_lines_grn_id_idx exists so each subquery is cheap, but there is no status filter, no supplier filter, no date range, and no offset — the purchasing list can only ever show the newest 200 documents with no way to find older ones. The PHP GRN list screen (routes /inventory/grn) supports browsing the full history. For a pharmacy that posts GRNs regularly this becomes a parity/UX gap within months of use, and the fixed cap silently hides records.
findings.recommendation: Add optional filters (supplier, status, date range, free-text invoice/grn-number) and pagination/offset to GrnRepository::list to match the PHP list screen; replace the per-row correlated count with a single LEFT JOIN ... GROUP BY if the row count grows. Surface a 'showing newest N' indicator in PurchasingPage.

findings.title: Test coverage gaps: duplicate-batch cost re-blend, multi-line shared-batch, and grn_documents money/scale assertions
findings.detail: grn_tests.cpp covers the happy paths and validation rejections well, but misses several GRN-document/line behaviors: (1) the dup-batch case asserts only quantity, not the re-blended cost_per_unit/mrp_per_unit after the second receipt (the UPDATE overwrites cost with the new line's blended cost — a stock-cost behavior that should be pinned); (2) no test that two lines in the same GRN target the same batch key and that qtyBefore/qtyAfter in the second movement reflect the first line's increment within the same transaction; (3) no assertion on the persisted grn_documents.subtotal/grand_total strings or grn_lines.line_total/unit_cost/mrp_per_base_unit stored values (only the returned res.subtotal and on-hand are checked); (4) no test that a posted GRN's inventory_movements qty_before/qty_after chain is consistent. Given these are the money/stock/expiry paths CLAUDE.md mandates testing, the document/line-level persisted values deserve explicit pins.
findings.recommendation: Extend grn_tests.cpp: assert cost_per_unit after a dup-batch re-receive, add a same-GRN same-batch two-line case asserting the second movement's qty_before == first line's qty_after, and read back grn_documents/grn_lines columns to assert the exact stored decimal strings. Mirror the corresponding PHP fixtures so the bit-for-bit claim is demonstrable.

findings.title: Lost-update / TOCTOU on current_qty: C++ adjuster drops the PHP FOR UPDATE row lock
findings.detail: PHP reads the batch with `SELECT ... FROM batches WHERE id = :id FOR UPDATE` (StockAdjuster.php:42-48) so the row is write-locked for the whole transaction; the qtyBefore -> qtyAfter compute-and-write is atomic. The C++ port does a plain `SELECT ... FROM batches WHERE id = ?` inside `m_db.transaction()`, which under SQLite's default DEFERRED transaction acquires only a SHARED read lock and does not escalate to RESERVED until the first write (the INSERT). Between the SELECT and the UPDATE, a second connection can read the same current_qty, so two concurrent adjustments (e.g. the POS sale path decrementing the same batch, or two adjustment windows) can both compute from the same qtyBefore and the later UPDATE silently overwrites the earlier one, while both inventory_movements rows record the same stale qty_before. This violates the ledger invariant (qty_after of one == qty_before of the next) and can leave stock wrong. Single-PC reduces but does not eliminate the risk (multiple windows / the sale + adjust paths share the DB).
findings.recommendation: Begin the transaction in IMMEDIATE/EXCLUSIVE mode (e.g. issue `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` via QSqlQuery before the reads, instead of QSqlDatabase::transaction() which emits a deferred BEGIN), so the writer lock is taken before the qty read. Add a concurrent-adjustment test (two transactions on one batch) asserting the second sees the first's committed qty and that the movement ledger chains correctly.

findings.title: Adjustment-number minting race: pg_advisory_xact_lock not reproduced
findings.detail: PHP serializes number minting with a per-day `pg_advisory_xact_lock` held for the rest of the transaction (StockAdjuster.php:130-150) so two concurrent adjustments cannot both read count()==N and mint identical ADJ-YYYYMMDD-NNNN. The C++ port has no lock: it does `SELECT count(*)` then probes 3 sequential candidates, falling back to a random 6-digit suffix. The unique index stock_adjustments_adjustment_number_key will reject a true collision, but the failing INSERT then aborts the entire transaction and surfaces as a generic error (ins.lastError) with no retry — the user sees a spurious 'rejected' for a perfectly valid adjustment. The count()-based scheme is also wrong if same-day rows were deleted (count drifts below the max suffix).
findings.recommendation: Take BEGIN IMMEDIATE (see prior finding) so the count()->insert sequence is serialized by the write lock, OR derive the suffix from `MAX(suffix)+1` rather than COUNT(*), and on a UNIQUE-violation INSERT retry the mint a few times instead of aborting. Add a test for duplicate-number handling.

findings.title: listRecent uses INNER JOINs on medicines/batches — adjustments vanish if a referenced row is gone
findings.detail: The history query INNER JOINs medicines and batches (`JOIN medicines m`, `JOIN batches b`). stock_adjustments.batch_id/medicine_id are NOT NULL with FKs, so today every adjustment has both. But the audit/ledger intent is that adjustments are an append-only record; if a batch or medicine is ever hard-deleted (no ON DELETE CASCADE is declared, so a delete would normally fail — but only if PRAGMA foreign_keys is actually ON for that connection), the corresponding adjustment rows would silently disappear from the 'Recent adjustments' list rather than show with a placeholder. For an auditable medical-retail history that is a quiet data-loss-in-view bug.
findings.recommendation: Use LEFT JOINs and COALESCE the medicine/batch display to a placeholder (e.g. '(deleted batch)'), matching the append-only intent of the adjustments record. Confirm PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON is set on this connection regardless.

findings.title: Repository LIMIT binding has no upper bound / negative guard
findings.detail: listRecent(int limit) binds the caller-supplied limit straight into LIMIT ?. The only caller passes a constant 200, so it is safe today, but the signature is public and a negative value binds as a negative LIMIT (SQLite treats negative LIMIT as unlimited), and a huge value would load the entire table into memory and build that many QTableWidgetItems. There is no pagination on the Recent table.
findings.recommendation: Clamp limit to a sane [1, N] range inside the method, or document the contract. Longer term, consider an offset/keyset paged query for the history table since adjustments grow unbounded.

findings.title: Cost impact is captured at adjust-time cost_per_unit but is not re-validated; no test pins scale-4 cost rounding
findings.detail: costImpact = Money::fromString(cost_per_unit).mul(|qtyDelta|).toString(ScaleMoney). This mirrors PHP's Money::round(Money::mul(cost, |delta|), 2). The existing test only covers a clean case (10 * 5.0000 = 50.00). There is no test for a scale-4 cost that forces HALF_UP rounding at the scale-2 storage boundary (e.g. cost_per_unit 0.3333 * 3 = 0.9999 -> 1.00, or 0.1250 * 1 -> 0.13 vs 0.12), which is exactly the money-path bit-for-bit guarantee CLAUDE.md mandates. cost_impact is also nullable in schema (DECIMAL(12,2)) but the port always writes a value — verify cost_per_unit being NULL/empty doesn't silently produce '0.00' divergent from PHP.
findings.recommendation: Add an adjustment test with a 4-dp cost that exercises HALF_UP rounding to scale 2 and compare against the PHP Money result. Confirm behavior when cost_per_unit is NULL.

findings.title: Hand-rolled audit JSON does not escape control characters < 0x20
findings.detail: The audit before/after payload is built by string interpolation through jesc(), which escapes only ", \, \n, \r, \t. Other control characters (e.g. 0x00-0x08, 0x0B, 0x0C, 0x1B) pass through unescaped, producing invalid JSON in audit_log if they ever appear. The interpolated fields here (adjustment_number, reason) are controlled enums/format strings so the practical risk is low, but this jesc pattern is reused and is fragile; notes are not part of this payload but could be in future.
findings.recommendation: Build the audit JSON with QJsonObject/QJsonDocument (which escapes correctly) rather than printf-style interpolation, or extend jesc to emit \u00XX for all control chars < 0x20.

findings.title: No audit row written when an adjustment is rejected (PHP parity is the same, but a rejected stock change still warrants a trail)
findings.detail: Validation failures (zero delta, bad reason, quarantine block, would-go-negative) return an error with no audit_log entry — matching PHP, which also only audits on success. For a controlled-substance-capable pharmacy this means attempted negative/oversize write-offs leave no record. Flagged as info because it is faithful to the source-of-truth, not a regression; raise only if the business wants attempted-adjustment logging beyond PHP behavior.
findings.recommendation: If desired beyond PHP parity, log rejected attempts at a lower audit action; otherwise leave as-is to preserve parity.

findings.title: Soft-delete auto-restore workflow not ported (re-adding a deleted SKU/barcode is wrongly rejected)
findings.detail: The PHP source (pos/frontend/pages/inventory/medicines.php:155-205) treats a collision with a SOFT-DELETED medicine as an auto-restore, not an error: it converts the INSERT into an UPDATE of the deleted row that clears deleted_at and applies the new data, keeping the SAME id so all historical references (batches, sales, inventory_movements, audit) keep resolving. It only errors if a live row collides, or if SKU and barcode point to two DIFFERENT deleted rows. The Qt port has no equivalent: skuInUse()/barcodeInUse() filter to live rows only (deleted_at IS NULL), and MedicineDialog rejects with 'SKU is already used' only on live collisions — but if the operator re-adds a previously deleted medicine, create() hits the partial-unique index... which also excludes deleted rows, so the INSERT actually SUCCEEDS and creates a NEW id, orphaning the old deleted row's batch/sale history under a different medicine_id. PHP would have revived the original id. This silently forks inventory history.
findings.recommendation: Add a restoreOrCreate path: before INSERT, look up a soft-deleted row by sku and (if present) barcode; if found and both point to the same id, UPDATE that row setting deleted_at=NULL and apply the draft (audit as MEDICINE_RESTORED); if they point to two different deleted ids, return a friendly error matching PHP. Cover with a test that deletes, then re-adds the same SKU and asserts the id is preserved.

findings.title: Admin catalog on-hand diverges from PHP (extra expiry_date filter)
findings.detail: list() computes on_hand as SUM(current_qty) over batches with current_qty>0 AND is_quarantined=0 AND is_expired=0 AND b.expiry_date > date('now'). The PHP admin medicines list (pos/frontend/pages/inventory/medicines.php:349-351) does NOT include the expiry_date predicate — it sums current_qty>0 AND is_quarantined=FALSE AND is_expired=FALSE only. So a batch that is physically on the shelf and not yet flagged is_expired but whose expiry_date has just passed counts as on-hand in PHP but is hidden in the Qt admin catalog. The admin list is meant to show physical/book stock (including soon-to-be/just-expired-but-unflagged), distinct from the POS sellable view. This makes the catalog on-hand column understate stock vs the source app.
findings.recommendation: Remove the 'AND b.expiry_date > date('now')' clause from the list() on_hand subquery to match PHP exactly (keep current_qty>0, is_quarantined=0, is_expired=0). The POS searchForPos subquery should keep its expiry filter (PHP keeps it there). Add a test that stocks a batch with a past expiry_date but is_expired=0 and asserts list() on_hand includes it while searchForPos in_stock excludes it.

findings.title: Audit records drop before-value and never emit MEDICINE_RESTORED
findings.detail: PHP captures the full prior row as before_value JSON on update (Audit::write(... $before, ['sku'=>..., 'brand_name'=>...])) and distinguishes MEDICINE_RESTORED from MEDICINE_UPDATED. The Qt create/update/softDelete pass an empty before-value and only {"sku":...} as after-value (no brand_name), and there is no RESTORED action. Audit.cpp supports beforeJson but the repo never reads the old row to populate it. For a medical-retail audit trail this loses who-changed-what detail (e.g. price/control-schedule edits) that the PHP app preserves, weakening compliance review.
findings.recommendation: In update(), SELECT the existing row first and pass it as beforeJson; include brand_name in afterJson to match PHP. Emit MEDICINE_RESTORED when reviving a soft-deleted row. Keep the JSON shape consistent with the PHP audit_log entries.

findings.title: create/update INSERT and Audit::write are not wrapped in a transaction
findings.detail: create() and update() run the medicine INSERT/UPDATE and the subsequent Audit::write as two independent statements with no surrounding transaction. CLAUDE.md mandates that every multi-statement change be wrapped in a transaction. If Audit::write fails (e.g. audit_log constraint, disk error) the medicine row is already committed, producing a stock-catalog change with no audit record — exactly the kind of gap the audit guardrail exists to prevent. The return value also ignores Audit::write's bool, so a failed audit is invisible.
findings.recommendation: Wrap the INSERT/UPDATE plus Audit::write in QSqlDatabase::transaction()/commit(), rolling back and returning failure if either step fails. Check Audit::write's return value.

findings.title: No enum/length validation at the repository layer; SQLite schema has no CHECK on form
findings.detail: The SQLite schema deliberately omits a CHECK on the form column ('enforced in the C++ domain layer'), but the only enforcement is in MedicineDialog::accept (MedicineForm::isValid). MedicineRepository::create/update perform no validation of form, controlled_schedule, tax_code_value, units_per_purchase>=1, or field lengths. Any other caller (e.g. CatalogImporter at src/data/CatalogImporter.cpp, or future code) can write an invalid form string or an over-length sku/brand (Postgres had VARCHAR(40)/(160) limits; SQLite TEXT does not), which would round-trip into the DB and only surface as a corrupt row. PHP validates these server-side in the page controller regardless of the UI.
findings.recommendation: Move enum/length/units validation into the repository (or a shared MedicineDraft::validate()) so all write paths enforce it, mirroring the PHP controller checks (form/schedule/tax in allowed sets, sku<=40, brand/generic<=160, units_per_purchase>=1, reorder>=0). Optionally add the CHECK lists to the schema for defense in depth.

findings.title: Admin list() search lacks the GTIN-14/13 normalization branch the POS/PHP admin uses
findings.detail: searchForPos() correctly parses a scanned barcode and matches primary_barcode IN (:g14,:g13). The admin list() does NOT — it only LIKEs the raw string against brand/generic/sku/manufacturer/barcode. PHP's admin medicines page (medicines.php:315-324) DOES include the scan branch: when the query parses as a barcode it matches primary_barcode IN (:gtin14, :gtin13) OR = :raw. So scanning a 13-digit EAN in the admin catalog finds nothing in Qt when the row stores the 14-digit GTIN-padded form, whereas PHP normalizes and finds it.
findings.recommendation: Mirror the searchForPos barcode-scan branch in list(): when Barcode::parse(q).isBarcode, add primary_barcode IN (:g14,:g13) to the OR group. Reuse the existing parse logic.

findings.title: Both POS and admin barcode search omit the raw-GS1-verbatim match (primary_barcode = :raw)
findings.detail: PHP MedicineSearch (and the admin page) match the scanned barcode against primary_barcode IN (:g14,:g13) OR primary_barcode = :raw — the :raw clause covers legacy rows where the full GS1 string (with AIs) was stored verbatim in primary_barcode. The Qt searchForPos only binds :g14/:g13 (the parsed GTIN forms) and drops the raw-input match entirely. Rows seeded with a verbatim GS1 string in primary_barcode will not be found by scan in the Qt port even though PHP finds them. Given the 318-row Postgres seed pending import, some rows may carry verbatim barcodes.
findings.recommendation: Add the raw-input term (primary_barcode = :raw bound to the trimmed query) to the searchForPos and list() barcode branches, matching PHP. Add a test with a medicine whose primary_barcode is a full GS1 string and assert it is found by scanning that string.

findings.title: list() LIMIT 200 vs PHP LIMIT 100 (and no test asserting cap/order)
findings.detail: The admin list() caps at LIMIT 200 while PHP medicines.php caps at LIMIT 100. Minor parity drift; with 318 seed rows an empty-query catalog view shows up to 200 rows in Qt vs 100 in PHP, changing which medicines are visible/hidden. No test covers the limit or the ORDER BY brand_name behavior, and no test exercises the manufacturer/barcode LIKE columns of list() (the existing test only searches by sku substring).
findings.recommendation: Decide on the intended cap (match PHP's 100 unless product wants more) and document it. Add tests for ORDER BY and for search hits via manufacturer and barcode columns.

findings.title: Supplier DML and audit_log write are not in a single transaction
findings.detail: create(), update(), and softDelete() execute the suppliers INSERT/UPDATE and then call Audit::write() as two separate auto-committed SQLite statements. There is no QSqlDatabase::transaction()/commit() wrapping them. If the supplier write succeeds but the audit insert fails (Audit::write returns bool, which is ignored here), the supplier change is persisted with no audit record. CLAUDE.md explicitly requires 'wrap every multi-statement change in a transaction' and 'reproduce who-did-what-when for sales and stock adjustments'; supplier master edits feed every GRN and belong on that audit trail. The PHP app runs inside its request/DB layer; the port must add an explicit transaction.
findings.recommendation: Wrap each mutating method in db.transaction() ... if (!Audit::write(...)) { db.rollback(); return failure; } db.commit(). Treat a false return from Audit::write as a hard failure and roll back the supplier change.

findings.title: payment_terms no longer validated against the PHP allowlist
findings.detail: PHP suppliers/index.php defines $TERMS_OK = ['CASH','CREDIT_7','CREDIT_15','CREDIT_30','CREDIT_45','CREDIT_60','CREDIT_90','COD','ADVANCE'] and coerces any value not in that set to 'CASH'. The C++ repo only replaces an EMPTY term with 'CASH' and otherwise stores the raw string verbatim. SupplierDialog uses an EDITABLE QComboBox (setEditable(true)) offering just 4 of the 9 terms, so a user can type any free-text term and it is persisted unchecked. This diverges from the spec and lets invalid terms flow into GRN defaults; the schema column is plain VARCHAR(60) with no CHECK, so the DB will not catch it either.
findings.recommendation: Port the $TERMS_OK allowlist into the repo (the trust boundary) and coerce any value not in the set to 'CASH', exactly as PHP does. Also offer all 9 terms in SupplierDialog or make the combo non-editable.

findings.title: update() reports success when no row matched
findings.detail: The UPDATE has '... WHERE id=? AND deleted_at IS NULL'. If the id does not exist or the supplier is already soft-deleted, q.exec() still succeeds (0 rows affected) and the method returns true, then writes a SUPPLIER_UPDATED audit row for a change that never happened. The caller (SupplierDialog) shows a success and reloads, masking the no-op. softDelete() has the same property.
findings.recommendation: Check q.numRowsAffected() == 0 after exec and return false with an error like 'Supplier no longer exists', and skip the audit write in that case. Apply the same guard to softDelete().

findings.title: No tests for supplier CRUD, uniqueness, or terms coercion
findings.detail: Grep across tests/ shows grn_tests.cpp and returns_tests.cpp but nothing for suppliers. There is no coverage for: case-insensitive duplicate-name rejection (create and update self-exclusion), payment_terms defaulting/coercion, NULL-vs-empty handling via the nz() helper, soft-delete filtering in list()/find(), or the LIKE ESCAPE search. CLAUDE.md requires tests on critical paths and suppliers are referenced by every GRN. A regression in the uniqueness or terms logic would silently corrupt the supplier-returns workflow (the PHP comment at lines 34-44 calls this out explicitly).
findings.recommendation: Add tests/cases/supplier_tests.cpp covering duplicate detection (incl. case-insensitive and update self-exclusion), terms allowlist coercion, NULL handling, and that list()/find() exclude soft-deleted rows.

findings.title: Audit after_value payload dropped vs PHP
findings.detail: PHP calls Audit::write(..., null, ['name' => $name]) recording the supplier name in the after_value JSON. The C++ calls pass no before/after JSON, so the audit rows carry only entity_id with no human-readable context. Audit::write supports beforeJson/afterJson parameters that are simply not used here.
findings.recommendation: Pass an afterJson like {"name":"..."} on create/update to match PHP, and ideally a beforeJson snapshot on update/delete (read the existing row first) for a useful audit trail.

findings.title: Name length not enforced at the repository trust boundary
findings.detail: PHP enforces mb_strlen($name) > 160 server-side (the schema is VARCHAR(160)). SupplierDialog sets m_name->setMaxLength(160) in the UI, but the repo — the real trust boundary and the layer tests would target — performs no length check. SQLite does not enforce VARCHAR length, so an over-160 name from any future caller or import path would be stored, unlike Postgres/PHP which reject it.
findings.recommendation: Validate name non-empty and length <= 160 in create()/update() (mirroring PHP), returning a clear error, rather than relying on the dialog.

findings.title: Duplicate-name check is a TOCTOU with no DB-level unique guarantee
findings.detail: create() does a SELECT-then-INSERT for the duplicate-name check with no surrounding transaction, and the schema has no unique index on lower(name) (suppliers_pkey is the only constraint; there is only a non-unique name/is_active/deleted_at index). On a single-PC SQLite app the race window is small, but the application-level uniqueness the PHP comment relies on for supplier-returns integrity has no database backstop.
findings.recommendation: Perform the dup check and insert inside one transaction (covered by the fix above), and consider a partial unique index on lower(name) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL in the SQLite schema to enforce it at the DB layer.

findings.title: Manager-PIN override has no rate limiting (brute-forceable), unlike the PHP spec
findings.detail: verifyManagerOverride() (UserRepository.cpp:443-492) bcrypt-verifies the entered PIN against every active MANAGER/ADMIN and returns ok on first match, with no throttle. The PHP source of truth (../pos/backend/services/ManagerOverride.php:32-39) rate-limits per 'override:<action>:<ip>' key (5 attempts / 15 min) BEFORE scanning, and audits OVERRIDE_RATE_LIMITED. Worse, the C++ comment at UserRepository.cpp:455-456 explicitly claims 'An attacker is rate-limited long before the scan cost matters' — but no rate limit exists anywhere in the Qt port (callers at PosTerminalPage.cpp:474/498 and ReturnsPage.cpp:555 call it directly with no throttle). For a system with short numeric PINs, an attacker at the POS can brute-force a manager override (discount auth, void, controlled-substance witness) unboundedly. OVERRIDE_DENIED is audited but nothing slows or blocks repeated guessing.
findings.recommendation: Add a per-action lockout/backoff for failed overrides mirroring the login lockout (or a RateLimit equivalent of the PHP keyed limiter), and update/remove the misleading comment. Track consecutive failures (e.g. in a rate_limits-style table or in-memory per process) and refuse to scan once the threshold is hit.

findings.title: Lockout never decays: failed_attempts is only reset on success, so windows escalate indefinitely
findings.detail: registerFailedLogin() (UserRepository.cpp:347-396) increments users.failed_attempts and, at/after threshold 5, sets locked_until via exponential backoff using over = newCount - kLockoutThreshold (line 370). failed_attempts is ONLY zeroed by clearFailedLogins() on a successful login (lines 398-407); secondsLockedOut() (329-345) only checks locked_until>now and never clears the counter. Consequently, once a window expires, the user is allowed to try again (secondsLockedOut==0) but a single new failure computes a larger 'over' and re-locks them for a longer time (60s, then 120s, ...), with no decay back toward zero. The PHP source (../pos/backend/RateLimit.php:38-49) uses a 15-minute sliding window that FULLY RESETS to count=1 once expired, so a legitimate user who returns later starts fresh. This is a behavioral divergence from the spec and can permanently degrade a real user who occasionally mistypes.
findings.recommendation: On a successful or expired-window login attempt, reset failed_attempts to 0 before counting the new failure (or store a window/reset_at and start fresh when it has elapsed), to match the PHP sliding-window semantics. At minimum, reset failed_attempts when locked_until has passed.

findings.title: No tests for verifyManagerOverride, findForLogin, backoff schedule, or Bcrypt
findings.detail: tests/cases/auth_tests.cpp covers only the basic lock-after-5, clear, and single-failure cases. There is NO test for: verifyManagerOverride (success match, forbidUserId exclusion, empty PIN, denied path, audit rows) — a security gate guarding discounts/voids/controlled-substance witness; findForLogin (case-insensitive lookup, inactive/deleted exclusion, mustRotatePin/branchId mapping); the exponential-backoff schedule (30s->60s->120s cap at 900s) which is asserted only as '>0'; Bcrypt::hash/verify interop with PHP $2y$ hashes; and last-active-admin protection in updateUser. CLAUDE.md mandates tests on the auth/security path; these are the highest-value untested branches.
findings.recommendation: Add cases for verifyManagerOverride (matching manager, excluded cashier id, empty/whitespace PIN, no-match denial), findForLogin (case-insensitive, is_active/deleted filtering, field mapping), the precise backoff seconds at counts 5..8, otherProtections in updateUser, and a Bcrypt round-trip plus a known PHP $2y$ hash verify.

findings.title: registerFailedLogin lock window omits failed_attempts continuity in audit, and re-uses pre-fetched count under no row lock
findings.detail: registerFailedLogin() reads failed_attempts (line 357-365) then computes newCount = old+1 and, in the locked branch, writes 'failed_attempts = failed_attempts + 1' (line 377) rather than = newCount. The increment is done by SQL relative to the row value, while the backoff 'over' is computed from the pre-read newCount. In single-PC SQLite with a transaction this is fine, but the two values are derived inconsistently (one from app-side read, one from SQL). If a concurrent path ever incremented between the SELECT and UPDATE, the lock window would be computed from a stale count. Minor for a single-PC app but a latent inconsistency.
findings.recommendation: Compute lockSeconds from the post-increment count read inside the same statement, or write 'failed_attempts = ?' with the app-computed newCount so the stored count and the backoff window are always derived from the same number.

findings.title: pinAgeDays returns 0 (not 'large') when pin_changed_at is unknown, contradicting its contract
findings.detail: The header comment (UserRepository.h:102) says 'Days since pin_changed_at ... Large if unknown.' The implementation (UserRepository.cpp:308-319) returns 0 when the row/value is missing. Returning 0 means an unknown/edge user appears to have a freshly-set PIN and would never be prompted to rotate, the opposite of the documented fail-safe. PHP enforces rotation at >= ROTATION_DAYS (Auth.php:131-132); a 0 here silently disables that for affected rows.
findings.recommendation: Return a large sentinel (e.g. INT_MAX) when pin_changed_at is NULL/missing so the rotation policy fails safe, matching the documented contract.

findings.title: Audit JSON is built by string interpolation — unescaped username/role can corrupt audit records
findings.detail: createUser (UserRepository.cpp:181), recordLogin (326), and verifyManagerOverride (483, 489) build JSON via QStringLiteral(...).arg(username/role/action). usernames are validated at the login UI (LoginDialog.cpp:57-58 allows [A-Za-z0-9._-]), but createUser/recordLogin take arbitrary strings, and the audit_log is the tamper-evident who-did-what record CLAUDE.md requires. A username/full-context containing a double-quote or backslash produces invalid JSON in the audit detail column, breaking later parsing and weakening the integrity guarantee. recordLogin is called with the raw submitted username even on failed logins.
findings.recommendation: Use QJsonObject/QJsonDocument to serialize audit detail (proper escaping) instead of arg()-interpolated string literals, in all Audit::write call sites here.

findings.title: updateUser is not wrapped in a transaction while writing both the user row and an audit row
findings.detail: updateUser() (UserRepository.cpp:191-226) executes the UPDATE then Audit::write() with no surrounding transaction, unlike createUser/setPin which do. CLAUDE.md requires multi-statement changes to be transactional. If the audit write fails after the user update commits, the role/active change is applied with no audit trail — a gap in the who-did-what record for a privileged operation (changing roles / deactivating users).
findings.recommendation: Wrap the UPDATE + Audit::write in m_db.transaction()/commit() with rollback on failure, consistent with createUser() and setPin().

findings.title: secondsLockedOut relies on stored timezone matching datetime('now') (UTC); mismatch could mis-time lockouts
findings.detail: secondsLockedOut (UserRepository.cpp:334-339) and registerFailedLogin (line 378) both use SQLite datetime('now')/julianday('now'), which return UTC. last_login_at and other timestamps use CURRENT_TIMESTAMP (also UTC in SQLite) so this is internally consistent today. But the comparison assumes locked_until is stored in the same UTC frame; if any code path ever stored a localtime value into locked_until, the remaining-seconds math would be off by the UTC offset, either freeing a locked account early or over-locking. Worth an explicit invariant/test given this is a security control.
findings.recommendation: Add a test asserting the backoff window length end-to-end (set N failures, assert secondsLockedOut is within the expected band) and document/assert that locked_until is always UTC datetime('now', ...).

findings.title: One-OPEN-shift-per-cashier UNIQUE index missing in SQLite schema — open-session uniqueness is a TOCTOU check only
findings.detail: The PHP/Postgres layer enforces at most one OPEN session per cashier with a partial UNIQUE index `cashier_sessions_one_open_per_user ON cashier_sessions(cashier_id) WHERE status='OPEN'` (db/triggers/phase9_concurrency_hardening.sql). Sessions.php explicitly relies on this as the 'suspenders' to currentFor()'s belt and catches the 23505 violation. The SQLite schema only creates `cashier_sessions_cashier_opened` and `cashier_sessions_status` non-unique indexes — the partial-unique constraint was NOT ported. openSession() therefore relies solely on the openSessionId() read-then-INSERT in SessionRepository.cpp:51-67, which is a classic time-of-check/time-of-use gap: two concurrent open-shift attempts (single PC is largely serial, but Qt SQL re-entrancy or a double-click can still interleave) can both pass the check and create two OPEN rows for one cashier, leaving the drawer in an ambiguous state.
findings.recommendation: Add `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX cashier_sessions_one_open_per_user ON cashier_sessions(cashier_id) WHERE status='OPEN';` to schema_sqlite.sql (SQLite supports partial indexes), and have openSession() treat the resulting constraint failure on INSERT as the 'already have an open session' message, mirroring the PHP 23505 handling. Add a test that simulates the race.

findings.title: Negative-amount defense-in-depth guard dropped from open/close validation
findings.detail: PHP open()/close() validate the regex AND then re-check `Money::cmp(Money::round($x,2),'0') < 0` to reject negatives explicitly. The Qt port keeps only isMoneyInput() (regex `^\d+(\.\d{1,2})?$`). In practice the regex already excludes a leading '-', so behavior is currently equivalent, but the parity is incomplete: if isMoneyInput is ever loosened or reused, the negative-rejection invariant the PHP guarantees would silently vanish. This is a minor maintainability/parity gap, not a live bug.
findings.recommendation: Mirror PHP by adding an explicit post-round negative check (or document that the regex subsumes it). Low priority but cheap.

findings.title: SESSION_CLOSE_DENIED audit row not written on ownership mismatch
findings.detail: PHP close() audits the security-relevant denial: when (int)session.cashier_id != closedBy it calls Audit::write(closedBy,'SESSION_CLOSE_DENIED',...,{reason:'cashier_mismatch',session_owner:...}) BEFORE throwing. This is a deliberate tamper-detection trail ('a tampered session_id lets one cashier close another's drawer and harvest the variance'). The Qt port performs the ownership check (good) but returns false with only an error string and writes NO audit row. An attempted cross-cashier drawer close therefore leaves no forensic record, breaking the who-tried-what audit guarantee CLAUDE.md requires for sessions.
findings.recommendation: Write a SESSION_CLOSE_DENIED audit row (with reason + session_owner) before returning false on the ownership-mismatch branch, matching PHP. Note it should be committed independently of the (aborted) close.

findings.title: `notes` parameter not ported on closeSession — cashier close-note is lost
findings.detail: PHP close() accepts an optional `$notes` and persists it via `notes = COALESCE(:notes, notes)`. The Qt closeSession(sessionId, countedCash, userId) has no notes parameter and the UPDATE (SessionRepository.cpp:138-143) never touches the notes column. The schema column exists (schema_sqlite.sql:362) and the Reconciler relies on the closing cashier's note being present (it prefixes '[reconciled] ' and preserves prior notes). Closing cashiers thus cannot record a shift note, and downstream reconciliation parity is reduced.
findings.recommendation: Add an optional `const QString &notes = QString()` parameter and persist it with COALESCE semantics like PHP, so the reconcile flow can append to it.

findings.title: bumpForSale silently no-ops when the linked session is missing or not OPEN
findings.detail: Inside a committed sale, bumpForSale reads `SELECT total_cash_sales ... WHERE id=? AND status='OPEN'`; if the row is absent or the session is CLOSED/RECONCILED it returns true (no-op) so as not to fail the sale. The intent (don't unwind a sale) is reasonable, but the effect is that a CASH sale recorded against a session that was concurrently closed gets a sales row whose cash never lands in any drawer total — silently producing a false-zero variance at close with no audit/log signal. The PHP path links the session at sale time and does not have this swallow-on-closed branch in the same shape. There is no error_log/audit breadcrumb for the dropped bump.
findings.recommendation: Keep the sale non-fatal, but emit a log/audit breadcrumb (e.g. a movement/audit note) when a CASH bump is dropped because the session is gone or not OPEN, so reconciliation discrepancies are traceable. Consider whether a sale should even be allowed to commit against a non-OPEN session.

findings.title: Ownership-denial and concurrency paths have no test coverage
findings.detail: sessions_tests.cpp covers open/close, expected/variance math, surplus/shortage, CARD-vs-CASH bump, no-op bump, and reconcile — good money coverage. But every closeSession call passes the SAME cashier id (cid) as both owner and userId. The ownership guard at SessionRepository.cpp:116 (a security control) is never exercised with a mismatched userId, and there is no test asserting that closing another cashier's shift is rejected (and, per the finding above, audited). There is also no test for the double-open race / unique-index behavior, nor for closing an already-CLOSED session via the WHERE status='OPEN' guard returning numRowsAffected!=1.
findings.recommendation: Add tests: (1) close with a non-owner userId returns false and (when implemented) writes SESSION_CLOSE_DENIED; (2) closing an already-closed session fails cleanly; (3) once the unique index is added, a second OPEN insert for the same cashier is rejected.

findings.title: list() omits total_refunds_paid, so the admin view cannot show or re-derive expected cash
findings.detail: SessionRow/list() expose opening_float, total_cash_sales, counted_cash, cash_variance but not total_refunds_paid (it is only in SessionSummary). Expected cash = opening_float + total_cash_sales − total_refunds_paid; without refunds the list cannot display or sanity-check expected drawer per row, and any per-row expected computed from the list fields would be wrong whenever refunds were paid. PHP's session/Reconciler views carry refunds through. Minor since the detail summary has it, but the list parity is incomplete.
findings.recommendation: Add total_refunds_paid to the list() SELECT and SessionRow if the admin sessions grid needs to show expected/variance consistently.

findings.title: Audit JSON payloads built via string interpolation rather than escaped JSON
findings.detail: SESSION_OPENED/SESSION_CLOSED audit `after` payloads are assembled with QStringLiteral(...).arg(...) interpolating Money strings directly into a JSON literal. The values here are validated Money decimal strings so injection is not currently possible, but this hand-rolled JSON pattern is fragile: if a notes field or any free-text value is ever added (see the notes finding), an unescaped quote/newline would corrupt the append-only audit JSON. Prefer QJsonObject/QJsonDocument for any audit payload that may contain non-numeric values.
findings.recommendation: Build audit payloads with QJsonObject + QJsonDocument::Compact so values are always properly escaped, especially before adding notes to the close payload.

findings.title: Settings changes are never written to the audit_log (PHP writes SETTINGS_UPDATED on every save)
findings.detail: The PHP settings screen (../pos/frontend/pages/admin/settings.php:55,93) calls Audit::write($adminId,'SETTINGS_UPDATED','settings',...) on both the branding 'save' action and the 'save_theme' action, so every settings/theme change is recorded in the append-only audit_log with the acting admin. In the Qt port, SettingsRepository::set/setMany take an updatedBy id but only stamp the settings row's updated_by column — they never emit an audit entry, and neither AdminPage::savePharmacy/savePrinter/saveBackup nor SetupWizard::accept write a SETTINGS_UPDATED audit row. grep for SETTINGS_UPDATED across src/ returns nothing. This breaks the CLAUDE.md guardrail requiring who-did-what-when for configuration changes and is a regression from the spec.
