findings.recommendation: Have AdminPage (and/or SettingsRepository) write an AuditRepository SETTINGS_UPDATED entry recording the acting user and the changed keys, mirroring the PHP Audit::write calls for both the branding save and the theme save. Reuse the existing AuditRepository already included in AdminPage.cpp.

findings.title: Callers ignore set()/setMany() return value — failed saves are reported as success
findings.detail: SettingsRepository::set returns bool and records m_error on failure, but AdminPage::savePharmacy (lines 554-561) discards the return of all eight s.set(...) calls and unconditionally shows QMessageBox::information(... 'Settings saved.'). savePrinter (590-592) and saveBackup (764-785) do the same. If any upsert fails (locked DB, FK violation, disk full), the user is told the save succeeded while data was silently lost — and because there is no transaction (see next finding) some keys may persist and others not. Only SetupWizard::accept (line 96) actually checks the setMany result.
findings.recommendation: Check the boolean result of every set/setMany call (or have savePharmacy use setMany and inspect its return), and on failure show s.errorString() instead of a success message.

findings.title: No transaction around multi-key settings saves — partial writes possible
findings.detail: setMany loops issuing one independent INSERT...ON CONFLICT per key with no transaction (the header comment explicitly notes 'does not open its own transaction'), and savePharmacy bypasses setMany entirely with eight separate set() calls. If a write fails midway, earlier keys are already committed, leaving the settings inconsistent (e.g. new pharmacy_name saved but theme/logo not). CLAUDE.md requires multi-statement changes to be wrapped in a transaction. SetupWizard relies on the caller to wrap it, but AdminPage does not wrap anything.
findings.recommendation: Add a transactional setMany path (BEGIN/COMMIT with rollback on first failure) or wrap AdminPage::savePharmacy's group of upserts in a QSqlDatabase transaction so the settings set is atomic.

findings.title: Per-field validation (required + length limits) from PHP was dropped
findings.detail: PHP enforces REQUIRED=['pharmacy_name'] plus explicit max lengths (pharmacy_name 160, pharmacy_address 500, pharmacy_phone 60, pharmacy_ntn 40, return_policy_text 2000, receipt_footer_message 200) and trims values before storing (settings.php:65-85). The Qt savePharmacy only checks that pharmacy_name is non-empty and trims; it enforces none of the length caps. Since the SQLite settings.value is unbounded TEXT, an admin can paste arbitrarily long content that then flows onto printed receipts, diverging from PHP behavior and risking layout breakage on the thermal printer.
findings.recommendation: Reproduce the PHP REQUIRED and LIMITS maps in the settings UI (or in SettingsRepository) and reject over-length / empty-required values with the same messages before upserting.

findings.title: Upsert overwrites updated_by/updated_at on conflict — PHP intentionally does not
findings.detail: PHP's settings upsert is 'ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE SET value = EXCLUDED.value' — it touches ONLY value and leaves updated_by/updated_at unchanged (settings.php:51-54, 88-91). The Qt version additionally sets updated_at = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP and updated_by = excluded.updated_by on conflict. This is a semantic deviation from the source of truth. Arguably the Qt behavior is better (the columns exist precisely to track this), but it should be a deliberate, documented choice rather than an accidental divergence, and it only matters if the audit gap above is addressed by relying on these columns.
findings.recommendation: Confirm this is intentional and note it as a documented improvement; if strict parity is desired, drop updated_at/updated_by from the ON CONFLICT UPDATE clause. Either way, do not rely on updated_by alone as the audit trail (see SETTINGS_UPDATED finding).

findings.title: get()/getAll() swallow SQL errors and report indistinguishably from a missing key
findings.detail: In get(), if q.exec() fails (e.g. table missing, DB locked) the code falls through to 'return fallback' exactly as it would for a legitimately absent key, and m_error is never set (only set() touches m_error). getAll() likewise returns an empty map on exec failure with no error signal. A read failure thus masquerades as 'unconfigured', so receipts silently fall back to defaults instead of surfacing a real DB problem, and callers have no way to tell the two cases apart.
findings.recommendation: On exec() failure in get/getAll, set m_error (mutable QString already exists) and consider logging; keep returning the fallback but make the failure observable so callers/tests can distinguish a DB error from an unset key.

findings.title: No unit tests for SettingsRepository despite settings feeding receipts
findings.detail: tests/cases/ has 20 test files (money, fefo, sale, returns, sessions, etc.) but none for SettingsRepository; grep -rln SettingsRepository tests/ is empty. There is no coverage for the upsert/insert-then-update path, the updatedBy<0 → NULL binding, get() fallback behavior, getAll() round-trip, or setMany failure handling. Pharmacy name/address/footer/return-policy and theme all flow from here onto printed receipts, so regressions would be silent.
findings.recommendation: Add a settings_tests.cpp covering: insert then update of the same key (value changes, no duplicate row), updatedBy=-1 stores NULL and a valid id stores it, get() returns fallback for an unknown key, getAll() returns all rows, and setMany propagates failure. Use the existing in-memory test DB harness.

findings.title: HMAC tamper-evidence chain is not implemented — audit_log is editable-blocked but not tamper-EVIDENT
findings.detail: The PHP source-of-truth (db/triggers/audit_log_immutable.sql) provides TWO independent guarantees: (1) append-only via BEFORE UPDATE/DELETE rejection, and (2) a cryptographic HMAC-SHA256 chain (row_hmac = hex(HMAC(secret, prev_hmac || canonical_payload))) whose explicit purpose is that 'dropping the trigger and forging history still fails verification', plus an offline verifier (tools/audit-verify.php). The Qt port implements ONLY guarantee (1). Audit::write inserts rows with prev_hmac/row_hmac left at their schema DEFAULT '' (never computed), and there is no verifier tool. CLAUDE.md explicitly allows simplifying the HMAC chain for single-PC SQLite but says 'keep the audit records' tamper-evident; here an attacker (or buggy code) with raw file access to the SQLite DB can edit/delete history with sqlite3 CLI (bypassing the app-layer triggers entirely, which only fire for the app's own connection) and nothing detects it. Notably the project already has working HMAC-SHA256 chaining via QMessageAuthenticationCode in src/service/ZReportArchive.cpp:88, so the capability exists but was never applied to audit_log.
findings.recommendation: Port the chain: on each Audit::write, read the current chain tip (highest id with non-empty row_hmac), build the same pipe-separated canonical payload the PHP function uses (timestamp|user_id|action|entity_type|entity_id|before|after|reason|ip|ua), compute QMessageAuthenticationCode HMAC-SHA256 over prev_hmac||payload with a host-stored secret, and store prev_hmac/row_hmac. Serialize concurrent inserts (single-PC makes this trivial). Add a verify routine mirroring audit-verify.php and a test that flips a byte and detects the break. At minimum, document loudly that the SQLite log is only edit-blocked, not tamper-evident.

findings.title: Audit payloads built by raw string interpolation — malformed JSON / stored-injection on quotes & backslashes
findings.detail: Several Audit::write callers build the after_value JSON with QStringLiteral("...").arg(value) and NO escaping. recordLogin() interpolates the raw login username: {"username":"<username>"} (UserRepository.cpp:326). SaleService.cpp:347-368 interpolates receipt number and override id into the SALE_COMPLETED / CONTROLLED_DISPENSED / DISCOUNT_AUTHORIZED payloads. requireOverride interpolates the action label (UserRepository.cpp:483,489). Any value containing a double-quote, backslash, or control char produces invalid JSON, and an attacker-controlled username (login form) can inject arbitrary key/values into the audit record — e.g. typing a username of `x","role":"ADMIN` forges fields in the stored audit JSON. Because the audit log is supposed to be the forensic record of who-did-what (and would feed the HMAC canonicalization), corrupting it defeats the trail. Note StockAdjuster.cpp:169 and ParkedCartRepository correctly use jesc()/QJsonDocument, so the safe pattern already exists in-tree and was simply not applied to the auth/sale paths.
findings.recommendation: Build every audit payload with QJsonObject/QJsonDocument(Compact) (as ParkedCartRepository already does) or route all string fields through the existing jesc() helper. Add a test that audits an entity whose name/username contains a double-quote and asserts the stored after_value parses as valid JSON with the literal value intact.

findings.title: Audit::write return value is never checked — a failed audit insert silently succeeds the business transaction
findings.detail: Audit::write returns bool (q.exec()), but no caller inspects it (grep of all call sites shows none assign or branch on the result). In the critical sale path (SaleService.cpp:347), if the audit INSERT fails (e.g. a CHECK/length issue, or the malformed-JSON column constraint in a future schema), the sale still commits at SaleService.cpp:371 with no audit record and no error surfaced. For a medical-retail system the audit record of a controlled-substance dispense (CONTROLLED_DISPENSED) or a manager discount override is a compliance artifact; losing it silently while completing the sale is a guardrail violation. The PHP Audit::write throws on json_encode failure (JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR) and Db::execute throws on SQL error, so the PHP behavior is fail-loud; the C++ port is fail-silent.
findings.recommendation: Make Audit::write throw (or have callers check the bool and roll back) when invoked inside a business transaction so a failed audit write aborts the same transaction it documents — mirroring the PHP fail-loud semantics. At minimum, log a hard error on false return.

findings.title: PHP `reason` audit field dropped from the C++ Audit::write signature
findings.detail: PHP Audit::write (backend/Audit.php:25-32) has a dedicated `?string $reason` parameter stored in the audit_log.reason column, and that column is part of the canonical HMAC payload. The C++ Audit::write signature has no reason parameter at all, so the reason column (which exists in schema_sqlite.sql:383) is ALWAYS NULL. Callers work around this by stuffing the reason into the JSON after_value (e.g. StockAdjuster.cpp:168 embeds "reason":"..." in JSON). This diverges from the PHP record shape, means any report/query filtering on audit_log.reason returns nothing, and the audit reports screen (../pos/frontend/pages/reports/audit.php) parity is broken for the reason column.
findings.recommendation: Add the optional `reason` parameter to Audit::write matching the PHP signature, bind it to the reason column, and update stock-adjustment / override / return-adjudication callers to pass the operator-entered reason there (in addition to, or instead of, the JSON blob).

findings.title: ip_address / user_agent columns are dead in the port (no parity, but they bloat the chain payload)
findings.detail: The schema keeps ip_address and user_agent columns (carried over from the web app) but the C++ Audit::write never sets them — they are always NULL. For a single-PC desktop app these are arguably meaningless, so this is acceptable, but two issues: (1) the columns are part of the PHP HMAC canonical payload, so when the chain is eventually implemented the canonicalization must agree on how NULL serializes ('' in PHP) to stay verifiable, and (2) carrying always-NULL columns with no comment invites future confusion. This is informational/parity housekeeping.
findings.recommendation: Either drop ip_address/user_agent from the SQLite schema (single-PC) and document the divergence, or, if kept for parity, add a schema comment that they are intentionally always NULL on desktop and ensure the future HMAC canonicalization treats NULL as '' exactly like PHP.

findings.title: AuditRepository read view has no filtering, pagination, or entity drill-down — parity gap with reports/audit.php
findings.detail: AuditRepository::list() returns only the most-recent 500 rows ordered by id DESC with no filters and exposes only timestamp/userName/actionType/entityType/entityId — it drops before_value/after_value/reason entirely, so the UI cannot show WHAT changed. The PHP audit report (../pos/frontend/pages/reports/audit.php) typically supports filtering by user/action/entity/date and viewing the before/after diff. With a hard LIMIT 500 and no date/action filter, older compliance records become unreachable through the UI even though they exist in the table (and indexes audit_log_action / audit_log_user_timestamp / audit_log_entity exist precisely to support such filtering but are unused here).
findings.recommendation: Compare against reports/audit.php and add date/user/action/entity filters plus the before/after payload to AuditRow, using the existing indexes. At minimum allow paging beyond the newest 500 rows so the full append-only history is viewable.

findings.title: Failed-login audit write executes outside any transaction during a hot brute-force path
findings.detail: On a failed login, LoginDialog calls recordLogin() (audit LOGIN_FAILED) then registerFailedLogin() (lockout counter) as two separate un-batched statements with no surrounding transaction. The audit write and the lockout-counter increment are not atomic: if the process is killed or the DB errors between them, you can get an audit row without a lockout increment (or vice versa), weakening the brute-force record. Combined with finding #3 (return value ignored), a failed LOGIN_FAILED insert is invisible. For an auth/lockout path this is the exact place auditing must be reliable.
findings.recommendation: Wrap the failed-login audit write + failed-login counter increment in a single transaction (and the success path's clearFailedLogins + touchLastLogin + LOGIN_SUCCESS likewise), and check the audit write result.

findings.title: No test asserts audit COMPLETENESS for the critical money/stock/auth events
findings.detail: Existing tests cover (a) append-only triggers reject UPDATE/DELETE (smoke.cpp:122-132) and (b) a single USER_CREATED row appears (smoke.cpp:330-333). There is NO test asserting that a completed sale writes SALE_COMPLETED, that a controlled-substance sale writes CONTROLLED_DISPENSED, that a discount override writes DISCOUNT_AUTHORIZED, that a stock adjustment writes STOCK_ADJUSTED with the correct entity_id, or that the stored after_value is valid parseable JSON. CLAUDE.md requires the money/stock/expiry/auth paths to be covered by tests; the audit side of those paths is essentially untested, so a regression that drops an audit write (very easy given finding #3) would pass CI.
findings.recommendation: Add tests that drive SaleService / StockAdjuster / ReturnService / requireOverride end-to-end and assert the expected action_type + entity_id rows exist and that before_value/after_value parse as valid JSON. Once the HMAC chain lands (finding #1), add a tamper-detection test.

findings.title: Refunds per-medicine breakdown filters by disposition; PHP counts all returns
findings.detail: refundsReport() restricts the per-medicine query to status IN ('APPROVED_RESTOCK','RETURN_TO_SUPPLIER','WRITE_OFF'), excluding PENDING_REVIEW. The PHP source (reports/refunds.php, $byMedicine query lines 75-87) has NO status filter — it groups every return in the date range regardless of disposition, ordered by SUM(refund_amount). As a result the Qt per-medicine table understates refund counts/amounts whenever returns are still awaiting manager adjudication, and the per-medicine total will not reconcile with the headline total (which the Qt code DOES compute over all returns at line 436). The misleading comment at line 432 even claims it matches PHP. PHP also surfaces 'by reason' and 'by disposition' breakdowns that the Qt port omits entirely.
findings.recommendation: Drop the status IN (...) filter so the per-medicine breakdown matches PHP (all dispositions). If the by-reason and by-disposition breakdowns are in scope for parity, add them. Add a test asserting a PENDING_REVIEW return appears in byMedicine.

findings.title: Compliance report only lists controlled lines and adds filters PHP doesn't have
findings.detail: complianceReport() joins sale_items/medicines with 'AND m.controlled_schedule <> \'NONE\'', so the GROUP_CONCAT 'items' column lists ONLY the controlled lines of each sale. The PHP compliance.php (lines 16-33) joins ALL sale_items (no controlled filter on the join) and STRING_AGGs every line — so a compliance row shows the full basket, not just the controlled drug. The Qt query also adds 'AND s.status <> VOIDED' (PHP has none) and formats the schedule as 'Brand [SCHEDULE]' whereas PHP uses 'Brand (SCHEDULE)'. PHP also caps at LIMIT 500; the Qt query has no limit. These change what auditors/regulators see on a controlled-drug report.
findings.recommendation: Match PHP: remove the controlled-only restriction on the items join (keep the controlled qualifier only in the WHERE/EXISTS gate), use '(SCHEDULE)' formatting, drop the VOIDED exclusion (or confirm with the business it is intentional), and add LIMIT 500. Add a test selling a controlled + a non-controlled line and asserting the items string contains both.

findings.title: Velocity report drops PHP's LIMIT 200 and adds a HAVING filter, changing rows returned
findings.detail: velocityReport() adds 'HAVING SUM(... -90 days ...) > 0' so medicines with no 90-day sales are dropped, and omits PHP's 'LIMIT 200'. PHP velocity.php (lines 13-24) returns up to 200 rows including zero-velocity active medicines (ORDER BY d30 DESC NULLS LAST LIMIT 200). The Qt version therefore shows a different (potentially much longer or shorter) set: it hides slow movers that PHP would show as 0/0/0 and can return more than 200 rows. Tie-break ordering also differs (PHP NULLS LAST). For a velocity/reorder screen these row-set differences are user-visible.
findings.recommendation: Decide the intended behavior and document it; to match PHP, drop the HAVING and add LIMIT 200 with stable ORDER BY d30 DESC. If filtering zero-velocity rows is a deliberate improvement, note it in MEMORY php-vs-qt gaps and test the row count/ordering.

findings.title: Narcotic register item separator differs from DRAP-format PHP output
findings.detail: narcoticRegister() joins 'Brand × qty unit' with ', ' (comma). PHP narcotic-register.php line 28 uses '; ' (semicolon): STRING_AGG(... , '; '). For a regulated DRAP register and its CSV export, the field delimiter inside the items cell should match the spec, and a comma separator inside an un-quoted-looking field is also more error-prone for downstream parsing. Minor, but it is a verbatim regulatory document.
findings.recommendation: Use '; ' to match PHP. Cheap to fix; covered by a string-content assertion in the existing narcotic test.

findings.title: Tax report per-bucket rounding order differs from PHP (round-per-row vs round-at-display)
findings.detail: PHP tax.php rounds base and tax to scale-2 PER BUCKET (Money::round(...,2) at lines 69-76) and accumulates the already-rounded values into the grand totals. The Qt taxReport() keeps base/tax at scale-4 internally (ratioMul returns scale-4) and only rounds when calling .toString() for display, accumulating the unrounded scale-4 values into grandBase/grandTax. For inclusive tax, base = gross/(1+rate) rarely lands exactly on 2dp, so the Qt grand totals can differ from PHP by 1 paisa per bucket. For an FBR return this is a reconciliation discrepancy against the PHP system it replaces.
findings.recommendation: Round each bucket's base/tax/total to scale-2 before accumulating the grand totals, mirroring PHP's Money::round(...,2) order. Add a test with STANDARD_18 inclusive on an odd gross (e.g. 100.01) asserting the exact base/tax the PHP would produce.

findings.title: Report tests assert existence/sign but not exact amounts vs PHP-computed values
findings.detail: P&L and top-sellers have good exact-value delta assertions (50.00/20.00/30.00), but the tax test only checks '!tx.total.isEmpty()' (line 102) — it never verifies the inclusive/exclusive base/tax math, so the rounding-order divergence above is invisible to CI. Refunds tests check totalCount>=1 and amount not-zero/not-negative but never assert the exact refund amount (16.00) or the per-medicine amount. Compliance/narcotic tests only assert the receipt is present, not the items string, doctor/patient/witness fields, or that non-controlled lines are/aren't included — exactly the fields where the port diverges. CLAUDE.md mandates the money/expiry/stock paths be covered by tests comparing against PHP behavior; the report money paths are under-covered.
findings.recommendation: Add assertions for exact tax base/tax per bucket, exact refund amount (16.00) and per-medicine amount, and compliance/narcotic items-string contents (including a non-controlled line in the same sale). These directly catch findings 1, 2, and 5.

findings.title: Refund netting in P&L/top-sellers ignores returns with no in-range sale and can over-net across periods
findings.detail: profitAndLoss() and topSellers() skip a return entirely when 'agg' has no sales row for that medicine in range (line 137: 'if (!agg.contains(mid)) continue'). PHP pl.php uses sales_agg LEFT JOIN refund_agg, which also only nets refunds onto medicines that had sales in range — so this matches PHP for the common case. However, the proportional COGS reduction cogsNet = cogs − refunds×(cogs/revenue) can drive a row negative when refunds in the window exceed the same window's sales (e.g. sold last month, returned this month), and the result is then sorted/limited differently than PHP only if the float-derived NULLIF path in PHP yields NULL. Worth a documented decision, since refund-COGS netting on cross-period returns is an inherent approximation the PHP comment (pl.php lines 18-23) flags as imperfect.
findings.recommendation: Confirm the cross-period behavior matches PHP bit-for-bit with a targeted test (sale in month A, refund in month B, report month B) and document the approximation. Low severity because it mirrors the PHP limitation rather than introducing a new one.

findings.title: Reports silently swallow query failures, returning zeroed/partial results with no signal
findings.detail: Every query uses 'if (sq.exec()) { ... }' with no else branch and no logging (e.g. lines 114, 134, 212, 296, 320, 404, 441, 458; SalesReportRepository.cpp:28,62). If a query fails (schema drift, locked DB, bad date), the method returns an empty or partially-populated report that looks like 'no activity in this period' rather than surfacing an error. For financial/regulatory reports a silent zero is dangerous — a manager could conclude there were no controlled sales when the query actually errored. PHP fails loudly (PDO exception) instead.
findings.recommendation: On exec() failure, log lastError() and propagate a failure signal (return an error/throw, or set a status flag the UI shows) instead of returning a misleadingly empty report. Mirror PHP's fail-loud behavior.

findings.title: load() and discard() are not scoped by cashier_id — any cashier can resume/delete another cashier's parked bill
findings.detail: PHP scopes both resume and discard with `WHERE id = :id AND cashier_id = :cid` and rejects the row if it belongs to a different cashier (terminal.php:390-394, 413-417). The Qt load() (`SELECT ... WHERE id = ?`) and discard() (`DELETE ... WHERE id = ?`) ignore cashier ownership entirely. ParkedBillsDialog has the cashierId in hand (m_cashierId) but never passes it to load/discard, and resumeSelected()/discardSelected() act on any id. In a multi-cashier shop this lets cashier B resume cashier A's suspended cart (taking over their customer/total) or delete it. The list() picker only shows the current cashier's bills, but selectedId() returns a raw id with no server-side ownership re-check, so the guarantee is purely cosmetic.
findings.recommendation: Add a cashierId parameter to load() and discard() and append `AND cashier_id = ?` to both queries (treating cashierId<=0 as match-NULL like park/list do). Have ParkedBillsDialog and PosTerminalPage pass m_cashierId/m_userId through. Verify the DELETE affected exactly one row (q.numRowsAffected()==1) before auditing success.

findings.title: Resume is non-atomic: load → mutate UI cart → separate discard(), with discard failure ignored
findings.detail: resumeBill() copies the parked items into m_cartLines and then calls `ParkedCartRepository(m_db).discard(pc.id, m_userId)` with its return value discarded. PHP does this in one request: set session cart, DELETE the row, audit (terminal.php:396-399). In the Qt port, if discard() fails (DB locked, row already gone, FK/trigger error), the cart is still loaded into the terminal AND the parked row survives — the cashier can complete the sale, then reopen Parked bills and resume the same cart again, double-selling stock. There is no transaction wrapping the load+delete, and no user feedback on discard failure during resume.
findings.recommendation: Provide an atomic repo method (e.g. resume(id, cashierId, ParkedCart* out)) that, inside a single transaction with PRAGMA foreign_keys on, loads the row, deletes it (checking numRowsAffected==1), writes the SALE_RESUMED audit, and commits — returning the items only on success. The UI should populate the cart only after the repo confirms the row was consumed; surface an error and abort the resume otherwise.

findings.title: Park drops customer name/phone/CNIC/note and collapses pack lines to base units — parity loss vs PHP cart_json
findings.detail: PHP stores the full cart_json (sold_unit_label, sold_unit_factor, units_per_purchase, brand/generic, controlled_schedule, prescription_required) plus customer_name, customer_phone, customer_cnic and note as first-class columns (terminal.php:154-168, 355-367). The Qt port serializes only {medicine_id, name, base_unit, unit_mrp, qty} and folds pack quantities into base units (`c.qty * c.factor`, comment lines 542-544). Consequences: a bill parked as e.g. 2 packs resumes as N loose base units (the cashier's pack grouping, and any pack-level pricing context, is lost), and customer identity / pharmacist note attached at park time vanish on resume. For a pharmacy bill that may carry CNIC for controlled-drug audit, silently dropping it is a compliance regression.
findings.recommendation: Either (a) document this as an accepted simplification in CLAUDE.md / PHP_APP_MAP gaps, or (b) preserve sold_unit_factor and unit_label per line in items_json and add customer/note fields (the SQLite parked_carts table currently lacks them) so resumed carts reconstruct the original line structure and customer context.

findings.title: No expiry/cleanup of stale parked carts (PHP expires after 24h and prunes on every /pos load)
findings.detail: The PHP schema gives parked_carts an expires_at (CURRENT_TIMESTAMP + 24h) and an expires_idx, and terminal.php:430-435 runs `DELETE FROM parked_carts WHERE expires_at < CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` on every POS page load, flagging is_expired in the picker. The SQLite parked_carts table has no expires_at column at all (only created_at), and the repository has no cleanup/expiry concept. Parked bills therefore accumulate forever and a day-old cart with stale prices can be resumed and sold at its parked MRP with no warning, diverging from current pricing and from PHP's expiry guard.
findings.recommendation: Add expires_at to the SQLite schema (or compute age from created_at), prune expired rows on POS open, and surface an expired/stale indicator in ParkedBillsDialog. At minimum re-validate each line's current MRP/stock on resume and warn if changed.

findings.title: Audit action names don't match PHP and resume is logged as a discard
findings.detail: PHP records SALE_PARKED, SALE_RESUMED, SALE_PARK_DISCARDED (terminal.php:370,399,420). The Qt port uses CART_PARKED and CART_DISCARDED, and crucially the resume path calls the same discard() (CART_DISCARDED) to consume the row (PosTerminalPage.cpp:573). So in the audit trail a resume is indistinguishable from an intentional discard, and no SALE_RESUMED event with items_count is ever written. This breaks who-did-what-when reporting and any cross-system reconciliation that keys on PHP action names. Additionally, discard()'s audit captures no `before` JSON, whereas PHP passes the full $row as the before image.
findings.recommendation: Align action_type strings with PHP (SALE_PARKED/SALE_RESUMED/SALE_PARK_DISCARDED) or document the rename in the audit mapping. Give resume its own audit event distinct from discard, and capture the row's before-image (label, item_count, total) in the discard/resume audit `before` field.

findings.title: Park and audit write are not wrapped in a transaction (audit can desync from the parked row)
findings.detail: CLAUDE.md mandates that multi-statement changes go through a single transaction and Audit.h states write() 'must be called inside the caller's transaction when part of a larger change.' park() does INSERT then Audit::write as two separate auto-committed statements; discard() does DELETE then Audit::write likewise. If the audit insert fails (e.g. HMAC trigger, lock) the parked row is created/deleted without a matching audit record, violating the append-only who-did-what guarantee for these operations. Lower severity than the sale path since no stock moves, but still an audit-integrity gap.
findings.recommendation: Wrap each of park() and discard() (and the future resume()) in db.transaction()/commit() with rollback on any failure including the Audit::write call, mirroring the sale-commit pattern.

findings.title: medicine_id serialized through double in JSON — silent precision loss for large ids
findings.detail: itemsToJson stores medicine_id as `static_cast<double>(it.medicineId)` and itemsFromJson reads it back via `.toDouble()` then casts to qint64. qint64 ids above 2^53 lose precision, and even below that the double round-trip is fragile. Current ids are small so no live bug, but it's an avoidable correctness landmine for a primary-key field, and inconsistent with how the rest of the codebase treats ids.
findings.recommendation: Store medicine_id as a JSON string (or use QJsonValue from a qint64 via toString) and parse with toLongLong on the way back, eliminating the floating-point hop.

findings.title: No tests cover cashier-scoping, non-empty-resume guard, double-resume, or malformed items_json
findings.detail: parked_tests.cpp covers the happy path (empty rejected, park/list/load/discard round-trip, totals) well, but there are no tests for: (1) cross-cashier isolation — load/discard of another cashier's id (which currently succeeds, the security bug above); (2) resume consuming the row exactly once / not being resumable twice; (3) malformed or non-array items_json (itemsFromJson returns empty silently, which would make a corrupt cart resume as empty with no error); (4) discard of a non-existent id (currently returns true and writes a spurious audit row even though nothing was deleted). Per CLAUDE.md the quantity/pricing path here must be covered against PHP behavior.
findings.recommendation: Add cases asserting that load/discard with a foreign cashier id fail; that a resumed row cannot be resumed again; that corrupt JSON is reported as an error rather than silently emptying the cart; and that discard of a missing id returns false (after adding numRowsAffected checks).

findings.title: Enum fields (form, controlled_schedule, tax_code) are imported without validation
findings.detail: CatalogImporter never validates dosage form or the controlled/tax enums before INSERT. `d.form` is taken verbatim from the CSV (CatalogImporter.cpp:148) and the schema deliberately has NO CHECK on `form` ("enforced in the C++ domain layer", sql/schema_sqlite.sql:76-85) — yet the importer bypasses the very validator that exists for this, src/domain/MedicineForm.h:isValid(). So an out-of-enum form value (e.g. a column-shifted ' 500ml' or 'Zingiber officinale', which naive parsing of this very file surfaces) would be inserted silently, producing a medicine the GUI form-picker cannot represent or round-trip. Conversely controlled_schedule (CatalogImporter.cpp:153) and tax_code_value (157) DO have DB CHECKs; an invalid value there fails the INSERT and is counted as a bare ++result.failed (176) with no reason recorded. The current seed happens to be all-NONE/all-EXEMPT so this is latent, but it is a real correctness/observability hole for any other export.
findings.recommendation: Before create(), validate d.form with MedicineForm::isValid() and d.controlledSchedule/d.taxCode against ControlledSchedule::all()/TaxCode::all(); on failure increment failed and record the row number + offending column/value into a per-row error list returned in Result, rather than relying on the DB CHECK to reject silently.

findings.title: Failed rows carry no diagnostic — Result reports only a count
findings.detail: When repo.create() returns <=0 the importer does `++result.failed` (CatalogImporter.cpp:174-176) and discards the SQL error (repo.errorString() / q.lastError() is captured into the repo's m_error but never read by the importer). The CLI then prints only 'imported X, skipped Y, failed Z' (tools/import_catalog.cpp:66-69). For a 318-row medical-catalog seed, an operator who sees 'failed 4' has no way to know which SKUs failed or why (CHECK violation? unique barcode collision? NOT NULL on brand/generic?), making the import effectively un-debuggable in the field on AlmaLinux.
findings.recommendation: Extend Result with a list of {rowNumber, sku, reason} for failed/skipped rows (pull reason from repo.errorString()), and have the CLI print or write them. This turns a blind count into actionable output.

findings.title: Ragged / short rows are silently dropped without being counted
findings.detail: Rows with fewer columns than the header are skipped with a bare `continue` (CatalogImporter.cpp:126-128) and counted as neither imported, skipped, nor failed. A genuinely malformed data row (e.g. an unescaped embedded newline that splits one logical record into two short physical rows, or a truncated export) therefore vanishes with zero signal — imported+skipped+failed will silently not sum to the data-row count. For a pharmacy catalog, silently losing a medicine is worse than failing loudly.
findings.recommendation: Count short/ragged rows into failed (or a dedicated 'malformed' counter) with the row number recorded, and make the totals reconcile against the number of data rows. Consider asserting imported+skipped+failed == rows.size()-1.

findings.title: No shipped or GUI catalog-seed path for a real AlmaLinux install
findings.detail: medicines_export.csv lives at the PMS root but is not in resources/resources.qrc and is not bundled by CMake, so the AppImage does not contain it. The only seed path is the pharmadesk_import CLI (CMakeLists.txt:142), which (a) is 'Not shipped in the GUI' per its own header and (b) requires the operator to have the loose 318-row CSV on disk. Project memory confirms a 'setup-wizard import starter catalog step is still deferred.' On a fresh single-PC AlmaLinux deployment the pharmacy would start with an empty catalog and no in-app way to load the 315 medicines — a clear gap versus the PHP app, which ships its data in Postgres.
findings.recommendation: Either embed medicines_export.csv as a Qt resource and add a first-run/setup-wizard 'import starter catalog' step that calls CatalogImporter, or document and ship the CLI + CSV as part of the AppImage install procedure. At minimum bundle the CSV so the CLI has something to point at.

findings.title: Per-row audit + single mega-transaction: an abort discards all audit context
findings.detail: The entire import runs in one db.transaction()/commit() (CatalogImporter.cpp:118,179) and each successful create() writes a MEDICINE_CREATED audit row inside that transaction (MedicineRepository.cpp:165). This is correct for atomicity, but if commit() fails (179-183) the rollback discards everything including the audit trail, and there is no record that an import was even attempted. For a 318-row seed a single transaction is fine on size, but there is no audit of the import operation itself (counts, file path, partial failures) — only per-medicine create events that vanish on rollback.
findings.recommendation: Write one IMPORT_CATALOG audit event (file path, imported/skipped/failed counts) on successful commit, outside the per-row noise, so the operation is traceable even when individual creates were the only writes.

findings.title: No UTF-8 BOM handling — a BOM would corrupt the first header column
findings.detail: parseCsv consumes QString::fromUtf8(f.readAll()) (CatalogImporter.cpp:97) with no BOM stripping. The current file has no BOM (verified: first bytes 69 64 2c = 'id,'), but Postgres COPY/psql and especially Excel re-saves commonly prepend an EF BB BF BOM. That would make the first header cell '﻿sku' instead of 'sku', failing the required-column check at CatalogImporter.cpp:109-116 with a confusing 'missing required column: sku' error even though the column is visibly present.
findings.recommendation: Strip a leading U+FEFF from the decoded text before parsing (e.g. if text starts with QChar(0xFEFF), remove it).

findings.title: Test coverage misses enum/form validation, error rows, and barcode-collision idempotency
findings.detail: catalog_tests.cpp covers the happy path well (t/f booleans, quoted comma, soft-delete skip, NARCOTIC mapping, column-order independence via header map, and re-import idempotency). But there is no test for: an invalid form value, an invalid controlled_schedule/tax_code (the ++failed path), a ragged/short row, an empty required field (brand/generic), a duplicate primary_barcode across two live rows (which would hit the partial-unique index and fail one row), or a UTF-8 BOM. Given CLAUDE.md mandates tests on anything touching batch numbers/pricing and the importer is the catalog's only data-entry funnel, the failure/validation branches are untested.
findings.recommendation: Add cases for: out-of-enum form (asserting it is rejected, not silently inserted), bad tax/schedule (failed count + reason), duplicate live barcode, short row counted as failed, and a BOM-prefixed header parsing correctly.

findings.title: units_per_purchase coercion silently masks bad data via qMax(1, toInt())
findings.detail: d.unitsPerPurchase = qMax(1, cell(...).toInt()) (CatalogImporter.cpp:152) silently turns a missing, non-numeric, zero, or negative units_per_purchase into 1. units_per_purchase drives base-unit conversion for sales/pricing (sold_unit_factor), so silently defaulting a garbage value to 1 could mis-scale stock and price for that medicine without any warning. The current seed has no bad values (verified, 0 bad of 318), so this is defensive only, but a wrong factor here is a pharmacy-grade quantity bug.
findings.recommendation: Treat a non-positive / non-numeric units_per_purchase as a failed row (with reason) rather than coercing to 1, so the operator must fix the source rather than shipping a silently mis-scaled medicine.

findings.title: Receipt-number generation is race-prone and silently degrades to a non-monotonic random suffix
findings.detail: nextReceiptNumber() does count(*) of today's sales then formats INV-YYYYMMDD-(count+1). PHP guarded this exact read-then-write with a per-day pg_advisory_xact_lock held for the whole transaction (Sale.php nextReceiptNumber). The Qt port dropped the lock (header says single-PC SQLite doesn't need it) but kept the read-then-write. The SELECT count(*) here runs BEFORE m_db.transaction() begins (commit() opens the txn at line 202, after this returns at line 207 — actually it is called at line 207 inside the txn, but SQLite's default deferred transaction does not take a write lock until the first write, so the count is not isolated from another connection). If a second connection (e.g. a future reporting/return process, or a background sync) ever inserts a sale concurrently, both can read the same count and mint the same INV number; the UNIQUE index then aborts the loser's INSERT and the sale fails with a raw SQL error. The defensive fallback (line 51-52) produces a 6-digit RANDOM suffix that breaks the monotonic INV-YYYYMMDD-NNNN sequence cashiers and auditors rely on, and can itself collide. There is also a TOCTOU window between the chk SELECT (line 44-49) and the actual INSERT at line 235.
findings.recommendation: Make the receipt number derive from an authoritative monotonic source inside the same write transaction: either a dedicated per-day counter row updated with UPDATE ... RETURNING under the write lock, or rely on the sales PK and format from lastInsertId. At minimum, begin the transaction in BEGIN IMMEDIATE mode so the count is taken under a write lock, and on UNIQUE violation retry the count-based candidate (not a random suffix) so the sequence stays monotonic. Add a test that asserts no INV number ever contains a random fallback suffix.

findings.title: Audit rows are written but the HMAC/append-only chain is not enforced or verifiable
findings.detail: CLAUDE.md and PHP_APP_MAP require an append-only, HMAC-chained audit_log (audit_log_immutable.sql) reproducing who-did-what-when, simplified for single-PC but with the audit records kept. SaleService calls Audit::write for SALE_COMPLETED / CONTROLLED_DISPENSED / DISCOUNT_AUTHORIZED, and Audit::write does a plain INSERT with no chaining or prev-hash linkage. There is no tamper-evidence and no test verifying the chain. For a controlled-substance (narcotic) register this is the legally sensitive record. Additionally the JSON payloads are built by raw QString interpolation (e.g. line 349-351, 356-360): prescriber_license and receipt_number are concatenated unescaped, so a license string containing a quote or backslash produces invalid JSON in the audit row.
findings.recommendation: Either implement the simplified hash-chain (store prev_hash + row_hash so the chain is verifiable, matching the immutable-trigger intent) or document explicitly that chaining was intentionally dropped. Build audit detail JSON with QJsonObject/QJsonDocument instead of QString interpolation so special characters in license/receipt are escaped. Add a test that a license like LIC"-\x produces valid JSON and that the audit chain verifies.

findings.title: Stored sale subtotal (client MRP) can diverge from the sum of sale_items line_subtotal (batch MRP) with no reconciliation
findings.detail: The sales-header subtotal/grand_total are computed from the CLIENT-supplied row.unitMrp (line 79-86), but each sale_items row is written with the BATCH's mrp_per_unit (alloc.batch.mrpPerUnit, line 290/309) and line_total is set equal to that batch-MRP line_subtotal. If the cart's unitMrp does not match the batch mrp_per_unit (stale price in the cart, a price change between scan and commit, or a deliberately tampered client value), the header total and the sum of line items will silently disagree — the header drives the cash drawer / change while the items drive margin and tax reporting. This is faithfully ported from PHP (same structure), so it is port-parity rather than a new bug, but it is a real inconsistency that should at least be detected. No test asserts that sum(sale_items.line_total) == grand_total + discount.
findings.recommendation: After allocation, assert that the recomputed sum of batch-MRP line subtotals equals the client-derived subtotal (or refuse the sale / re-price from the batch like a real POS). At minimum add a guard + test that flags a mismatch instead of persisting two disagreeing totals. Confirm with the team whether header should be repriced from batches.

findings.title: DISCOUNT_AUTHORIZED audit semantics diverge from PHP (self-authorized managerial discounts now logged as authorized)
findings.detail: PHP writes the DISCOUNT_AUTHORIZED audit row only when input.discount_authorized_by was explicitly supplied (if (!empty($input['discount_authorized_by']) && discount>0)). The Qt port writes it whenever discountPositive && discountAuthBy > 0, and discountAuthBy is set to m_cashierId for a managerial cashier self-authorizing (line 197). So a manager/admin who applies a discount to their own sale now generates a DISCOUNT_AUTHORIZED row attributed to themselves, which PHP would not emit. This changes the meaning of the discount audit trail. The discount-auth test (13.3) only checks the sales.discount_authorized_by column, not the audit row, so the divergence is untested.
findings.recommendation: Decide intended behavior and align with PHP: either only audit when an external authorizer differs from the cashier, or document the deliberate change. Add a test asserting whether a self-authorized managerial discount does/does not create a DISCOUNT_AUTHORIZED audit row.

findings.title: Post-commit receipt-name lookup runs outside the transaction and can leave receipt lines showing a medicine id
findings.detail: Each result line's display name is initialized to QString::number(medicineId) (line 336) and only replaced after commit by a SELECT brand_name/strength (line 378-388). If that SELECT fails (the name query is best-effort: no error handling), the receipt line shows a bare numeric id to the cashier/customer. The lookup is also a separate query per line after the sale is already committed, so a failure cannot be rolled back. Functionally the sale is fine, but the printed receipt can be wrong. Fetching the name inside the main loop (where the medicine is already known) before commit would be more robust and avoid N extra round-trips.
findings.recommendation: Resolve the display name during the per-line loop (one query, or join it into the batch fetch) before commit, and fall back to a readable placeholder (e.g. 'Item') rather than the raw id if the name is missing.

findings.title: Witness/license re-validation trusts a UI-resolved witness id without verifying the PIN belongs to that user server-side
findings.detail: The two-person controlled gate and discount override are re-validated server-side (good: witness must be active MANAGER/ADMIN, != cashier; discount authorizer must be active mgr/admin != cashier). However the actual PIN verification happens only in the UI (PosTerminalPage verifyManagerOverride), and SaleService receives an already-resolved controlledWitnessUserId / discountAuthorizedBy integer. SaleService is the domain boundary that is supposed to be 'defense in depth', but it cannot tell whether that id was genuinely PIN-authenticated this transaction or simply set by a caller. Any future caller (tests already do this) can pass an arbitrary manager id and pass the gate. For a narcotic register the binding between the witnessing PIN and the recorded witness_user_id is the whole point.
findings.recommendation: Pass the witness/authorizer PIN (or a short-lived verified token) into SaleService and have it perform the bcrypt verification within the same call, so the audit/witness binding is established at the domain layer rather than trusting an id. If that is intentionally a UI responsibility, document it and ensure no non-UI path can mint controlled sales.

findings.title: No test for rollback integrity when a write fails mid-transaction (the core 'never inconsistent stock' guarantee)
findings.detail: sale_tests.cpp is thorough on validation rejections (which fail before the transaction opens, lines 600-781) and on insufficient-stock (which throws during allocation before any batch is decremented). But there is NO test that forces a failure AFTER the first batch UPDATE/sale_items/inventory_movements insert has succeeded — e.g. a second line that fails on a DB constraint — to prove the rollback actually reverts the already-decremented stock and removes the partial sale_items/movements rows. The CLAUDE.md guardrail 'never leave stock in an inconsistent state on error' and the rollback paths at lines 401/406/413 are therefore unverified for the mid-transaction case. There is also no concurrency/duplicate-receipt test.
findings.recommendation: Add a test that commits a multi-line sale where a later line is engineered to fail (e.g. a constraint violation or an injected error) and assert: ok==false, no sales/sale_items/inventory_movements rows for that receipt exist, and every batch current_qty is back to its pre-sale value. This directly exercises the rollback guarantee.

findings.title: Controlled-substance schedule query and batch fetch ignore SQL errors / partial results, weakening the gate
findings.detail: The schedule lookup (line 141-153) runs sq.exec() and only reads rows if it succeeded; on exec failure it silently proceeds with an EMPTY schedules list, which means anyControlled/anyRequiresWitness return false and a narcotic sale could bypass the witness/license gate entirely if that one query fails. The gate is supposed to be defense-in-depth. (The batch fetch at 256 does throw on error — good — so the inconsistency is only in the compliance query.) Because the query failing also likely means the subsequent inserts would fail, the practical risk is low, but a fail-open compliance check is the wrong default for a narcotic register.
findings.recommendation: Throw SaleError on sq exec failure (fail closed) instead of continuing with an empty schedule set, mirroring the strict error handling used for the batch/insert queries.

findings.title: Express commitReturn(restock=true) skips the quarantine/expired guard that adjudicate enforces
findings.detail: adjudicate() refuses APPROVED_RESTOCK when the batch is now is_quarantined or is_expired (lines 350-369), preventing QA-flagged stock from re-entering saleable inventory. The express commitReturn() path with restock=true loads only current_qty (line 626-630) and unconditionally does current_qty += qtyReturned and writes a RETURN_RESTOCK movement (lines 632-659). It never reads is_quarantined/is_expired and never applies the guard. A counter operator can therefore restock returned goods straight into a batch that has been quarantined or has expired — exactly the unsafe state adjudicate() exists to prevent. This is a pharmacy stock-safety invariant.
findings.recommendation: In commitReturn(), when restock==true, read is_quarantined/is_expired from the batch and apply the same refusal as adjudicate() before bumping current_qty. Share a single helper so the invariant cannot drift between the two paths.

findings.title: RETURN_QUARANTINE ledger row records qty_delta=0, diverging from PHP (qty_delta=baseQtyToReturn)
findings.detail: The Qt initiate() inserts the RETURN_QUARANTINE inventory_movements row with a hardcoded qty_delta=0 and qty_before==qty_after==current_qty. PHP Returns::initiate inserts the same row with qty_delta = baseQtyToReturn (Returns.php:185, ':delta' => $baseQtyToReturn) while still keeping qty_before==qty_after==batchQty. The ledger meaning differs: PHP records how many units physically left into quarantine; the Qt port records nothing in the delta column. The SQLite schema has no qty_after = qty_before + qty_delta CHECK, so it does not error, but any report or reconciliation that sums RETURN_QUARANTINE deltas (or compares against the PHP ledger) will diverge. CLAUDE.md mandates bit-for-bit ledger parity on stock paths.
findings.recommendation: Set qty_delta to qtyReturned in the RETURN_QUARANTINE insert to match PHP, keeping qty_before==qty_after unchanged. Add a test asserting the movement's qty_delta equals the returned quantity.

findings.title: bumpSessionRefund silently ignores exec() failure — refund cash may go unrecorded in the open shift
findings.detail: bumpSessionRefund() calls q.exec() (line 84) but never checks the return value or throws on failure. It runs inside the caller's transaction. If the UPDATE fails (e.g. schema drift, locked row), the failure is swallowed: the return still commits but total_refunds_paid is not incremented, so the Z-report / Day-Close expected-cash math under-counts cash that left the drawer. PHP runs the same UPDATE via Db::execute, which throws on error and aborts the whole transaction. The Qt port should fail closed the same way rather than committing a financially inconsistent state.
findings.recommendation: Check q.exec() in bumpSessionRefund and throw ReturnError on failure so the enclosing transaction rolls back, matching PHP's fail-closed Db::execute behavior.

findings.title: Witness rejection branches (witness == operator, witness not active manager/admin) are untested
findings.detail: requireWitnessIfControlled enforces three distinct rejections for NARCOTIC returns: missing witness (line 57), witness equal to operator (line 62), and witness not an active MANAGER/ADMIN (line 65). returns_tests.cpp case 14 (lines 766-804) only covers the missing-witness rejection and the happy path with a valid manager. The two-person-integrity rules that the witness must differ from the operator and must be an active manager/admin — the core of the DRAP narcotic control — have no test. A regression in UserRepository::isActiveManagerOrAdmin or the operator-equality check would pass silently. CLAUDE.md requires controlled-substance paths be covered by tests.
findings.recommendation: Add test cases: (a) controlled return with witnessUserId == operator is refused; (b) controlled return with a CASHIER/inactive/deleted witness is refused; for both initiate() and the express commitReturn() path.

findings.title: Express commitReturn() path has no PHP equivalent and no dedicated controlled/restock-guard tests
findings.detail: commitReturn() is a Qt-only one-step path (initiate + immediate final disposition) with no counterpart in Returns.php, so there is no source-of-truth to compare against and extra scrutiny is warranted. It is exercised heavily for non-controlled refunds in the tests, but there is no test that commitReturn() of a NARCOTIC medicine enforces the witness, and (per finding 1) no test that restock onto a quarantined/expired batch is refused on this path. Because it duplicates ~150 lines of initiate()+adjudicate() logic inline, divergences from the two-step path (like the missing restock guard) are easy to introduce and currently uncaught.
findings.recommendation: Add controlled-medicine and quarantined/expired-restock tests for commitReturn(); consider refactoring commitReturn() to delegate to initiate()+adjudicate() (or shared helpers) so the safety invariants are defined once.

findings.title: nextReturnNumber count query ignores exec failure and lacks the per-day serialization PHP uses
findings.detail: The initial count() query (line 92) calls q.exec() without checking the result; on failure count stays 0 and generation proceeds. PHP nextReturnNumber takes a per-day pg_advisory_xact_lock to serialize concurrent minting (Returns.php:439-441); the Qt port drops this and instead relies on a 3-attempt probe loop plus a random 6-digit fallback. On a single-PC SQLite target concurrent minting is unlikely, so the lock omission is acceptable, but the unchecked exec plus the silent random fallback can yield a RET-YYYYMMDD-NNNNNN number that breaks the otherwise sequential RET-YYYYMMDD-0001 format without any audit note. Minor, but worth tightening for traceability.
findings.recommendation: Check exec() on the count query and on the uniqueness probe; if falling back to the random suffix, emit an audit/log note. Optionally rely on the return_number UNIQUE constraint with a retry rather than a probe.

findings.title: Audit before-image for RETURN_ADJUDICATED uses a hardcoded PENDING_REVIEW status instead of the real prior row
findings.detail: The RETURN_ADJUDICATED audit writes before='{"status":"PENDING_REVIEW"}' literally. This matches the (admittedly imperfect) PHP, which builds $beforeRow=['status'=>'PENDING_REVIEW'] and even leaves a dead $before placeholder (Returns.php:285-286). Since adjudicate() already guards status==PENDING_REVIEW before proceeding, the value is always correct in practice, so this is faithful-but-fragile parity rather than a bug. Flagging for maintainability: if the pre-guard ever changes, the audit before-image would silently lie.
findings.recommendation: Use the status value already read into the local 'status' variable (line 344) for the audit before-image instead of a literal, so it stays correct if the guard is ever relaxed.

findings.title: voidSale restock does not check is_quarantined/is_expired before re-adding stock
findings.detail: voidSale() restocks every sale line (current_qty += qty, RETURN_RESTOCK movement) without checking whether any batch is now quarantined or expired. This mirrors a same-day reversal where the goods were never really gone, so re-adding to a now-flagged batch is a smaller risk than the express-return case, and the PHP equivalent for void was not provided here to compare. Noting it for completeness: a sale voided after one of its batches was quarantined would silently return flagged stock to saleable on-hand.
findings.recommendation: Confirm against the PHP void implementation whether quarantine/expiry should block per-line restock on void; if so, apply the same guard (or skip-and-write-off flagged lines) used in adjudicate().

findings.title: received_qty update formula deviates from PHP spec, skewing received/FOC totals after sales
findings.detail: PHP Grn.php updates an existing batch with `received_qty = current_qty + :delta` (Grn.php, the UPDATE batches block). The C++ port intentionally changes this to `received_qty = received_qty + :delta` (lines 156-162) with a comment calling the PHP behavior a 'quirk' and asserting 'current_qty is identical'. That assertion only holds on the very first receipt into a batch. Once any stock from that batch is sold, current_qty < received_qty, so on the NEXT receipt into the same (medicine, batch#, expiry) the two formulas diverge: PHP would set received_qty = (depleted current_qty) + delta, the port sets received_qty = (full prior received_qty) + delta. CLAUDE.md states 'The PHP app is the specification... do not change business rules unless explicitly asked' and the audit ground-truth says deviations are bugs unless CLAUDE.md says otherwise — this divergence is documented only in a code comment, not in CLAUDE.md. received_qty feeds purchasing/received-stock reports, so reports will silently disagree with the PHP system bit-for-bit. current_qty (the safety-critical value) is computed identically in both, so stock-on-hand is unaffected.
findings.recommendation: Either match PHP exactly (received_qty = current_qty + delta) to preserve report parity, or get explicit sign-off and record the deviation + rationale in CLAUDE.md / PHP_APP_MAP.md rather than only in a source comment. Add a test that sells from a batch then re-receives into it and asserts the received_qty value against the chosen spec.

findings.title: Draft→post lifecycle collapsed: lost FOR UPDATE re-read guard against double-posting, no busy_timeout
findings.detail: PHP Grn::post() runs SERIALIZABLE and re-reads the GRN row `FOR UPDATE`, bailing if another session already flipped status to POSTED — explicitly to stop two concurrent posts from double-receiving stock. The port collapses create+post into one step (documented as acceptable in the header and CLAUDE.md), so there is no pre-existing draft to double-post; each call creates a fresh grn_documents row, which structurally avoids that exact double-post. However SQLite has no SERIALIZABLE/FOR UPDATE; the post relies on m_db.transaction() (a DEFERRED txn that takes no write lock until the first write). On a single-PC target this is low risk, but Database.cpp sets WAL with NO `PRAGMA busy_timeout` (verified absent in src/), so if any second connection (e.g. a report query, future feature) writes concurrently, a write will fail immediately with SQLITE_BUSY and the GRN post rolls back rather than waiting.
findings.recommendation: Set a busy_timeout (e.g. PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000) in Database.cpp when opening the connection, and/or begin the GRN transaction as IMMEDIATE so the write lock is acquired up front. Document the single-step lifecycle decision is unchanged.

findings.title: nextGrnNumber() count query is not lock-protected; relies on unique index + bounded retry
findings.detail: nextGrnNumber() runs `SELECT count(*) ... WHERE date(created_at,'localtime')=date('now','localtime')` and builds GRN-YYYYMMDD-NNNN. PHP does the same but inside a SERIALIZABLE txn. Here, two near-simultaneous posts could read the same count and generate the same candidate; the grn_documents_number_key unique index would reject the second INSERT and roll back the whole post. The 3-attempt loop inside nextGrnNumber does NOT help because each retry re-runs the same count (yielding count+1, count+2, count+3 candidates) before any insert — it guards against pre-existing duplicates, not against a concurrent inserter. After 3 attempts it falls back to a random 6-digit suffix. Single-PC usage makes a true collision unlikely, but the failure mode is a hard rollback of a valid receipt rather than a retried number.
findings.recommendation: Acquire the write lock before computing the number (BEGIN IMMEDIATE), or catch the unique-constraint failure on the grn_documents INSERT and regenerate the number + retry the insert instead of failing the whole post. Add a test simulating an existing same-number row.

findings.title: Dup-batch merge silently overwrites cost_per_unit/mrp_per_unit with no test coverage
findings.detail: When a batch already exists for (medicine, batch#, expiry), the UPDATE sets cost_per_unit = blendedCost and mrp_per_unit = mrpPerBase computed from THIS receipt's line only — it does not re-blend against the existing on-hand quantity/cost. This mirrors PHP (which also overwrites), so it is correct parity, but it is a subtle and high-impact behavior (the per-unit cost used for valuation/margin reporting jumps to the latest receipt's blended value, ignoring residual stock at the old cost). grn_tests.cpp case 4 ('dup batch merges to 5') asserts only the merged quantity and that it is a single row — it never asserts the resulting cost_per_unit or mrp_per_unit after a merge, so a regression that broke cost/MRP refresh-on-merge would pass.
findings.recommendation: Add a test: receive batch DUP at cost A, then re-receive same batch at cost B, and assert cost_per_unit == B's blended value and mrp_per_unit == B's per-base value (matching PHP). Document the overwrite (vs re-blend) semantics near the UPDATE.

findings.title: No test for HALF_UP rounding boundary on blended cost / mrp_per_base
findings.detail: CLAUDE.md mandates the money/cost paths be 'covered by tests comparing results against PHP behavior' and 'Match these results bit-for-bit'. grn_tests.cpp exercises only clean values: 5.0000, 8.3333 (1000/120, truncated not a rounding edge), and 8.0000. There is no case that lands exactly on the scale-4 HALF_UP boundary (e.g. a division whose 5th fractional digit is 5, or a value like x.xxxx5 that must round UP not to-even/down). Money.h documents a non-obvious optimization ('8-dp truncation can't change a 4-dp HALF_UP decision' via divByInt at internal scale 4) — exactly the kind of claim that needs a boundary test against the PHP bcmath result.
findings.recommendation: Add CostBlender/Money tests with inputs chosen so blendedCostPerBaseUnit and mrpPerBaseUnit hit a 5-at-the-rounding-digit case, asserting the exact scale-4 string equals the PHP Money::round output. Include a negative/zero and a large-value (near DECIMAL(12,4) range) case.

findings.title: Validation rejection tests never assert that NO grn_documents/lines/movements rows were written on rollback
findings.detail: Case 5 verifies rejected posts return ok=false and that batches.onHand(m6) == 0, which confirms stock was not incremented. But it does not assert the transaction fully rolled back — e.g. that no orphan grn_documents header (inserted at line 71-86 before the failing line is processed), grn_lines, or inventory_movements rows survive. Since the header INSERT happens before per-line validation can throw (a medicine-not-found or past-expiry on line 2 of a multi-line GRN throws after the header and earlier lines were inserted), a regression that committed instead of rolling back would leak a POSTED header with partial lines and the onHand check alone would not catch it.
findings.recommendation: After a rejected post, assert SELECT count(*) FROM grn_documents (and grn_lines, inventory_movements) for the would-be GRN is unchanged. Add a multi-line case where line 2 fails validation and assert line 1's batch/movement were also rolled back.

findings.title: Audit detail JSON built via string interpolation — injection / malformed-JSON risk if grnNumber ever contains a quote
findings.detail: The GRN_POSTED audit row's after-JSON is assembled with QStringLiteral("{\"grn_number\":\"%1\",...}").arg(grnNumber, subtotalStr). grnNumber is system-generated (GRN-date-NNNN or random suffix) so today it is safe, but the pattern hand-rolls JSON instead of using a JSON serializer. If the format string source ever changes (e.g. including supplier name, invoice number, or notes — all user-controlled) a value containing a double-quote or backslash would produce invalid JSON or allow field injection into the audit record, which is meant to be a tamper-evident trail. PHP passes a structured array to Audit::write and lets the encoder escape it.
findings.recommendation: Build the audit payload with QJsonObject/QJsonDocument so values are properly escaped, matching the PHP approach of passing structured data rather than pre-formatted JSON. This future-proofs against adding user-controlled fields.

findings.title: Hard-coded branch_id = 1 in every insert; medicine's branch / GRN branch not honored
findings.detail: All inserts (grn_documents, batches, inventory_movements) hard-code branch_id = 1. PHP threads branch_id through (createDraft takes $branchId, and post() copies $grn['branch_id'] into the batch and movement inserts). The port is single-branch by design for the single-PC target, so this is acceptable today, but the literal '1' is repeated across three statements and the GrnResult/post signature has no branch parameter, so a future multi-branch requirement would need edits scattered through the method.
findings.recommendation: Introduce a single branchId constant/member (default 1) and reference it in all three inserts so the single-branch assumption lives in one place and is trivially generalizable. No behavior change required now.

findings.title: Audit::write() return value ignored — a failed audit row silently commits the adjustment
findings.detail: Every other DB call in the transaction checks its result and throws AdjustError on failure (ins.exec, ub.exec, mv.exec). The Audit::write() call returns a bool but its value is discarded. If the audit insert fails (e.g. schema/constraint/HMAC-chain issue), the code proceeds straight to m_db.commit() and the stock adjustment is persisted WITHOUT an audit trail. For a medical-retail system whose CLAUDE.md mandates an append-only who-did-what-when audit on every stock change, a stock movement that commits without its audit row is a compliance hole, not a cosmetic one. The PHP version runs inside Db::transaction(); if Audit::write throws, the whole tx rolls back — so this is also a behavioral divergence from the source of truth.
findings.recommendation: Wrap the Audit::write call: `if (!Audit::write(...)) throw AdjustError{QStringLiteral("Failed to write audit record.")};` so a failed audit aborts and rolls back the adjustment, matching PHP's all-or-nothing semantics.

findings.title: Sequence-count query in nextAdjustmentNumber() does not check exec() and silently defaults to 0
findings.detail: q.exec(...) on the COUNT(*) query is not checked. On failure count stays 0, so the candidate becomes ADJ-yyyymmdd-0001. The subsequent 3-attempt uniqueness loop and random fallback prevent an actual unique-constraint violation, so this won't corrupt data, but a silent query failure here is a latent maintainability/observability gap and inconsistent with the rest of the file which checks every exec().
findings.recommendation: Check the exec() result (or at least require q.next()); if it fails, treat it as an error rather than assuming a count of 0.

findings.title: Adjustment-number minting drops PHP's advisory lock; relies on collision-retry instead of serialization
findings.detail: PHP's nextAdjustmentNumber() takes pg_advisory_xact_lock keyed on the day so two concurrent adjustments cannot both read count()==N and mint the same ADJ-...-NNNN. The Qt port replaces this with a read of COUNT(*) outside any lock plus a 3-attempt existence check and a 6-digit random fallback. The count query also runs against the same connection inside the open transaction but the candidate-existence checks (chk) would not see uncommitted rows from a *different* connection. For the documented single-PC, single-instance SQLite deployment, writes are effectively serialized so a real collision is improbable, and the random fallback prevents a hard failure — but the comment parity with PHP's locking guarantee is lost, and the random fallback produces a number in a different format (ADJ-date-6digits) than the canonical ADJ-date-4digits, which may surprise downstream report/UI consumers.
findings.recommendation: Document explicitly that the single-instance lock makes the advisory lock unnecessary, or compute the next number from MAX(adjustment_number) for the day rather than COUNT(*) so deletions/gaps don't cause silent reuse attempts. Confirm the 6-digit random fallback format is acceptable to any code that parses adjustment_number.

findings.title: Adjustment number derives date prefix from local clock while uniqueness count uses created_at; cross-midnight edge
findings.detail: today is QDate::currentDate() (local), and the count filters date(created_at,'localtime') = date('now','localtime'). These are consistent under normal conditions and mirror the PHP intent. However created_at is written by the DB DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP (UTC in SQLite) and converted back with 'localtime' for counting, while the prefix uses the C++ local clock at a slightly earlier instant. An adjustment minted at 23:59:59.9 local could in principle get a prefix for one day while its stored created_at counts under the same day — generally fine, but there is no test covering a date-boundary scenario and the two clocks (QDate vs SQLite) are independent. Low risk for a single PC.
findings.recommendation: Optional: derive the prefix from the same SQLite expression used for counting (SELECT strftime('%Y%m%d','now','localtime')) so prefix and count always agree on the day. Otherwise document the accepted edge.

findings.title: Missing test coverage for invalid reason, non-existent batch, and audit-row emission
findings.detail: The suite covers positive/negative/negative-guard/zero/OTHER-notes/quarantine paths well, but per CLAUDE.md's mandate to cover stock + audit paths, three gaps remain: (1) no test that an unknown reason string is rejected (the kReasons guard at line 72 is untested); (2) no test for a non-existent batchId returning 'Batch not found' with no side effects; (3) no test asserting that a STOCK_ADJUSTED audit_log row is actually written with the correct adjustment_number/qty_delta/reason/cost_impact JSON — the very thing finding #1 shows can silently fail. The cost-impact rounding test only exercises an exact value (50.00); there is no fractional/HALF_UP case (e.g. cost 5.0050 * odd qty) to guard the scale-4→scale-2 boundary.
findings.recommendation: Add tests: invalid-reason rejection, batch-not-found, an audit_log existence/content assertion after a successful adjust, and a HALF_UP cost-impact case (e.g. cost_per_unit '0.3350' * 3 = 1.0050 -> 1.01).

findings.title: Audit 'before' state is empty for STOCK_ADJUSTED — no record of qty_before/cost in the audit JSON
findings.detail: The audit row passes an empty 'before' JSON and an 'after' JSON containing only adjustment_number/qty_delta/reason/cost_impact. This faithfully mirrors the PHP call (which also passes null for before), so it is correct port parity. Noting it only because the inventory_movements ledger already captures qty_before/qty_after, so reviewers should not expect the audit row to carry the pre-image. No change needed unless the team wants richer audit detail beyond PHP parity.
findings.recommendation: No action required for parity. If richer audit is desired later, include qty_before/qty_after in the after-JSON, but do this in both PHP and Qt to keep them aligned.

findings.title: Variance recomputed from raw columns instead of the stored expected_cash_in_drawer snapshot (spec divergence)
findings.detail: Reconciler.php derives the recount variance against the persisted snapshot column: variance = round(counted - s['expected_cash_in_drawer']). It SELECTs expected_cash_in_drawer and never re-derives it from opening_float/total_cash_sales/total_refunds_paid. The Qt port instead ignores the stored expected_cash_in_drawer column entirely and recomputes expected = openingFloat + cashSales - refundsPaid (line 63). SessionRepository::closeSession already wrote expected_cash_in_drawer at close time (SessionRepository.cpp:141). The two only coincide because the refund bump targets status='OPEN' only (ReturnService.cpp:80-84), so the inputs happen to be frozen after close. The moment that invariant changes — or if a session's stored expected was ever computed differently (e.g. a future correction, manual data fix, or a refund path that doesn't gate on OPEN) — the reconciled variance silently diverges from PHP and from what the cashier was told at close. This is the source-of-truth column for an auditable cash drawer.
findings.recommendation: Mirror PHP: SELECT expected_cash_in_drawer from cashier_sessions and compute variance = round(counted - expected_cash_in_drawer, 2) rather than re-deriving expected from the component columns. Add a reconcile test that records a CASH refund-after-close scenario (or a stored expected that differs from the live recompute) and asserts the variance matches the stored snapshot.

findings.title: Audit 'after' payload diverges from PHP — omits 'expected', uses wrong field name path, hardcodes non-null 'before'
findings.detail: PHP writes Audit::write(..., before=null, after=['counted_cash'=>counted, 'expected'=>expected, 'variance'=>variance]). The Qt port writes before='{"status":"CLOSED"}' (PHP passes null) and after={"status":"RECONCILED","counted_cash":...,"variance":...} — it drops the 'expected' figure that PHP records and adds a 'status' field PHP does not. For a cash-drawer audit trail the expected-vs-counted-vs-variance triple is exactly what an auditor needs; losing 'expected' weakens the record relative to spec. (The return value of Audit::write is also ignored, but that is a consistent project-wide pattern incl. the critical SaleService path, so not a Reconciler-specific defect.)
findings.recommendation: Match the PHP audit shape: pass an empty/null before and include expected in the after JSON: {"counted_cash":..,"expected":..,"variance":..}. This requires SELECTing expected_cash_in_drawer anyway (see prior finding), so the two fixes pair naturally.

findings.title: recountedCash is not validated for format or non-negativity — invalid input silently becomes 0.00
findings.detail: A non-empty recountedCash is fed straight into Money::fromString(recountedCash).toString(ScaleMoney). Money::fromString returns zero on invalid input (per Money.h:22 'Invalid → zero'). SessionRepository::closeSession guards counted cash with isMoneyInput() and rejects negatives (SessionRepository.cpp:121-125); the PHP close() uses the regex ^\d+(\.\d{1,2})?$ and a negative check. The reconcile recount path has NO such guard in either PHP or Qt — but in Qt the consequence is worse: a manager typo like 'abc' or '12.999' or a negative '-50' is accepted and written as a counted_cash/variance with no error, corrupting the drawer record under the manager's name. Because recount overrides the cashier's figure, this is a silent data-integrity hole on a money field.
findings.recommendation: Validate recountedCash with the same isMoneyInput()/non-negative rule used by closeSession before accepting the recount; return ReconcileResult{ok=false, error=...} on bad input instead of coercing to zero.

findings.title: TOCTOU on session status — re-check is not part of the UPDATE WHERE clause
findings.detail: Status is read (line 50), validated to be 'CLOSED' (line 57), then the UPDATE sets status='RECONCILED' WHERE id = ? with no '... AND status = 'CLOSED'' predicate (line 82-84). On single-PC SQLite within one transaction this is largely theoretical, but SessionRepository::closeSession deliberately uses 'WHERE id = ? AND status='OPEN'' plus a numRowsAffected()==1 guard (SessionRepository.cpp:143,153) for exactly this race. The reconciler is inconsistent with that hardening pattern and would happily re-reconcile or clobber a concurrently-changed row.
findings.recommendation: Add 'AND status = ''CLOSED''' to the UPDATE WHERE clause and assert uq.numRowsAffected() == 1 (rolling back otherwise), matching closeSession.

findings.title: No test asserts the SESSION_RECONCILED audit row is actually written / well-formed
findings.detail: The reconcile tests (R1-R4) verify status transition, counted_cash, variance, and refusal paths, but none query audit_log to confirm a SESSION_RECONCILED row exists with the expected manager userId and JSON payload. Given CLAUDE.md mandates an audit trail for stock/cash changes and the audit payload diverges from PHP (see finding above), an absent audit row or a malformed payload would pass the current suite undetected.
findings.recommendation: Add an assertion in R1/R2 that audit_log contains exactly one SESSION_RECONCILED row for the session with user_id = manager and the expected counted_cash/expected/variance fields in after_json.

findings.title: Reconcile does not enforce a manager/admin role — any caller-supplied managerId is trusted
findings.detail: The constructor takes managerId and the class header documents this as a 'manager reviews ... and signs it off' operation. Neither the constructor nor reconcile() verifies that managerId actually has a manager/admin role; it trusts the caller (UI) entirely and writes the audit row under that id. PHP's reconcile likewise trusts $managerId, so this is at-parity — but it means authorization rests solely on UI gating. For a cash-variance sign-off (the control that detects till skimming) a defense-in-depth role check at the service boundary is warranted, especially since the audit record's accountability depends on managerId being genuine.
findings.recommendation: Optionally verify managerId resolves to a user with MANAGER/ADMIN role (and is active) before reconciling, returning an error otherwise; at minimum document that the UI must enforce this and ensure no non-manager path can construct a Reconciler.

findings.title: No signature verification / tamper-detection path in the Qt port
